chapterTitle: I. Overview of the Nervous System

questions.text: In adults, the spinal cord ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically terminates at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). In neonates, it ends at L3.
questions.keyConcept: Adult spinal cord ends at L1; neonatal spinal cord ends at L3

questions.text: Which of the following is not present in the sacral canal?
questions.explanation: The sacral canal contains the filum terminale, cauda equina, cerebrospinal fluid, and the dural/arachnoid tube extending to S2. The ligamentum denticulatum anchors the spinal cord to the dura and does not extend into the sacral canal.
questions.keyConcept: Ligamentum denticulatum is absent in the sacral canal

questions.text: The spinal dura extends from the level of the foramen magnum to the level of which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2). Below this, the filum terminale continues as the coccygeal ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal dura extends from foramen magnum to S2

questions.text: In adults the spinal cord usually terminates at the:
questions.explanation: In adults, the conus medullaris typically ends at the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is important clinically to avoid spinal cord injury during lumbar puncture, which is performed below this level.
questions.keyConcept: Adult conus medullaris ends at lower border of L1
options: Upper border of the 12th thoracic vertebra.
Lower border of the 1st lumbar vertebra.
Upper border of the 4th lumbar vertebra.

questions.text: To do lumbar puncture in an adult a needle is introduced:
questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed below the level of the conus medullaris (which ends at L1–L2 in adults) to avoid cord injury. The needle is typically introduced at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace.
questions.keyConcept: Lumbar puncture performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5 to avoid conus medullaris
options: Below or above tip of 4th L spine.

questions.text: At birth, the conus medullaris ends at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: At birth, the conus medullaris is located at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). It ascends to L1–L2 by adulthood due to differential growth.
questions.keyConcept: Birth conus medullaris at L3; ascends to L1–L2 in adults

questions.text: As regards the spinal cord; choose the INCORRECT statement:
questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater does NOT continue below L1 as the filum terminale. The filum terminale is a pial structure extending from the conus medullaris to the coccyx, pierced by the dura and arachnoid at S2. The dura itself ends at S2.
questions.keyConcept: Filum terminale is pial, not dural; dura ends at S2
options: In adults, it ends at lower border of L1.
It is anchored to the dura mater by denticulate ligaments.
Its covering dura mater below the level of L1 forms filum terminale.
Lumbar puncture may be done between L3 and L4.

questions.text: Describe shape of spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly, extending from foramen magnum to the lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements (cervical at C5-T1 and lumbar at L2-S3) and shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus). It tapers inferiorly to form the conus medullaris. This shape is clinically important for lumbar puncture and understanding segmental anatomy.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord cylindrical shape, flattening, extensions, and conus medullaris
questions.modelAnswer: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly. It extends from foramen magnum to lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements: cervical (C5-T1) and lumbar (L2-S3). It shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus) and gradual tapering at its lower end (conus medullaris).

questions.text: Describe the site of exit of spinal nerves from vertebral column.
questions.explanation: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves (C1-C7) exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebra. From T1-L1, nerves exit BELOW their corresponding vertebra. Below L1, the cauda equina (L2-S5 nerves) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective sacral foramina. This somatotopic arrangement is essential for interpreting segmental neurological deficits.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nerve exit above/below vertebrae and cauda equina arrangement
questions.modelAnswer: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves exit above their corresponding vertebra (C1-C7 exit above C1-C7). From T1-L1, nerves exit below their corresponding vertebra. The cauda equina (L2-S5) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective foramina.

questions.text: An old man developed UMNL paralysis of muscles of lower part of the face while muscles of upper part of face were preserved.
questions.explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). Lower facial muscles are affected because they receive mainly contralateral input. The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
questions.keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches

subQuestions.explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
subQuestions.keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches

questions.text: Reappearance of the grasp reflex occurs in lesion of:
questions.explanation: Area 6 (premotor area) lies anterior to the primary motor cortex. Lesions here cause reappearance of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex, as this area normally has an inhibitory influence on these reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 lesion causes return of grasp reflex

questions.text: Changes in judgment & intelligence occur in lesion of:
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe, particularly the prefrontal cortex, is responsible for higher cognitive functions including judgment, reasoning, planning, and personality expression. These functions are lost in frontal lobe lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe controls judgment and intelligence

questions.text: Match cortical area in left column with its lesion in right column: Area 6.
questions.explanation: Area 6 (premotor area) lies anterior to the primary motor cortex. Damage can cause release of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex, as this area normally suppresses such reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 controls grasp reflex suppression

questions.text: A lesion of frontal cortex in the dominant hemisphere results in all but one of the following:
questions.explanation: Receptive aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia) is caused by lesions of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the frontal lobe. Frontal lobe lesions cause expressive aphasia, contralateral paralysis, and behavioral changes.
questions.keyConcept: Receptive aphasia is temporal, not frontal lobe lesion

questions.text: Regarding motor speech center, all statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: Receptive aphasia is caused by Wernicke's area lesion, not Broca's area. Broca's area is the motor speech center; its lesion causes expressive/motor aphasia, not receptive aphasia.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's lesion causes motor, not receptive aphasia
options: Found in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Its lesion leads to receptive aphasia.
Lies in area of rami of lateral sulcus.

questions.text: Astereognosis & receptive aphasia characterize lesions in:
questions.explanation: Astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and receptive aphasia (inability to understand language) are both features of dominant parietal lobe lesions, particularly involving the angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Dominant parietal lobe lesions cause astereognosis

questions.text: The facial recognition areas are found in the undersurface of:
questions.explanation: The facial recognition areas (fusiform face area) are located on the undersurface of both temporal and occipital lobes. These areas specifically recognize familiar faces.
questions.keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal and occipital undersurface

questions.text: A patient presents with inability to understand words and speaks non understandable words. Lesion is most likely in Brodmann areas number:
questions.explanation: Brodmann areas 39 and 40 (angular gyrus and supramarginal gyrus) in the dominant parietal-temporal region are responsible for language comprehension. Lesions cause Wernicke's receptive aphasia where speech is fluent but meaningless.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 39-40 lesion causes receptive aphasia

questions.text: A lawyer suffered a bad fall that resulted in head trauma. His motor, sensory, and language skills were intact after the incident, and he had no visual problems. In the following weeks, he began to lose interest in his work and did not seem to care much about his family. The trauma most likely affected the:
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex controls personality, social behavior, and executive functions. A lawyer losing interest in work and not caring about family indicates damage to the prefrontal area, consistent with frontal lobe trauma.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal lesion causes personality/behavior changes

questions.text: Enumerate structures within crus cerebri.
questions.explanation: The crus cerebri contains somatotopically organized descending fibers: MEDIAL 1/5 (most medial): Frontopontine fibers (from frontal lobe to pontine nuclei); MIDDLE 3/5: Corticospinal fibers (arm fibers anterior, leg fibers posterior) and corticobulbar fibers; LATERAL 1/5: Parietopontine and temporopontine fibers (from parietal and temporal lobes to cerebellum via pontine nuclei). The corticospinal fibers are somatotopically organized.
questions.keyConcept: Crus cerebri: medial frontopontine, middle corticospinal/corticobulbar, lateral parieto/temporopontine fibers
questions.modelAnswer: ARTERIAL SUPPLY OF MEDULLA: (1) ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY - supplies medial medulla (pyramids, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nucleus); (2) VERTEBRAL ARTERIES - supply lateral and posterior regions; (3) POSTERIOR INFERIOR CEREBELLAR ARTERY (PICA) - supplies lateral medulla including橄榄, inferior cerebellar peduncle; (4) Direct medullary branches from vertebral arteries.

questions.text: Infection in the mastoid air cells may spread to which sinus?
questions.explanation: The sphenoparietal sinus is a tributary of the cavernous sinus, running along the lesser wing of sphenoid. It drains the dura of the frontal and parietal lobes.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenoparietal sinus tributary of cavernous sinus

questions.text: The sinus that runs along the junction between the flax cerebri and the tentorium cerebelli is the:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is a fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres. It contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses in its upper and lower borders respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri between cerebral hemispheres with sagittal sinuses

questions.text: Falx cerebri:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is a fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres, attached to the crista galli anteriorly and the tentorium cerebelli posteriorly. It contains the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri is dura between hemispheres
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process.

questions.text: Describe relations of cavernous sinus.
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is a paired venous sinus situated on either side of the sella turcica in the middle cranial fossa. Its anatomical relations are clinically significant because of the many important structures that pass through or adjacent to it.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus relations: temporal lobe laterally, pituitary/sphenoidal air sinus medially, optic chiasma superiorly, pons posteriorly.
questions.modelAnswer: The cavernous sinus lies on either side of the sella turcica in the middle cranial fossa. Superiorly: it is related to the optic chiasma and internal carotid artery as it emerges. Inferiorly: related to the sphenoidal air sinus. Medially: related to the pituitary gland (separated by dura). Laterally: related to the temporal lobe of the brain. Anteriorly: related to the superior orbital fissure. Posteriorly: related to the apex of the petrous temporal bone, trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave, and the petroclinoid ligament.

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei relays auditory impulses?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body is a thalamic relay nucleus for auditory information. It receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects via acoustic radiation to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. The lateral geniculate body relays visual impulses, not auditory.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body relays auditory impulses from inferior colliculus to auditory cortex.

questions.text: Arterial supply of the speech areas is from:
questions.explanation: The speech areas (Broca's area in the inferior frontal gyrus and Wernicke's area in the superior temporal gyrus) are supplied by the middle cerebral artery. The MCA also supplies the motor cortex for the face and hand. Broca's area is typically dominant in the left hemisphere for language function.
questions.keyConcept: Middle cerebral artery supplies speech areas (Broca's and Wernicke's areas).

questions.text: Occlusion of this artery in dominant hemisphere results in sensory aphasia:
questions.explanation: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the posterior temporal lobe including Wernicke's area (sensory speech area). Occlusion of the PCA in the dominant hemisphere results in sensory aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia), characterized by fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension. Wernicke's area is located in the superior temporal gyrus.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior cerebral artery supplies Wernicke's area; PCA occlusion in dominant hemisphere causes sensory aphasia.

questions.text: For the Retrolentiform part of the internal capsule, choose its appropriate statement from the right column.
questions.explanation: The retrolentiform part of the internal capsule is located posterior to the lentiform nucleus. It contains the optic radiations (visual fibers from the lateral geniculate body to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe) and parietotemporopontine fibers. Damage causes visual field defects such as homonymous hemianopia.
questions.keyConcept: Retrolentiform part contains optic radiations (visual fibers from lateral geniculate body to visual cortex).

questions.text: The structure(s) derived from spongioblasts of neural crest is (are):
questions.explanation: Spongioblasts (neural crest cells) give rise to chromaffin cells (adrenal medulla), which secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine. Microglia come from mesoderm ( monocytes), not neural crest. Oligodendrocytes and astrocytes come from neuroepithelial cells (glial precursors). Dura and pia mater are mesodermal.
questions.keyConcept: Chromaffin cells (adrenal medulla) derived from neural crest/spongioblasts; microglia from mesoderm, not neural crest.

questions.text: Each of the following cells is derived from the neuroepithelial cells EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS and are derived from MONOCYTES (mesodermal origin), NOT from neuroepithelial cells. Neuroepithelial cells give rise to ependymal cells, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes (all neuroglia), and motor neurons. Microglia are unique among CNS cells in being mesodermal in origin.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocytes), NOT from neuroepithelial cells. All other glial cells and neurons come from neuroepithelial cells.

questions.text: Neuroepithelial cells give rise to:
questions.explanation: Neuroepithelial cells (radial glial cells) in the ventricular zone of the developing neural tube give rise to all the cellular elements of the CNS: neuroblasts (neurons), glioblasts (astrocytes and oligodendrocytes), and ependymal cells (lining the ventricles and central canal). The marginal zone contains axon tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroepithelial cells give rise to neuroblasts (neurons), glioblasts (astrocytes/oligodendrocytes), and ependymal cells.

questions.text: The spinal cord in newly born infant reaches the level of:
questions.explanation: In the newborn infant, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris (end of spinal cord) reaches L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar punctures—needle insertion below L3 avoids spinal cord injury in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord in newborn reaches L3 vertebra; in adults it ends at L1-L2 (conus medullaris).

questions.text: During a normal child delivery, the attending physician noticed a swelling at the back of a newly born infant, giving a suspicious look for a birth defect. An urgent MRI was requested to assess the structure of the spinal cord. Where should u expect the spinal cord to end in this infant
questions.explanation: In a newborn, the spinal cord extends to the level of the 3rd lumbar vertebra (L3) because the vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord. By adulthood, the conus medullaris ends at L1-L2. This is clinically important for lumbar puncture, epidural anesthesia, and avoiding spinal cord injury. This infant's spinal cord would end at L3.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord ends at L3 in newborns; by adulthood it ends at L1-L2. Vertebral column grows faster than spinal cord.

questions.text: A 50-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of right-sided hemiparesis. She reports that she woke up this morning and was unable to move her right arm or leg. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: The precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) in the frontal lobe is the region responsible for voluntary motor control. Hemiparesis (weakness of right arm and leg) indicates a lesion in the LEFT precentral gyrus (contralateral to the affected side). The postcentral gyrus is somatosensory; the angular gyrus is for reading and language; Broca's area is for speech production.
questions.keyConcept: Right-sided hemiparesis = lesion in the LEFT precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex); contralateral motor control.
options: The opercular and triangular parts of the inferior frontal gyrus
Superior lip of posterior ramus of lateral sulcus

questions.text: Regarding the motor speech center, all the statements are true Except:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, not the anterior cerebral artery. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes. All other statements about motor speech center are true.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area supplied by MCA; damage causes expressive aphasia; connected to Wernicke's area.
options: Found in the inferior frontal gyrus
Its lesion leads to expressive aphasia
Is supplied by anterior cerebral artery

questions.text: What is the site of first somatosensory area?
questions.explanation: The first somatosensory area (S1) is located in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and extends onto the posterior part of the paracentral lobule (representing the lower limb). The face is represented in the lower part near the lateral sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: First somatosensory area: postcentral gyrus + posterior paracentral lobule (leg representation).
questions.modelAnswer: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and posterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). The body representation is inverted: face near Sylvian fissure, upper limb in middle, trunk higher up, lower limb on medial surface (paracentral lobule).

questions.text: What is the site of inferior parietal lobule?
questions.explanation: The inferior parietal lobule consists of the supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus) and the angular gyrus (around the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus).
questions.keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule: supramarginal gyrus + angular gyrus. Part of Wernicke's area for language.
questions.modelAnswer: Supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of lateral sulcus) and angular gyrus (around the posterior end of superior temporal sulcus).

questions.text: What are the 3 speech centers?
questions.explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech, inferior frontal gyrus), Wernicke's area (sensory speech, posterior superior temporal gyrus), and the supplementary motor area (medial frontal gyrus).
questions.keyConcept: Speech centers: Broca's (expressive), Wernicke's (receptive), supplementary motor area (planning).
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Broca's area - pars triangularis and opercularis of inferior frontal gyrus (expressive speech). 2) Wernicke's area - posterior superior temporal gyrus (receptive speech). 3) Supplementary motor area - medial frontal gyrus (speech planning and initiation).

questions.text: What is the site of primary motor area?
questions.explanation: The primary motor area (area 4) is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe and extends onto the anterior part of the paracentral lobule on the medial surface (representing the lower limb).
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor area: precentral gyrus + anterior paracentral lobule (leg). Body representation is inverted.
questions.modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus of frontal lobe and anterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). Representation is upside-down and contralateral: face near lateral sulcus, upper limb above, trunk, lower limb on medial surface.

questions.text: What is the site of premotor area?
questions.explanation: The premotor area (area 6) is located in front of area 4, extending across the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri and onto the medial surface of the hemisphere. It programs movements without direct cortical input to motor neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area: in front of area 4, superior/middle/inferior frontal gyri and medial surface.
questions.modelAnswer: In front of area 4, in the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri, and on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere. It lies anterior to the precentral gyrus.

questions.text: Mention the external relations of the cavernous sinus.
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is a paired venous sinus on each side of the sella turcica. Its external relations include: anteriorly - superior orbital fissure; posteriorly - apex of petrous temporal and crus cerebri; medially - pituitary gland and sphenoid sinus; laterally - temporal lobe; superiorly - optic tract and ICA; inferiorly - foramen lacerum.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus relations: laterally = temporal lobe; medially = pituitary; anteriorly = superior orbital fissure; posteriorly = petrous apex.
questions.modelAnswer: Anteriorly: superior orbital fissure and apex of orbit. Posteriorly: apex of petrous temporal bone and crus cerebri of midbrain. Medially: pituitary gland and sphenoidal air sinus. Laterally: temporal lobe of cerebrum. Superiorly: optic tract and internal carotid artery. Inferiorly: foramen lacerum.

questions.text: Mention the derivatives of neural crest.
questions.explanation: Neural crest cells migrate to form sensory ganglia (neuroblasts), autonomic ganglia, melanocytes, chromaffin cells, Schwann cells, meninges (pia and arachnoid), odontoblasts, and skeletal elements of branchial arches.
questions.keyConcept: Neural crest cell derivatives and migration
questions.modelAnswer: Neuroblast, Spongioblast, Melanocyte, Chromaffin cells, Odontoblasts and cartilaginous elements of the branchial arches

questions.text: The falx cerebri
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri separates the cerebral hemispheres and contains the superior sagittal sinus in its superior border; the diaphragma sellae separates the pituitary from the brain.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri anatomy
options: Is attached anteriorly to anterior clinoid process

questions.text: Match the named cerebral vessels in left column with their corresponding anatomical sites in right column.
questions.explanation: The matching pairs are: Posterior cerebral winds round crus cerebri; Circulus arteriosus (circle of Willis) is in interpeduncular fossa; Basilar lies in median pontine groove; Anterior cerebral runs above corpus callosum; Middle cerebral lies in lateral sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral vessel anatomical relationships

pairs.target: b. Median groove on ventral surface of pons
e. above trunk of corpus callosum

questions.text: A 28-year-old man sustains a head injury. After recovery, his family reports marked personality change. Which area is affected?
questions.explanation: Damage to the frontal lobe can cause personality changes, poor judgment, and inappropriate social behavior (pseudopendulous swinging describes cerebellar ataxia, not frontal lobe damage).
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe damage causes executive dysfunction and behavioral changes rather than primary motor deficits.

questions.text: Which part of the brain controls motor function of the right leg?
questions.explanation: The leg area of the primary motor cortex is located on the medial surface of the hemisphere in the paracentral lobule, controlling the contralateral lower limb.
questions.keyConcept: Motor control of the leg is represented medially in the paracentral lobule of the primary motor cortex.

questions.text: Loss of sensation from the left upper limb indicates a lesion in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation: The left upper limb sensory representation is in the right postcentral gyrus (postcentral gyrus), located in the parietal lobe, specifically the upper part near the central sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Upper limb somatosensory cortex is located in the postcentral gyrus, above the lateral sulcus.

questions.text: Third order Neuron start in ......... going via ...........
questions.explanation: Third order neurons in sensory pathways start in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus and project via internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2).
questions.keyConcept: Third order somatosensory neuron

questions.text: Axon in proprioception ascend in:
questions.explanation: Proprioception fibers from the thalamus ascend via the posterior limb of the internal capsule (along with other sensory fibers) to the primary somatosensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule somatosensory fibers

questions.text: The first order neuron in proprioception from the upper half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: First order neurons in proprioception from the upper body also have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (spinal ganglia), same as lower body.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception first neuron upper body

questions.text: The second order neuron in proprioception from lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for lower body proprioception are in the gracile nucleus on the same side, which then decussates as internal arcuate fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception second neuron lower
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.

questions.text: In the urea cycle, which two compounds are end products (released from the cycle)?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle releases urea and fumarate; fumarate enters the citric acid cycle, linking the two cycles at the argininosuccinate step.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle products

questions.text: The inborn error of branched‑chain amino acid metabolism that causes a burnt‑sugar odour in urine is:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine with characteristic sweet odor.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD biochemistry

questions.text: Which vitamin is directly involved in one‑carbon transfer reactions (e.g., purine and thymidylate synthesis)?
questions.explanation: Folate (as N5, N10-methylene-THF) donates one-carbon units in purine synthesis and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Folate one-carbon transfer

questions.text: Which of the following releases free ammonia in the body?
questions.explanation: Amino acid catabolism releases free ammonia via transamination and oxidative deamination; this ammonia is converted to urea for excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia production

questions.text: The enzyme carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is activated by:
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate) is the essential allosteric activator of CPS I, the first urea cycle enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I activation

questions.text: Which compound links the urea cycle with the citric acid cycle?
questions.explanation: Fumarate links the urea and citric acid cycles; it is produced from argininosuccinate in the urea cycle and enters the CAC.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle CAC link

questions.text: The central nervous system is soft because it:
questions.explanation: The CNS is soft because it lacks connective tissue framework; neurons and glia are supported primarily by neuroglial cells, not connective tissue.
questions.keyConcept: CNS softness cause

questions.text: Mention the 3 ligaments supporting the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: The three ligaments supporting the spinal cord are the filum terminale (coccygeal ligament), ligamentum denticulatum, and subarachnoid septum.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal cord support
questions.modelAnswer: Filum terminale, ligamentum denticulatum, subarachnoid septum.

questions.text: Site of second somatosensory area:
questions.explanation: The second somatosensory area (S2) is located in the superior wall of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), deep to the parietal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: S2 location
questions.modelAnswer: Superior wall of lateral sulcus.

questions.text: 3 speech centers:
questions.explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech), Wernicke's area (comprehension), and the arcuate fasciculus connecting them.
questions.keyConcept: Speech centers
questions.modelAnswer: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, arcuate fasciculus.

questions.text: Site of primary motor area:
questions.explanation: The primary motor area (M1) is located in the precentral gyrus (area 4) of the frontal lobe, anterior to the central sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor area
questions.modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus (area 4) of frontal lobe.

questions.text: Lesion of area 4 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes spastic paralysis of contralateral muscles with hyperreflexia and positive Babinski sign.
questions.keyConcept: Area 4 lesion
questions.modelAnswer: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign on contralateral side.

questions.text: Site of premotor area:
questions.explanation: The premotor area (area 6) is located anterior to the precentral gyrus on the lateral and medial surfaces of the frontal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area location
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior to precentral gyrus on lateral and medial frontal lobe.

questions.text: External relations of cavernous sinus:
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is related anteriorly to the superior orbital fissure, posteriorly to the petrous apex and crus cerebri, medially to the pituitary gland and sphenoid sinus, laterally to the temporal lobe, superiorly to the optic tract and ICA, and inferiorly to foramen lacerum.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus relations: orbital fissure anterior, petrous apex posterior, pituitary medially, temporal lobe laterally.
questions.modelAnswer: Anterior: superior orbital fissure; Posterior: apex of petrous temporal and crus cerebri; Medial: pituitary and sphenoid sinus; Lateral: temporal lobe; Superior: optic tract and ICA; Inferior: foramen lacerum.

questions.text: Branches of cerebral part of ICA:
questions.explanation: The cerebral part of the internal carotid artery gives five branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, anterior cerebral, and middle cerebral arteries, supplying the orbit, diencephalon, and cerebral hemispheres.
questions.keyConcept: ICA cerebral branches: ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, ACA, MCA.
questions.modelAnswer: Ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, anterior and middle cerebral.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the condition of unilateral inattention (neglect)?
questions.explanation: Unilateral neglect syndrome involves ignoring stimuli from the contralateral side, often manifesting as failure to dress or groom that side, typically caused by right parietal lobe lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Neglect: ignoring contralateral stimuli, often with dressing/grooming deficits on that side.
options: Loss of all sensation on one side of the body
Ignoring stimuli from the opposite side, often with failure to dress or shave that side
Loss of proprioception with preserved touch

questions.text: The cauda equina is composed of:
questions.explanation: The cauda equina (horse's tail) consists of the dorsal and ventral roots of the lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal spinal nerves traveling within the subarachnoid space below L1-2.
questions.keyConcept: Cauda equina: dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral, coccygeal nerves.
options: The lower part of the spinal cord
Dorsal and ventral roots of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerves

questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic of the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The limbic system, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and cingulate gyrus, is fundamentally involved in emotional processing and memory formation, particularly through connections with the hypothalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic system: emotion and memory processing.
options: It is involved in emotion and memory.

questions.text: Contralateral sensation from the face and body is represented in the:
questions.explanation: SI (areas 3,1,2) maps the contralateral half of the body and face.
questions.keyConcept: Face represented upside down in somatosensory cortex, with larger areas for lips and fingers.

questions.text: The superior speech center is situated within the ……… area.
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA, medial area 6) is the superior speech center involved in planning and initiating speech movements, lying medial to premotor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Superior speech center: supplementary motor area.

questions.text: Choose the wrong statement about the speech areas:
questions.explanation: Speech areas are typically asymmetric; Broca's and Wernicke's areas are usually dominant in one hemisphere (left in right-handers), not equally present in both.
questions.keyConcept: Speech areas are not present equally in both hemispheres.
options: Motor area lies in the inferior frontal gyrus.
Sensory area lies in parietal and temporal lobes.
Sensory area is concerned with understanding visual and auditory information.
Both areas are present in both cerebral hemispheres.

questions.text: Myelination inside the CNS depends on:
questions.explanation: Myelination in the CNS is performed by oligodendrocytes, which can myelinate multiple axons. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.
questions.keyConcept: CNS myelination: oligodendrocytes (PNS: Schwann cells).

questions.text: The adult derivatives of the telencephalon are:
questions.explanation: The telencephalon develops into the cerebral hemispheres including the basal ganglia, hippocampus, and lateral ventricles, while thalamus, hypothalamus, and midbrain derive from diencephalon and mesencephalon.
questions.keyConcept: Telencephalon: cerebral hemispheres.

questions.text: The dural fold which is attached to the skull vault is:
questions.explanation: The falx cerebri is the dural fold attached to the skull vault along the midline, lying between the cerebral hemispheres with its anterior attachment at the crista galli.
questions.keyConcept: Falx cerebri: dural fold attached to skull vault.

questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerves is not related to cavernous sinus?
questions.explanation: The inferior sagittal sinus runs along the lower free margin of the falx cerebri and drains into the straight sinus. It receives blood from the medial aspects of the cerebral hemispheres.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior sagittal sinus in lower falx cerebri

questions.text: UMNL of cranial nerves can result from cerebrovascular accident affecting ……… artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies medial frontal and parietal regions including motor cortex areas controlling lower limbs; CVA here causes contralateral leg weakness and UMN signs.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: UMN lesion of cranial nerves (if affecting cortical areas).

questions.text: Which of the following is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) is the primary ion responsible for rapid depolarization during the upstroke of the action potential. Na+ channels open rapidly causing an influx of Na+, creating the spike. K+ is responsible for repolarization during the downstroke.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated sodium channels mediate the rapid depolarization phase of action potentials in most neurons and muscle fibers.

questions.text: Which structure is responsible for fine skilled movements of the index finger?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract originates from motor cortex including the precentral gyrus and premotor areas. The hand representation in area 4 controls skilled finger movements through lateral corticospinal fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Skilled hand movements are mediated by corticospinal neurons in the precentral gyrus hand area.

questions.text: The primary motor cortex (area 4) is chiefly responsible for:
questions.explanation: Area 4 executes movement; planning is premotor/SMA.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex (area 4): execution of voluntary movement.
options: Sensory perception of limb position in space
Converting the plan into actual movement

questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery is responsible for the supply of:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the motor and sensory areas for the contralateral lower limb due to its course along the medial cerebral hemisphere.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery: supplies contralateral lower limb motor/sensory areas.
options: Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral upper limb.
Sensory and motor areas of the contralateral lower limb.

questions.text: The thalamic nucleus that relays pain and temperature sensations from the head is the:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus receives somatosensory input specifically from the head and face. It receives the trigeminal lemniscus (carrying pain, temperature, and touch from the face) and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex. VPL handles the body; VPM handles the face.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus relays pain, temperature, and touch sensations specifically from the HEAD and face.

questions.text: A lesion in the Broca’s area of the cerebral hemisphere leads to:
questions.explanation: Broca's area is located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. It coordinates the motor aspects of speech production. Lesions here cause motor aphasia with hesitant, non-fluent speech but preserved comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Broca's area lesion causes motor aphasia

questions.text: Frontal lobe in dominant hemisphere contains the following areas Except:
questions.explanation: Wernicke's speech area is located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, not in the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe contains areas 4, 6, 8, and supplementary motor area.
questions.keyConcept: Wernicke's area is in temporal lobe, not frontal

questions.text: Parietal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following Except:
questions.explanation: Facial recognition is processed in the inferior temporal lobe (fusiform gyrus), not the parietal lobe. The parietal lobe is concerned with stereognosis, proprioception, and spatial processing.
questions.keyConcept: Facial recognition in temporal, not parietal lobe
options: Comprehension of received auditory & visual information.

questions.text: Cortical areas in temporal lobe include all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral eye movements is the occipital eye field (area 18), not the temporal lobe. The temporal lobe contains auditory areas and parts of Wernicke's area and facial recognition area.
questions.keyConcept: Involuntary eye movement control is occipital, not temporal
options: Area for control of involuntary conjugate lateral movements of eye.

questions.text: The frontal lobe of the non-dominant hemisphere is concerned with which of the following functions:
questions.explanation: The non-dominant hemisphere (usually right) is primarily responsible for control of behavior, emotional expression, and visuospatial functions. The dominant hemisphere handles speech and language.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant frontal lobe controls behavior/emotions

questions.text: A lady 55 years old, developed right sided hemiplegia mainly in the upper limb due to cerebrovascular accident as proved by MRI. The lesion affects the frontal and parietal lobes.
questions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
questions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.

subQuestions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Cerebrovascular accident (ischemic stroke) in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA), affecting the lateral aspect of the frontal and parietal lobes.

subQuestions.text: Which vessel is most likely affected?
subQuestions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Left middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the lenticulostriate branches or the main trunk, supplying the lateral surface of the frontal and parietal lobes and the internal capsule.

questions.text: Frontal lobe in the dominant hemisphere is concerned with the following functions Except:
questions.explanation: Understanding received auditory information (receptive language) is a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the frontal lobe. The frontal lobe handles speech production, skilled movements, eye movement initiation, and behavior control.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe functions: speech production (Broca), skilled movements, conjugate eye movements, behavior control.
options: Initiation of conjugate lateral eye movements

questions.text: Frontal lobe in the non-dominant hemisphere contains the following areas Except:
questions.explanation: Wernicke's speech area is located in the temporal lobe (superior temporal gyrus), not in the frontal lobe of the non-dominant hemisphere. The non-dominant hemisphere contains the same motor areas as the dominant but lacks speech areas.
questions.keyConcept: Non-dominant hemisphere frontal lobe contains motor areas (4,6,8) but NOT Wernicke's area (temporal lobe).

questions.text: What is the site of supplementary motor area?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (MII, area 6 on the medial surface) is located in the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the paracentral lobule. It is involved in speech planning and initiation.
questions.keyConcept: Supplementary motor area: medial frontal gyrus, medial surface of frontal lobe.
questions.modelAnswer: Medial frontal gyrus (medial surface of frontal lobe), anterior to the paracentral lobule. Also called MII or SMA, involved in planning and initiating complex movements including speech.

questions.text: Mention the relations of corpus callosum
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is related superiorly to the falx cerebri and anterior cerebral arteries, and inferiorly to the fornix and septum pellucidum, making it a key anatomical landmark in the interhemispheric fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Corpus callosum superior and inferior relations
questions.modelAnswer:
Superiorly: Falx cerebri and Anterior cerebral arteries
Inferiorly: Fornix and septum pellucidum

questions.text: What is the clinical feature that can assist in distinguishing Frontotemporal lobe degeneration from Alzheimer's Disease?
questions.explanation: Model Answer: Early prominent personality changes, behavioral disinhibition, and language difficulties (aphasia) suggest Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD), while early memory impairment with visuospatial dysfunction suggests Alzheimer's Disease. FTLD typically presents before age 65 with frontal/executive deficits.
questions.keyConcept: FTLD presents with early behavioral changes and preserved memory, distinguishing it from amnestic Alzheimer's presentation.
questions.modelAnswer: Clinical features distinguishing frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) from Alzheimer's disease include: 1) FTLD presents with early behavioral changes (disinhibition, apathy, compulsions) or language deficits, while memory and spatial orientation are relatively preserved early on. 2) AD presents with early anterograde amnesia and progressive memory loss. 3) FTLD onset is typically earlier (45-65 years) compared to AD. 4) FTLD shows frontal and temporal lobe atrophy on imaging, while AD shows hippocampal and medial temporal lobe atrophy.

questions.text: Where is the supplementary motor area located?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) is located in the medial surface of frontal lobe, anterior to the primary motor cortex (area 4), in Brodmann area 6.
questions.keyConcept: SMA is medial frontal cortex involved in motor planning, located anterior to primary motor cortex.

questions.text: Which function is primarily controlled by the primary motor cortex (area 4)?
questions.explanation: The primary motor cortex (area 4) controls discrete, fine voluntary movements, especially of the distal limbs. It contains large pyramidal neurons (Betz cells) in layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex mediates fine, skilled voluntary movements via Betz cells and corticospinal output.
options: Gives you the idea to move

questions.text: A 52‑year‑old man has had progressive headaches and concentration difficulties for two months. His behaviour becomes odd, and he then suffers a generalised seizure. MRI shows a large, necrotic mass in the left cerebral hemisphere that crosses the corpus callosum into the right hemisphere. Which neoplasm is most likely?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme typically crosses the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma), shows necrosis and ring enhancement, and has poor prognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma features

questions.text: Site of supplementary motor area:
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) is located on the medial surface of the frontal lobe anterior to the leg area of M1.
questions.keyConcept: SMA location
questions.modelAnswer: Medial frontal lobe above area 4.

questions.text: The genu of the corpus callosum is supplied mainly by the:
questions.explanation: The ACA supplies the genu of the corpus callosum.
questions.keyConcept: Genu of corpus callosum supplied by anterior cerebral artery.

questions.text: The supplementary motor area is located in the:
questions.explanation: The SMA lies on the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the leg area.
questions.keyConcept: Supplementary motor area located in medial aspect of frontal lobe (medial area 6).

questions.text: The frontal lobe of cerebral hemisphere DOESN'T include ……… area.
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory area (postcentral gyrus, area 1-3) is in the parietal lobe, not the frontal lobe. Frontal lobe contains premotor, prefrontal, and Broca's areas.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe doesn't include primary somatosensory (it's parietal).

questions.text: The area of reflex (involuntary) conjugate eye movement lies in ……… lobe of the cerebral hemisphere.
questions.explanation: The occipital lobe contains the area for reflex (involuntary) conjugate eye movements - the visual fixation center in the frontal eye field projects to superior colliculus for reflexive gaze.
questions.keyConcept: Reflex conjugate eye movement area: occipital lobe.

questions.text: The spinal dura mater ends at the vertebral level of:
questions.explanation: The spinal dura mater extends from the foramen magnum to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), where it fuses with the filum terminale to form the coccygeal ligament.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal dura mater ends at S2

questions.text: Arachnoid mater of spinal cord ends at the level of which vertebra:
questions.explanation: The spinal arachnoid mater extends to the level of the second sacral vertebra (S2), where it fuses with the filum terminale.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal arachnoid mater ends at S2

questions.text: A six-year old boy suffers from inability to control his micturition at night. On doing an X-ray, it showed a defect in the lower vertebral laminae with bulging meninges.
questions.explanation: The X-ray finding of a defect in the lower vertebral laminae with bulging meninges indicates spina bifida cystica (meningocoele). This results from failure of fusion of the dorsal portions of the vertebrae, leaving a midline defect through which meninges (and potentially spinal cord) protrude. The inability to control micturition suggests involvement of the cauda equina.
questions.keyConcept: Defect in vertebral laminae with bulging meninges = spina bifida cystica (meningocoele); from failure of posterior neural arch fusion.

subQuestions.text: TYPE: essay What is the name of this condition?
