questions.text: Mention the boundaries of lateral ventricle.
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricle boundaries include: lateral wall (caudate nucleus), medial wall (septum pellucidum), roof (corpus callosum), floor (thalamus and hypothalamus), anterior wall (paraterminal gyrus), and posterior wall (splenium of corpus callosum).
questions.keyConcept: Lateral ventricle anatomical boundaries
questions.modelAnswer:
Lateral wall: thalamus and hypothalamus
Roof: Layer of ependyma. Choroid plexus hangs from its roof.
Floor: optic chiasma, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mamillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, tegmentum of midbrain
Anterior wall: lamina terminalis, column of fornix, anterior commissure
Posterior wall: posterior commissure, pineal body, suprapineal recess

questions.text: The spinal cord is anchored to the dura mater by the
questions.explanation: Denticulate ligaments are pial extensions that anchor the spinal cord to the dura mater laterally; the coccygeal ligament (filum terminale externum) attaches the cord terminus to the coccyx.
questions.keyConcept: Denticulate ligaments spinal cord anchoring

questions.text: Concerning the lateral ventricle, choose one correct answer:
questions.explanation: The lateral ventricle is the only cavity in the telencephalon, with anterior horn in frontal lobe, body in parietal, and posterior/temporal horns in temporal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral ventricle structure
options: Its anterior horn lies in the parietal lobe.
Its posterior horn lies in the temporal lobe.
Is the only cavity in the telencephalon.

questions.text: A lesion of the anterior cerebral artery would most likely result in paralysis of:
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including the motor cortex representing the lower limb (paracentral lobule). Occlusion causes contralateral paralysis primarily affecting the leg and foot. The MCA supplies the lateral hemisphere (face, arm); the PCA supplies the occipital and inferior temporal regions.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery supplies medial hemisphere; occlusion causes contralateral LEG paralysis (paracentral lobule).

questions.text: List the cortical areas supplied by anterior cerebral artery.
questions.explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere (except occipital lobe), a one-inch strip of the superior lateral surface, and the medial part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cerebral artery cortical territories
questions.modelAnswer:
Medial surface: All except occipital lobe
Lateral surface: One inch strip superiorly
Inferior surface: Medial part of orbital surface

questions.text: Anterior cerebral artery supply:
questions.explanation: ACA supplies the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory for lower limb), medial aspect of frontal/parietal lobes; auditory cortex is supplied by MCA, not ACA.
questions.keyConcept: ACA supply territories

questions.text: Cortical branches of middle cerebral artery supply:
questions.explanation: MCA cortical branches supply lateral part of orbital surface, lateral surface (most except occipital), and temporal pole; occipital lobe and paracentral lobule are supplied by PCA and ACA respectively.
questions.keyConcept: MCA cortical supply

questions.text: Posterior cerebral artery supplies:
questions.explanation: PCA supplies: occipital lobe (visual cortex), lower border of temporal lobe, thalamus (central branches), and posterior limb of internal capsule; all of these are correct.
questions.keyConcept: PCA complete supply

questions.text: Occlusion of right anterior cerebral artery may lead to:
questions.explanation: Right anterior cerebral artery occlusion causes left lower limb paralysis (contralateral) since it supplies the medial motor cortex controlling the leg.
questions.keyConcept: Right ACA occlusion: left lower limb paralysis (contralateral).
options: Paralysis of the left upper limb.
Paralysis of the left lower limb.

questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty walking. He reports that he has been having trouble balancing and coordinating his movements for the past few months. He also has difficulty judging distances and reaching for objects. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: Difficulty balancing, coordinating movements, and judging distances (dysmetria) are classic signs of cerebellar dysfunction. The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements, maintains balance, and regulates muscle tone. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, and dysarthria. The frontal lobe controls motor planning; the parietal lobe processes sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesion = ataxia (difficulty balancing/coordinating), dysmetria (difficulty judging distances), intention tremor.

questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of difficulty paying attention. He reports that he has been having trouble staying focused on tasks and remembering things for the past few months. He also has difficulty controlling his impulses and making decisions. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation: The frontal lobe is responsible for executive functions including attention, working memory, impulse control, decision-making, and social behavior. Difficulty staying focused, remembering things, and controlling impulses indicates frontal lobe dysfunction. The prefrontal cortex is particularly important for these higher cognitive functions. The parietal lobe processes sensation; the cerebellum coordinates movement.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe = executive functions (attention, memory, impulse control, decision-making); damage causes frontal lobe syndrome.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT a character of Meissner’s corpuscle:
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscle has Schwann cells arranged in horizontal stacks (not spirally). The nerve fiber runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks. Merkel's disc has nerve fibers running spirally. Meissner's is encapsulated, in dermal papillae, and responds to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: Schwann cells in horizontal stacks, nerve fibers spiral; light touch receptor in dermal papillae.
options: It is an encapsulated nerve ending.
It is present in dermal papillae.
The Schwann cells are arranged in two cores.
The nerve fibers run spirally between the Schwann cells.

questions.text: Krause end bulb, all true except:
questions.explanation: Krause end bulbs have spherical structures with a gelatinous core, function as cold receptors, and are found in conjunctiva and oral cavity. They are mechanoreceptors. The statement about flattened Teloglia cells is incorrect - they have a different structure.
questions.keyConcept: Krause end bulb: cold receptor, mechanoreceptor, gelatinous core, found in conjunctiva and mouth.

questions.text: Pacinian corpuscle:
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric layers of Teloglia (not Schwann cells arranged transversely). They are located deep in the dermis (not dermal papillae), are encapsulated (not non-capsulated), and the nerve fiber runs centrally (not in spiral).
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle: concentric Teloglia layers, deep dermis, vibration receptor, encapsulated.
options: Lies in dermal papillae of skin.
Nerve fibers run in spiral coarse.

questions.text: The sensory nerve enters the Meissner’s corpuscle from:
questions.explanation: In Meissner's corpuscle, the sensory nerve enters from the SIDE (laterally), not from the lower part or central core. The nerve fiber then runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks within the corpuscle.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: sensory nerve enters from side; nerve fibers spiral between Schwann cell stacks.

questions.text: What is the site of Merkel’s tactile disc?
questions.explanation: Merkel's tactile discs are found in BOTH hairy and non-hairy skin, particularly in the deep layers of epidermis of palms, soles, and at transitional zones between hairy and non-hairy skin. They are slowly adapting touch receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Merkel's disc: deep epidermis of palms/soles and hairy-non hairy skin transitions; slowly adapting touch receptor.
options: Deep layers of the epidermis of the palmer surfaces of hands and planter surfaces of feet
Transitional sites between hairy & non-hairy skin

questions.text: Pacinian corpuscles are found in
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are found in deep tissues including dermis and hypodermis, as well as mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder, and other viscera. They detect deep pressure and vibration. Their wide distribution reflects their role in detecting deep mechanical stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles: deep dermis, hypodermis, mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder - deep pressure/vibration.

questions.text: About spinal nerve all true except:
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia contain nerve cells of VARIABLE size (not same size) - large neurons for proprioception, medium for touch, small for pain. Lateral division of dorsal root carries pain and temperature; medial division carries proprioception and fine touch. Thick myelinated fibers carry proprioceptive information.
questions.keyConcept: DRG neurons: variable sizes (large=proprioception, small=pain); lateral = pain/temp; medial = touch/proprioception.
options: Lateral division of dorsal root carry pain, temp
Dorsal root ganglia contain cells of same size.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion:
questions.explanation: DRG neurons are of variable size (pseudounipolar neurons with different diameters). The ganglion is located on the dorsal root OUTSIDE the CNS (not inside), surrounded by a connective tissue capsule. It is not located at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: pseudounipolar neurons of variable size, encapsulated, located on dorsal root outside CNS.
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.

questions.text: Nerve cells of dorsal root ganglia are characterized by:
questions.explanation: DRG cells are pseudounipolar with multiple processes (one peripheral, one central). They have eccentric nuclei, are associated with both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers, and are surrounded by satellite glial cells (not Schwann cells around the cell body itself).
questions.keyConcept: DRG cells: pseudounipolar, multiple processes, eccentric nucleus, satellite cells, myelinated + unmyelinated fibers.
options: Associated with myelinated & unmyelinated nerve fibers.
Have shwann cells around its cell bodies.

questions.text: The apical surface of ependymal Cells has:
questions.explanation: Ependymal cells have cilia on their apical surface that help circulate CSF. They also have microvilli but cilia are the distinguishing feature. The ciliary movement helps propel CSF through the ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymal cells: ciliated simple columnar epithelium lining ventricles; cilia circulate CSF.

questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ___ while microglia Is derived from ___:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (neural tube/glial precursors), same as neurons and astrocytes. Microglia are derived from mesoderm (monocyte-macrophage lineage), making them the only non-ectodermal glial cells in the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: neuroectoderm. Microglia: mesoderm (monocyte origin). Astrocytes: neuroectoderm.

questions.text: Which of the following cells Produce myelin sheath?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes form myelin sheaths in the CNS (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons). Schwann cells do this in the PNS. Astrocytes provide support; satellite cells support neurons in ganglia; ependymal cells line ventricles.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes: CNS myelin (multiple axons). Schwann cells: PNS myelin (one axon each).

questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells:
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in injury and disease to phagocytose debris. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are not phagocytic under normal conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages (phagocytic), mesodermal origin, activated in injury/disease.

questions.text: In the CNS Injury, which of the following cells are abundant:
questions.explanation: In CNS injury, astrocytes proliferate (gliosis) to form glial scars, and microglia activate to phagocytose debris. This reactive gliosis is a hallmark of CNS injury response. Oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells do not become abundant.
questions.keyConcept: CNS injury response: astrocyte proliferation (gliosis) + microglia activation (phagocytosis).

questions.text: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein specific to astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in histology and neuropathology. Oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells do not contain GFAP.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP: astrocyte marker (intermediate filament). Used to identify astrocytes in CNS.

questions.text: The outer band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL GRANULAR layer (layer IV). This band represents dense termination of thalamocortical fibers. The inner band of Baillarger is in the internal pyramidal layer (layer V).
questions.keyConcept: Outer Baillarger: layer IV (internal granular) - thalamocortical input. Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal).

questions.text: The inner band of baillarger is present in which layer
questions.explanation: The inner band of Baillarger is found in the INTERNAL PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V), which contains Betz cells in the motor cortex and other pyramidal neurons. The horizontal myelinated fibers form this band.
questions.keyConcept: Inner Baillarger: layer V (internal pyramidal) - contains Betz cells and corticospinal neurons.

questions.text: The cytoplasm of astrocytes contains
questions.explanation: Astrocytes contain microtubules (for transport), GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein - their intermediate filament marker), and thread-like mitochondria. These contents help identify astrocytes histologically. GFAP is the most specific marker.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocyte cytoplasm: GFAP (marker), microtubules, mitochondria. GFAP used for astrocyte identification.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about microglia?
questions.explanation: Microglia are present in CNS including retina and optic nerve (CNS outgrowths). They are small spindle-shaped cells with branching poles and fine spines on their surfaces. They are the resident macrophages of the CNS, derived from mesoderm.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia: CNS macrophages, spindle-shaped with branched spiny processes, mesodermal origin.
options: They are present in the retina and optic nerve
They are small spindle shaped cells with branching poles
The cell body and processes have minute spines on their surfaces

questions.text: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are seen in the UPPER level of closed medulla where the sensory decussation occurs. At the lower level, the motor decussation is occurring. In the open medulla, the medial lemniscus has already formed and ascended.
questions.keyConcept: Upper closed medulla: sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers). Lower closed medulla: motor decussation.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the dorsal root ganglion?
questions.explanation: Dorsal root ganglia are collections of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS (in the PNS), have variable-sized neurons, and are encapsulated by connective tissue. They are not inside the CNS or at viscera.
questions.keyConcept: DRG: outside CNS, variable size neurons, encapsulated connective tissue
options: It is a collection of nerve cells inside the central nervous system.
It is located at the viscera.
It has nerve cells of variable size.
It has no connective tissue capsule.

questions.text: Nucleus dorsalis (Claris nucleus), all true except:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (not ventral), located in lamina VII at C8-L3 levels. It has large cells with central nucleus, not eccentric nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus gives rise to DORSAL spinocerebellar tract (not ventral) - FALSE
options: In the medial aspect of the base of the posterior horn, in level from C8-L3.
Involved in lamina 7 of gray matter.
Give rise to ventral spinocerebellar tract.

questions.text: One of the following nuclei is not present in all segments of the spinal cord:
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) is NOT present at all spinal levels - it exists only from C8 to L3 segments. The other nuclei (postero-marginal, substantia gelatinosa, main sensory nucleus) are present in all segments.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus (C8-L3) is NOT present in all spinal segments - EXCEPTION

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning the lateral horn of the spinal cord is TRUE?
questions.explanation: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is most prominent at thoracic and upper lumbar levels (T1-L2/3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons (the origin of sympathetic preganglionic fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Lateral horn: origin of preganglionic sympathetic fibers, prominent at thoracic levels
options: Gives origin to pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibers.
It is most prominent at sacral levels.
It is present in all spinal cord levels.

questions.text: Anterior horn of spinal cord contains the following nuclei EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The anterior horn contains anteromedial, anterolateral, and posterolateral nuclei. There is no 'middle' nucleus in the anterior horn.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei: anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral (no 'middle' nucleus) - EXCEPTION

questions.text: The main sensory nucleus of spinal cord is:
questions.explanation: The main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius dorsalis) in the posterior horn receives touch and pressure sensations. Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) processes pain and temperature; posteromarginal nucleus is at the apex.
questions.keyConcept: Main sensory nucleus (nucleus proprius) is the primary sensory relay in posterior horn

questions.text: The second order neuron in proprioception from the lower half of the body is in:
questions.explanation: The second-order neuron for proprioception from the lower body is located in the gracile nucleus on the same side as the entry. Its axon decussates as internal arcuate fibers and ascends in the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Second-order proprioception neuron in gracile nucleus of SAME side
options: Gracile nucleus on the same side.
Cuneate nucleus on the same side.

questions.text: The oligodendrocyte is derived from ... while microglia is derived from ...
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm (like astrocytes), while microglia are derived from mesenchyme (monocyte-macrophage lineage). This distinction is important for understanding CNS pathology.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendrocytes from ectoderm, microglia from mesoderm

questions.text: In the CNS, which of the following are phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are the resident phagocytic cells of the CNS, derived from mesoderm. They become activated in CNS injury and disease, acting as macrophages.
questions.keyConcept: Microglia are the phagocytic cells of CNS (mesodermal origin)

questions.text: In the CNS injury, which of the following cells are abundant?
questions.explanation: After CNS injury, astrocytes (forming glial scars) and activated microglia (phagocytic response) increase in number. Ependymal cells and oligodendrocytes do not show the same abundance in injury responses.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytes and microglia are abundant in CNS injury (reactive gliosis)

questions.text: Cells of Cajal are present in:
questions.explanation: Cells of Cajal (horizontal cells) are found in the molecular layer (layer I) of the cerebral cortex. They have horizontal axons that run parallel to the surface.
questions.keyConcept: Cells of Cajal in molecular layer of cerebral cortex (layer I)

questions.text: Glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) is a marker of:
questions.explanation: GFAP (glial fibrillar acidic protein) is an intermediate filament protein found specifically in astrocytes. It is used as a marker to identify astrocytes in tissue and in astrocytoma diagnostics.
questions.keyConcept: GFAP is the specific marker for astrocytes (intermediate filament protein)

questions.text: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to:
questions.explanation: The dorsal motor nucleus of vagus gives rise to preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (GVE - General Visceral Efferent) that innervate cardiac, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal organs.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus: GVE (parasympathetic preganglionic)

questions.text: Psammoma bodies are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions) are characteristic of meningiomas, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and serous cystadenocarcinoma of ovary.
questions.keyConcept: Psammoma bodies characteristic of meningioma (and some carcinomas)

questions.text: The following tumor is always benign:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are benign tumors derived from arachnoid cap cells. Pilocytic astrocytoma can occasionally be aggressive; ependymomas and medulloblastomas can be malignant. Meningiomas are almost always benign.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma is the only tumor that is always benign

questions.text: Microscopic rosette formation is a characteristic feature of:
questions.explanation: Rosette formation (Homer-Wright rosettes) is characteristic of medulloblastoma and other primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNETs).
questions.keyConcept: Rosette formation characteristic of medulloblastoma (PNET)

questions.text: A female 50-year-old presented with brain tumor with focal erosion of the skull bones. The tumor was excised and examined histologically. It consisted of spindle-shaped & syncytial cells arranged in a whorly pattern. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas show spindle-shaped cells arranged in whorled patterns, sometimes with psammoma bodies. They arise from arachnoid cap cells and can erode skull bone.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma: spindle cells in whorled pattern, can erode skull bone

questions.text: Medulloblastoma is a:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is a tumor of undifferentiated/primitive neuroectodermal cells (PNET), not a glial tumor (astrocytoma/oligodendroglioma) or neuronal tumor. It arises from cerebellar granule cell precursors.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma: tumor of undifferentiated cells (PNET), not glial or neuronal

questions.text: The following tumor shows a whorly pattern of growth:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas characteristically show a whorled pattern of growth with spindle cells and psammoma bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma shows whorled pattern of growth

questions.text: Glioblastoma multiforme shows:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme shows vascular proliferation (neovascularization with abnormal vessels), necrosis with pseudopalisading, and highly anaplastic cells. Rosenthal fibers are in pilocytic astrocytomas; rosette formation in medulloblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma: vascular proliferation (not Rosenthal fibers or rosettes)

questions.text: The following histological picture is not characteristic of Glioblastoma multiforme:
questions.explanation: Papillary formation is NOT characteristic of glioblastoma multiforme. GBM shows highly anaplastic cells, necrosis, tumor giant cells, and vascular proliferation. Papillary architecture is seen in papillary ependymomas or papillary meningiomas.
questions.keyConcept: Papillary formation is NOT characteristic of glioblastoma - EXCEPTION

questions.text: The most common brain tumor in children:
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, occurring in the cerebellum. It is a PNET (primitive neuroectodermal tumor) with small round blue cells.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma is most common malignant brain tumor in children

questions.text: Which of the following tumors is malignant:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme is a malignant brain tumor (WHO grade IV). Meningiomas and schwannomas are usually benign; neurofibromas are typically benign.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma multiforme is the malignant tumor among the options

questions.text: A male patient 40 years old presented with hemiplegia & deafness. Radiological examination showed a tumor at the cerebellopontine angle. Biopsy from this tumor showed a neurogenic tumor formed of hypercellular and hypocellular areas. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Schwannomas (neurilemmomas) at the cerebellopontine angle show hypercellular (Antoni A) and hypocellular (Antoni B) areas. They arise from Schwann cells.
questions.keyConcept: Schwannoma: Antoni A and B areas, hypercellular/hypocellular, cerebellopontine angle

questions.text: The following tumor arises from the lining of the ventricular system:
questions.explanation: Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells that line the ventricular system and central canal of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma arises from ependymal lining of ventricular system

questions.text: Which sensation is primarily detected by Meissner’s corpuscles?
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors in the dermal papillae that detect crude touch and tactile discrimination, particularly in glabrous skin.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner corpuscle function

questions.text: Which statement about Clarke’s nucleus is correct?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is present at all thoracic levels (T1-L2) and is the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus distribution
options: Clarke’s nucleus is present at all levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all cervical levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all thoracic levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all lumbar levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all sacral levels

questions.text: Which of the following nuclei has motor function?
questions.explanation: The anteromedial nucleus (in the anterior horn) has motor function, containing motor neuron pools for axial and proximal limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn nuclei

questions.text: Inner Pyramidal cells are present in layer …. of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Inner pyramidal cells (also called Betz cells when giant) are found in layer V of the motor cortex, not in layers I-IV. Layer V is the internal pyramidal layer. The options I-IV are incorrect - inner pyramidal refers to layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Layer V (internal pyramidal): Betz cells, corticospinal neurons. Layer IV: thalamocortical input.

questions.text: Each of the following statements concerning closed medulla is true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In the closed medulla, the main inferior olivary nucleus is present, and it contains the gracile and cuneate nuclei on the dorsal aspect. The motor decussation is in the lower part, and sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibers) is at a higher level - making 'higher level has sensory decussation' TRUE, not the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Closed medulla: motor decussation lower, sensory decussation at higher level
options: In the lower part, there are motor decussation.
At a higher level, there are sensory decussation.
Contains the main inferior olivary nucleus.

questions.text: Which mechanoreceptor is primarily responsible for detecting vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic onion-like lamellar structure located in dermis and deeper tissues.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle function

questions.text: Which of the following share in the cerebellar islands:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar islands (islands of granular cells) contain rosettes of mossy fiber terminals surrounded by dendrites of granule cells. Mossy fibers synapse with granule cell dendrites in these glomeruli.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar glomeruli: mossy fiber rosettes + granule cell dendrites; input from spinal cord/brainstem.

questions.text: Cerebellar cortex:
questions.explanation: The cerebellar cortex is NOT uniform - different regions have different afferent inputs (vestibular, spinocerebellar, corticocerebellar). It has 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), not 6. It does show sulci (folia).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar cortex: 3 layers (molecular, Purkinje, granular), folia/sulci, non-uniform structure.
options: Contain martonitti cells in the molecular layer.
Is of uniform structure all over cerebellum

questions.text: Martinoti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells have axons directed UPWARDS (toward the cortical surface). Their dendrites extend laterally, cell bodies are multipolar (not rounded), and they use various neurotransmitters. They are inhibitory interneurons in the cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells: cortical interneurons with ascending axons; deliver inhibitory signals to superficial layers.

questions.text: Giant cells of Betz are present in which layer of cerebral cortex:
questions.explanation: Giant cells of Betz are found in the INNER PYRAMIDAL layer (layer V) of the motor cortex. These are the largest neurons in the CNS and give rise to corticospinal tract fibers. They are characteristic of the primary motor area.
questions.keyConcept: Betz cells: giant pyramidal neurons in layer V of motor cortex; corticospinal tract origin.

questions.text: Cerebral cortex is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Cerebral cortex has both laminar (6 layers) and columnar (functional minicolumns) organization. It has a folded surface (gyri and sulci), varying thickness, different neuron shapes in different layers, and shows plasticity.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex: 6 layers, columnar organization, folded surface, varying thickness, high plasticity.
options: Layers of the same thickness all over the brain

questions.text: All of the following are layers of cerebral cortex EXCEPT
questions.explanation: Purkinje layer is a layer of the CEREBELLAR cortex, not cerebral cortex. The cerebral cortex layers are: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), multiform (VI).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex 6 layers: I molecular, II external granular, III external pyramidal, IV internal granular, V internal pyramidal, VI multiform. Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje, granular.

questions.text: All of the following are cells of the cerebral cortex except:
questions.explanation: All of these - pyramidal cells, granular cells, fusiform cells, and Martinotti cells - ARE cells of the cerebral cortex. Pyramidal cells are the most common excitatory neurons. Granular cells are small interneurons. Fusiform cells are in the deep layer. Martinotti cells have ascending axons.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex neurons: pyramidal (main), granular, fusiform, Martinotti, basket, Chandelier cells.

questions.text: Martinotti cells of cerebral cortex are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Martinotti cells are characterized by being inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of the cerebral cortex. They have axons that ascend to the molecular layer.
questions.keyConcept: Martinotti cells are inner pyramidal cells (layer V) of cerebral cortex

questions.text: Giant cells of Betz are present in which layer of cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Giant cells of Betz are large pyramidal neurons found in layer V (inner pyramidal layer) of the primary motor cortex. They give rise to the corticospinal tract.
questions.keyConcept: Giant cells of Betz in layer V (inner pyramidal) of primary motor cortex

questions.text: All of the following are layers of cerebral cortex EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The cerebral cortex has six layers: molecular (I), external granular (II), external pyramidal (III), internal granular (IV), internal pyramidal (V), and multiform (VI). The Purkinje layer is in the cerebellar cortex, not cerebral cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje layer is in cerebellum NOT cerebral cortex (cerebral has 6 layers, not Purkinje)

questions.text: A 50-year-old man has a 3cm diameter left frontal lobe mass with areas of calcification. Microscopically, sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei surrounded by clear halo of cytoplasm are seen. Which of the following diagnosis is most likely to be made on microscopic examination of this mass?
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas have characteristic 'fried egg' cells (spherical nuclei with clear halo cytoplasm), often calcified, in the frontal lobe. They arise from oligodendrocytes and are slow-growing.
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma: 'fried egg' cells with clear halo, calcifications, frontal lobe

questions.text: The biopsy of a ring-enhancing tumor in the left parietal lobe of a 60-year-old patient reveals an astrocytic tumor that displays marked cellular atypia, mitotic activity, areas of pseudopalisading necrosis & multifocal microvascular hyperplasia. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Ring-enhancing tumor with pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular hyperplasia is diagnostic of glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV). These features distinguish it from lower-grade astrocytomas.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular hyperplasia = glioblastoma multiforme (grade IV)

questions.text: A 33-year-old male presents with seizures, MRI shows an ill-defined area of infiltrative tumor expanding the frontal lobe. Biopsy of this lesion shows glial tissue with slightly increased cellularity and mild nuclear pleomorphism. No mitotic activity, no necrosis & no vascular proliferation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Grade II astrocytomas show increased cellularity, mild nuclear pleomorphism, but no mitotic activity, necrosis, or vascular proliferation. They are diffuse astrocytomas in young adults, slower growing than anaplastic or GBM.
questions.keyConcept: Grade II astrocytoma: slightly increased cellularity, mild pleomorphism, no necrosis/mitosis

questions.text: A male patient 40 years presented with left-sided hemiplegia, brain MRI revealed a space-occupying lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere. Biopsy examination showed a highly cellular tumor with malignant cells, areas of necrosis & vascular proliferation. The most possible diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme shows highly cellular tumor with malignant cells, necrosis, and vascular proliferation. These features distinguish it from anaplastic astrocytoma (which lacks necrosis) and ependymoma.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma: necrosis and vascular proliferation = hallmark features

questions.text: Which statement is true regarding the layers of the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: The outer band of Baillarger (optic radiation fibers) is found in the inner granular layer (layer IV) of the cerebral cortex, while the inner band is in layer V.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral cortex layers
options: The outer band of Baillarger is present in the inner granular layer
The inner band of Baillarger is present in the molecular layer
The molecular layer contains large pyramidal cells
The inner granular layer lacks stellate cells
The multiform layer is the most superficial layer

questions.text: An 18-year-old male presents with a well-circumscribed mass involving the 4th ventricle. Diagnostic microscopical findings in this condition include:
questions.explanation: Ependymomas show both rosettes (true ependymal) and pseudorosettes (perivascular). Rosenthal fibers are in pilocytic astrocytomas; Verocay bodies in schwannomas; chicken wire calcification in oligodendrogliomas.
questions.keyConcept: Ependymoma: rosettes and pseudorosettes (not Rosenthal fibers or Verocay bodies)

questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma shows the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas show activation of the MAPK pathway and BRAF alterations (especially BRAF-KIAA1549 fusion). NF1 inactivation is seen in optic pathway gliomas. IDH1/IDH2 mutations are seen in adult diffuse astrocytomas, not pilocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: BRAF activation, MAPK pathway (NOT IDH1/IDH2 mutations)
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.

questions.text: A 65-year-old man develops new onset of seizures & headaches. A CT scan reveals a 6 cm left-sided intracerebral mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, presenting with seizures and headache. It is a diffusely infiltrating astrocytic tumor with necrosis and angiogenesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma multiforme: most common aggressive adult brain tumor, seizures, headache

questions.text: Astrocytoma is:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are tumors derived from astrocytes, classified as grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, malignant). They are the most common primary brain tumors, typically in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma: glial tumor from astrocytes, grades I-IV

questions.text: Meningioma shows:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are characterized by psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions), whorled patterns of spindle cells, and meningothelial cells. Rosenthal fibers are seen in pilocytic astrocytomas; vascular proliferation in glioblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma characteristic: psammoma bodies, whorled pattern

questions.text: The following is not a feature of meningioma:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas typically have a whorled cut surface (not whorly). The other statements about meningioma (adults, benign, psammoma bodies) are true. The question asks for what's NOT a feature.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma has whorled pattern, not whorly surface - minor terminology

questions.text: The following is not a type of glioma:
questions.explanation: Ganglioneuroma is a benign tumor of mature neurons (not a glioma). Astrocytomas, ependymomas, and glioblastomas are all gliomas (tumors of glial cells).
questions.keyConcept: Ganglioneuroma is NOT a glioma (it's a neuronal tumor) - EXCEPTION

questions.text: Oligodendroglioma is not a:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas are low-grade (grade II) tumors, not high-grade. They are glial tumors, cerebral tumors, and well-circumscribed. High-grade would be anaplastic oligodendroglioma (grade III).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma is a low-grade tumor, NOT high-grade - EXCEPTION

questions.text: Astrocytoma is a:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are glial tumors derived from astrocytes, the most common primary brain tumors. They range from grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, highly malignant).
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma is a glial tumor (from astrocytes)

questions.text: Oligodendrogliomas are not characterized by:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas do NOT typically show activation of the MAPK pathway. They characteristically have IDH1/IDH2 mutations and 1p/19q codeletion. MAPK activation is seen in pilocytic astrocytomas (BRAF fusion).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma: IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion (NOT MAPK activation) - EXCEPTION
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK).

questions.text: A 20 year old student was playing baseball when the ball hit him on the side of the head. He immediately fell to the ground unconscious. After 30 seconds he felt well & decided to sit & watch the match. An hour later, he felt so sleepy & then he became unconscious again. He was taken to the hospital & a skull X-ray showed a fracture in the region of the pterion.
questions.explanation: This patient presents with the classic clinical picture of extradural (epidural) hematoma following head trauma. The initial loss of consciousness represents the primary brain injury, the lucid interval represents temporary recovery, and the secondary deterioration is due to arterial bleeding causing expanding hematoma and increased intracranial pressure. Fracture at the pterion strongly suggests middle meningeal artery laceration.
questions.keyConcept: Pterion fracture with lucid interval = extradural hematoma from middle meningeal artery laceration.

subQuestions.explanation: This patient presents with the classic clinical picture of extradural (epidural) hematoma following head trauma. The initial loss of consciousness represents the primary brain injury, the lucid interval represents temporary recovery, and the secondary deterioration is due to arterial bleeding causing expanding hematoma and increased intracranial pressure. Fracture at the pterion strongly suggests middle meningeal artery laceration.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Pterion fracture with lucid interval = extradural hematoma from middle meningeal artery laceration.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: The pterion is the region where the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones meet. It is located approximately 4 cm above the zygomatic arch and 3.5 cm behind the frontozygomatic suture. It is the thinnest part of the lateral skull and is closely related to the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

subQuestions.text: TYPE: essay Why are fractures in this region extremely dangerous?
subQuestions.explanation: This patient presents with the classic clinical picture of extradural (epidural) hematoma following head trauma. The initial loss of consciousness represents the primary brain injury, the lucid interval represents temporary recovery, and the secondary deterioration is due to arterial bleeding causing expanding hematoma and increased intracranial pressure. Fracture at the pterion strongly suggests middle meningeal artery laceration.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Pterion fracture with lucid interval = extradural hematoma from middle meningeal artery laceration.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Fractures at the pterion are dangerous because: (1) the pterion is the thinnest part of the skull, making it easily fractured; (2) the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies immediately beneath it; (3) laceration of this artery causes rapid extradural hematoma; (4) the expanding hematoma compresses the brain and increases intracranial pressure, leading to brain herniation and death if not promptly treated.

questions.text: An old man starts to develop headache and by MRI proved to have tumors of the medial geniculate body.
questions.explanation: Medial geniculate body tumors present with auditory symptoms including tinnitus, hearing loss, and sensorineural hearing deficits because this nucleus is the thalamic relay for auditory information from the inferior colliculus. Headache results from mass effect. Efferent fibers project via the auditory radiation to Heschl's gyrus in the temporal lobe.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body tumor causes auditory deficits and tinnitus; relays auditory impulses from inferior colliculus to temporal auditory cortex.

subQuestions.text: TYPE: essay Where is the medial geniculate body located?
subQuestions.explanation: Medial geniculate body tumors present with auditory symptoms including tinnitus, hearing loss, and sensorineural hearing deficits because this nucleus is the thalamic relay for auditory information from the inferior colliculus. Headache results from mass effect. Efferent fibers project via the auditory radiation to Heschl's gyrus in the temporal lobe.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body tumor causes auditory deficits and tinnitus; relays auditory impulses from inferior colliculus to temporal auditory cortex.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Located below the posterior end of the thalamus.

subQuestions.text: TYPE: essay Where do its efferent fibers project to?
subQuestions.explanation: Medial geniculate body tumors present with auditory symptoms including tinnitus, hearing loss, and sensorineural hearing deficits because this nucleus is the thalamic relay for auditory information from the inferior colliculus. Headache results from mass effect. Efferent fibers project via the auditory radiation to Heschl's gyrus in the temporal lobe.
subQuestions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body tumor causes auditory deficits and tinnitus; relays auditory impulses from inferior colliculus to temporal auditory cortex.
subQuestions.modelAnswer: Its efferents form the auditory radiation which projects directly to the auditory area of cerebral cortex.

questions.text: Lateral medullary syndrome includes the following Except:
questions.explanation: Lateral medullary syndrome includes vestibular symptoms (vertigo, nystagmus) due to involvement of the vestibular nuclei. This is a key feature that distinguishes Wallenberg syndrome from medial medullary syndrome.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral medullary includes vestibular symptoms
options: Ipsilateral paralysis of palate, pharynx & larynx.
Contralateral pain & temperature loss from face.
Ipsilateral loss of taste of posterior 1/3 of tongue.

questions.text: The medial medullary syndrome includes:
questions.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome includes: ipsilateral tongue paralysis (hypoglossal), contralateral hemiparesis (pyramidal), and contralateral loss of proprioception/fine touch (medial lemniscus). Pain and temperature are preserved.
questions.keyConcept: Medial medullary syndrome includes tongue paralysis
options: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron lesion of XII.

questions.text: Crude touch sensation is:
questions.explanation: Crude touch is carried by Aδ fibers (lightly myelinated, 2-5 μm diameter, 5-15 m/s conduction). Option A is correct. Option B is wrong (crude touch is poorly localized, fine touch is sharply localized). Option C is wrong (crude touch is carried in anterior spinothalamic tract, not lateral). Option D is wrong (perceived at thalamic level, not cortex). Option E is wrong (receptors for crude touch are phasic, not tonic).
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch uses Aδ fibers and is carried in the anterior spinothalamic tract with poor localization.
options: Carried in the lateral spinothalamic tract.
Perceived at level of sensory cortex.

questions.text: Athetosis is associated with movement which is NOT:
questions.explanation: Athetosis movements are NOT decreased by emotions - they increase with emotional states. Option E is correct. Athetosis consists of slow, twisting, spontaneous movements that intensify with emotional stress, fatigue, and attempts at voluntary movement. Option A, B, C, D all correctly describe athetoid movements.
questions.keyConcept: Athetoid movements intensify with emotional states and voluntary attempts, distinguishing them from other movement disorders.

questions.text: Rigidity is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Rigidity is characterized by increased tone in antigravity muscles. Option A is correct. Rigidity (both lead-pipe and cogwheel) particularly affects anti-gravity muscles due to exaggerated extensor activity. Options B, C, D, E are incorrect: gamma cell hyperactivity alone doesn't cause rigidity; rigidity occurs in UMN lesions (not just associated); static tremors are Parkinsonian; circumduction gait is UMN, not rigidity.
questions.keyConcept: Rigidity preferentially affects antigravity muscles, reflecting the dominance of extensor muscles in human posture.
options: Due to increase gamma cells activities.

questions.text: Motor ataxia is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: Motor ataxia is characterized by FAILURE of coordination even with opened eyes. Option D is INCORRECT. Motor (cerebellar) ataxia shows poor coordination visible even with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which compensates with vision. Options A, B, C, E are correct features of motor ataxia: zigzag gait, staccato speech, kinetic tremors, and cerebellar origin.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar ataxia is manifest with eyes open due to loss of motor coordination, unlike sensory ataxia.

questions.text: Motor ataxia is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Motor ataxia is characterized by kinetic tremor. Option D is correct. Cerebellar motor ataxia presents with kinetic tremor (worse during movement), not the stamping gait or positive Romberg of sensory ataxia. Options A, B describe sensory ataxia features. Option C (normal speech) is not characteristic - cerebellar patients have dysarthria.
questions.keyConcept: Kinetic tremor worsens with intentional movement and is characteristic of cerebellar motor ataxia.

questions.text: An 83-year-old man was referred to a medical centre with a history of difficulty in walking. During examination: he was unsteady on his feet, dysarthric, negative Romberg’s sign, and appearance of tremor during movement were observed. What is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: Motor ataxia is the most probable diagnosis. Option A is correct. The patient has unsteady gait, dysarthria, negative Romberg (intact proprioception), and tremor during movement - all cerebellar signs. Sensory ataxia (B) would have positive Romberg. Vestibular ataxia (C) would have vertigo/nystagmus. Hysterical ataxia (D) lacks consistency.
questions.keyConcept: Negative Romberg with movement tremor and dysarthria points to cerebellar (motor) ataxia.

questions.text: A musician has lost his ability to play the piano with no signs of muscle paralysis. What is the probable site of lesion?
questions.explanation: Lesion within premotor area (area 6) is most probable. Option D is correct. Piano playing requires coordinated, skilled movements programmed by premotor cortex, not primary motor cortex (which executes fine movements). Area 8 is frontal eye fields; areas 1,2,3 are somatosensory. Loss without paralysis suggests premotor rather than primary motor lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area (area 6) programs skilled sequential movements; lesions disrupt coordination without paralysis.

questions.text: Spinal shock produces:-
questions.explanation: Spinal shock produces hypotension. Option B is correct. Loss of sympathetic outflow after spinal cord transection causes vasodilation and hypotension. Options A, C, D describe later effects (automatic micturition after shock, positive Babinski develops later, spasticity develops weeks later). During spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, loss of bowel/bladder, hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Acute spinal shock causes flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and hypotension due to loss of sympathetic tone.

questions.text: After falling down from a staircase, a young woman is found to have loss of voluntary movement on the right side of the body and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side below the mid thoracic region. The probable site of lesion is:
questions.explanation: Transection of the right half of spinal cord in upper thoracic region. Option A is correct. Right hemiplegia (right voluntary movement loss) and left pain/temperature loss indicate right Brown-Sequard syndrome. The motor fibers decussate at the cervicomedullary junction, so hemisection causes ipsilateral motor loss below the lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral motor paralysis with contralateral pain/temperature loss indicates hemisection on the side of motor deficits.
options: Transection of the right half of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of the left side of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region

Transection of the left half of the spinal cord in the lumbar region

questions.explanation: Mass reflex has pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder. Option B is correct. Options A, C, D are incorrect (upper limb rigidity is wrong, immediate occurrence is wrong, basoganglia involvement is wrong).

questions.text: Long-term effects of cord trans-section at T12 include:
questions.explanation: Long-term cord transection at T12: hypertonia and hyperreflexia in lower limbs. Option D is correct. questions.keyConcept: After spinal shock resolves, transection above T12 causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia in lower limbs.
options: Loss of tendon jerks in lower limbs.
Hypertonia and hyperreflexia in lower limbs.

questions.text: Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit - this is NOT true. Option E is INCORRECT. questions.text: Which statement is NOT true about Renshaw cells:
questions.explanation: Renshaw cells ACTIVATE nearby alpha motor neurons - NOT TRUE. Option C is INCORRECT. Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons that provide recurrent inhibition of alpha motor neurons, preventing overexcitation. questions.keyConcept: Renshaw cells provide recurrent inhibition via glycine to prevent alpha motor neuron overexcitation.

questions.text: Regarding the stretch reflex, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Stretch reflex is a polysynaptic reflex - NOT TRUE. Option C is INCORRECT. Stretch reflex is MONOsynaptic (one synapse between Ia afferent and alpha motor neuron). questions.keyConcept: The stretch reflex is the prototypical monosynaptic reflex with a single excitatory synapse.
options: Can be elicited by passive stretch.
Depends on the muscle spindle which is a mechanoreceptor present parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
Stretch of a muscle is followed by its contraction.
Is associated with simultaneous inhibition of the antagonist muscle.

questions.text: The resting membrane potential is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential (approximately -70 mV in neurons) closely matches the equilibrium potential of K+ (approximately -90 mV) because the membrane at rest is most permeable to potassium.
questions.keyConcept: The resting membrane potential approximates the K+ equilibrium potential due to high resting K+ permeability.

questions.text: Define ataxia. What are the causes and characteristic features of its different types?
questions.explanation: Ataxia is the loss of coordination of voluntary muscle movements, resulting in unsteady gait and movements. Types include: 1) Sensory ataxia - due to loss of proprioception (dorsal column disease), worse in darkness/closing eyes (positive Romberg), staggering gait with wide base; 2) Cerebellar ataxia - due to cerebellar lesions, has characteristic 'cerebellar speech' (scanning), truncal instability, intention tremor, past-pointing, dysmetria; 3) Vestibular ataxia - due to vestibular apparatus/nucleus lesions, accompanied by vertigo, nystagmus, falling to affected side; 4) Frontal ataxia - due to frontal lobe lesions causing gait apraxia. Differentiating features: sensory ataxia shows sensory loss and positive Romberg; cerebellar shows intention tremor and dysmetria; vestibular shows vertigo and nystagmus.

questions.text: Discuss briefly the effect of complete transection of spinal cord at mid thoracic level.
questions.explanation: Complete transection of the spinal cord at mid-thoracic level causes bilateral paralysis below the lesion. Immediate effects (spinal shock): 1) Flaccid paralysis of lower limbs; 2) Loss of all sensations below lesion; 3) Loss of reflex activity (areflexia); 4) Urinary retention; 5) Loss of bowel and bladder control; 6) Loss of temperature regulation below lesion. Delayed effects (after weeks, when spinal shock subsides): 1) Spastic paralysis below lesion (UMN signs: hyperreflexia, Babinski, spasticity); 2) Hyperactive bladder (spastic bladder); 3) Mass reflex (painful stimulus triggers flexor withdrawal with bladder emptying, sweating below lesion); 4) Autonomic dysreflexia (dangerous hypertension with baroreceptor reflex failure). The patient will have paraplegia and sensory loss below the umbilicus level.
questions.keyConcept: Mid-thoracic transection causes initial flaccid paralysis (spinal shock), followed by spastic paralysis with autonomic dysreflexia.

questions.text: Outline the process of normal speech & Differentiate between: Aphasia & Dysarthria.
questions.explanation: Normal speech production involves: 1) Formulation - Broca's area plans what to say; 2) Semantic processing - Wernicke's area selects words; 3) Motor planning - premotor area plans articulatory movements; 4) Execution - motor cortex controls larynx, tongue, lips, respiratory muscles; 5) Feedback monitoring - cerebellum and sensory cortex monitor output. The speech chain includes: linguistic, psychoacoustic, and motor levels. Aphasia vs dysarthria: Aphasia is a disorder of language processing (difficulty with word selection, grammar, comprehension) due to cortical lesions, while dysarthria is a motor speech disorder (difficulty with articulation, prosody, voice) due to damage to motor pathways or muscles. In dysarthria, language comprehension is preserved but speech production is impaired. Dysarthria types: flaccid (LMN), spastic (UMN), ataxic (cerebellar), hypokinetic (parkinsonian), hyperkinetic (choreiform).
questions.keyConcept: Aphasia is a language disorder (word/sentence processing); dysarthria is a motor speech disorder (articulation production).

questions.text: Gliosis means:
questions.explanation: Gliosis is the proliferation of glial cells (particularly astrocytes) in response to CNS injury. It represents a protective/scarring response rather than true regeneration. Brain tissue cannot regenerate neurons, so gliosis forms a glial scar. Option A (regeneration) is wrong because neurons don't regenerate in CNS. Option B (necrosis) is the cause of gliosis, not gliosis itself. Option C (fibrosis) occurs in other tissues but not brain - brain forms glial (astrocytic) scars, not fibrous scars. The correct answer is D (None of the above) because gliosis specifically means proliferation of neuroglial cells as a response to CNS injury, which is neither regeneration nor fibrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Gliosis is astrocyte proliferation forming a glial scar in response to CNS injury, not true regeneration or fibrosis.

questions.text: Concerning synapses:
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are widely distributed in the CNS, not rare. Electric synapses are characterized by rapid transmission without delay, are bidirectional (not unidirectional), and do not use gap junctions in the typical chemical synaptic cleft.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses: neurotransmitter-based, drug-sensitive, unidirectional, wide distribution in CNS.
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse

questions.text: The mechanism of synaptic transmission includes:
questions.explanation: Ca++ ions enter the presynaptic terminal (not released from it) to trigger vesicle fusion. Presynaptic knobs release both excitatory and inhibitory transmitters. Transmitters cause either EPSPs or IPSPs. Excitatory transmitters cause depolarization (not hyperpolarization).
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic transmission: Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis; transmitter binds specific receptors causing EPSP or IPSP.
options: Ca++ ions are released from the presynaptic knob
Presynaptic knobs release only an excitatory transmitter
Chemical transmission causes development of only excitatory postsynaptic state
Excitatory transmitters hyperpolarize the postsynaptic membrane
The released transmitter combines with specific receptors on postsynaptic membrane

questions.text:
Pain produced by tissue damage is due to release of:

A) Excess norepinephrine.
B) ATP.
C) Kinins.
D) Heparin.
E) Dopamine.
questions.explanation: Kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) are released during tissue damage and are potent pain-producing substances. They sensitize nociceptors. ATP also contributes but kinins are the primary algogenic substance among these options.
questions.keyConcept: Pain mediators: bradykinin, histamine, serotonin, ATP, prostaglandins - released from damaged tissue.

questions.text:
A patient who has had destruction of somatic sensory area I on the left side will show:

A) Total lack of pain sensation on the same side:
B) Total lack of temperature sensation of the same side.
C) Inability to identify objects put in the left hand.
D) Astereognosis in the right hand.
questions.explanation: Destruction of the left somatic sensory area I causes astereognosis (inability to identify objects) in the RIGHT hand because sensory pathways cross. Total loss of sensation would require bilateral lesions. Wernicke's area (temporal) handles auditory comprehension.
questions.keyConcept: Contralateral sensory cortex destruction causes astereognosis in opposite hand; object identification requires cortical processing.

questions.text:
Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:

A) They are larger and more numerous than gamma neurons.
B) They supply extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.
C) Alpha in the lateral part of anterior horn is concerned with fine movements.
D) Alpha of flexors is dorsally present to alpha of extensors
E) All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit.
questions.explanation: Alpha motor neurons that supply a specific muscle do NOT represent one motor unit; a motor unit is one alpha motor neuron plus ALL the muscle fibers it innervates. Multiple alpha neurons contribute to each muscle. The statement is false because it contradicts the definition of motor unit.
questions.keyConcept: Motor unit = 1 α-motor neuron + all muscle fibers it innervates; one muscle has many motor units.

questions.text: +ve Babinski sign is NOT present in:
questions.explanation: A positive Babinski sign (dorsiflexion of hallux with fanning) is normal in infants before age 1 year due to immature corticospinal tracts. It indicates UMN lesion in adults. It IS present in LMNL, chronic UMNL, deep sleep, and coma.
questions.keyConcept: Babinski positive = UMN lesion in adults; normal in infants <1 year; negative in LMN lesions.

questions.text: Physiologically, an intact innervated muscle can normally be made to contract by stimulation of which of the following neurons innervating that muscle?
questions.explanation: Alpha motor neurons directly innervate extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers and are the final common pathway for muscle contraction. Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal fibers and adjust spindle sensitivity but cannot directly cause visible muscle contraction.
questions.keyConcept: α-motor neurons: final pathway for skeletal muscle contraction; γ-motor neurons: adjust spindle sensitivity.

questions.text: Secondary evoked potential is characterized by:

Consists of a small +ve followed by a small –ve wave.

questions.explanation: Language comprehension is a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, not the prefrontal association area. The prefrontal area handles working memory, decision-making, personality, abstract thinking, and storage of vocalization programs.
questions.keyConcept: Prefrontal functions: executive function, working memory, personality, decision-making. Language = temporal/parietal areas.

questions.keyConcept: Speech centers: Broca's (frontal), Wernicke's (temporal), auditory/visual association areas. Somatic sensory association is NOT required for speech.

questions.text: Sensory aphasia occurs with lesion in:
questions.explanation: Sensory aphasia occurs with lesion in Wernicke's area or auditory association area, causing poor comprehension and fluent but meaningless speech. Visual pathway lesions cause blindness; Broca's/Exner cause motor aphasia; tongue muscles cause dysarthria.

questions.text: Concerning learning:
questions.explanation: Sensitization occurs by presynaptic facilitation of sensory neurons.
