questions.keyConcept: Broca's/Exner's area: motor aphasia (difficulty producing speech). Wernicke's: sensory aphasia (difficulty understanding).

questions.text: Short-term memory is:
questions.explanation: Short-term memory involves transient synaptic modifications like increased neurotransmitter release. It is limited capacity, stored in hippocampal/prefrontal areas initially (not neocortex directly). It requires hours for cortical storage. Gene activation is for long-term memory.
questions.keyConcept: Short-term memory: transient synaptic changes, limited capacity (7±2 items), hippocampal. Long-term: structural changes, unlimited.
options: Stored after 2 hours from getting the information.
Brain capacity for it is unlimited.
Encoded and stored in the neocortex.
Due to transient synaptic modifications such as increased release of neurotransmitters.
Involves gene activation and protein synthesis

questions.text: Long-term memory is:
questions.explanation: Long-term memory involves gene activation, protein synthesis, and structural synaptic changes (not transient neurotransmitter release). Capacity is unlimited. Stored in neocortex eventually (not frontal lobe only). Hippocampus is for consolidation, not permanent storage.
questions.keyConcept: LTM: gene activation, protein synthesis, new synapses; unlimited capacity; stored in neocortex.
options: Stored immediately after getting the information.
Brain capacity for it is limited.
Encoded in hippocampus and stored in the frontal lobe.
Due to transient synaptic modifications such as increased release of neurotransmitters.
Involves gene activation and protein synthesis.

questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true regarding consolidation of memory:
questions.explanation: Consolidation takes much longer than 5 minutes - it can take hours to days. Consolidation is the conversion of STM to LTM through synaptic changes and takes time for structural modifications. Completed in 5 minutes is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Memory consolidation: conversion of STM to LTM; takes hours-days; requires protein synthesis.
options: It is the conversion of short-term memory to a long-term one.
Represents the time needed for the structural and functional synaptic changes to take place.
Increases and fastens by focusing and rehearsal.

questions.text: Mechanisms of long-term memory do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Transient synaptic modifications are characteristic of SHORT-term memory, not long-term. LTM mechanisms include increased presynaptic terminals, structural/functional synaptic changes, new synapses, and gene activation/protein synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: STM: transient changes. LTM: structural changes, new synapses, gene activation.

questions.text: Habituation:
questions.explanation: Habituation is decreased response to repeated benign stimuli due to decreased neurotransmitter release (not inactivation of postsynaptic Ca++ channels). It does not involve new synapse formation or operant conditioning (that's sensitization).
questions.keyConcept: Habituation: decreased transmitter release from sensory neurons → decreased response to benign stimuli.
options: Is the gradual increase in response in presence of a repeated stimulus.
Explained by gradual inactivation of Ca++ channels in the postsynaptic neuron.
Leads to the formation of new synapses.
Is due to gradual decrease in the neurotransmitter release in the involved pathway.

questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true about sensitization:
questions.explanation: Sensitization can last much longer than 60 seconds - it can persist for days in long-term sensitization. It does involve serotonergic facilitation, operates in both short and long-term memory, and is associated with noxious stimuli paired to benign ones.
questions.keyConcept: Sensitization: enhanced response to stimuli after noxious input; serotonergic facilitation; can be short or long-term.
options: A prolonged augmented response occurs when a noxious stimulus paired to a benign stimulus.
It is due to serotonin-induced facilitation.
It continues up to 60 seconds after removal of the stimulus.

questions.text: Post-tetanic facilitation:
questions.explanation: Post-tetanic facilitation is explained by Ca++ accumulation in the presynaptic terminal after rapid stimulation, leading to increased neurotransmitter release. It is not gradual loss (that's habituation), not continuation after stimulus removal (that's post-tetanic potentiation), and not basis of classical conditioning.
questions.keyConcept: Post-tetanic facilitation: Ca2+ accumulation → increased transmitter release → enhanced response during tetanus.
options: Is a gradual loss of response to a repeated benign stimulus.
The postsynaptic response continues as long as the presynaptic stimulation is maintained.
Explained by accumulation of Ca++ in the presynaptic neuron upon rapid short-term stimulation.
Is associated with decrease postsynaptic response after removal of presynaptic stimulation.
Is the basis of classical conditioning.

questions.text: In long-term depression:
questions.explanation: LTD (long-term depression) involves slow, prolonged low-frequency stimulation that decreases synaptic strength. LTP involves rapid repeated tetanic stimulation that increases strength. Sensitization involves noxious stimuli causing facilitation. Classic conditioning involves CS-US pairing.
questions.keyConcept: LTD: low-frequency stimulation → decreased transmission (cerebellum). LTP: high-frequency → increased transmission (hippocampus).
options: A rapid repeated brief stimulation leads to a persistent enhancement of response.
A slow, prolonged, low frequency stimulation leads to decrease strength of synaptic transmission.
A rapid tetanizing presynaptic stimulation leads to continuation of postsynaptic response after removal of the stimulus.
A noxious stimulus leads to presynaptic facilitation of a habituated pathway.
A continuous benign stimulus leads to gradual increase in response.

questions.text: Functions of the limbic system do NOT include:
questions.explanation: Olfactory perception and discrimination is primarily a function of the olfactory bulb and temporal lobe, not the limbic system. The limbic system controls feeding, maternal/sexual behaviors, emotions, water balance, and motivations.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic functions: emotions, motivation, feeding, sexual behavior, memory. Olfaction: olfactory bulb/piriform cortex.
options: Control of feeding, maternal & sexual behaviors.

questions.text: Define synapse
questions.explanation: A synapse is a specialized functional junction between two neurons (or a neuron and an effector) where information is transmitted via neurotransmitter release, allowing communication between electrically separate cells.
questions.keyConcept: Synapse definition and functional significance
questions.modelAnswer: It is the site of contact between 2 neurons with separate protoplasm (functional junction)

questions.text: Enumerate functions of synapses
questions.explanation: Synaptic functions include unidirectional impulse transmission, convergence (multiple inputs to one neuron for intensity encoding), divergence (one neuron to multiple targets), and are primary sites of drug action.
questions.keyConcept: Synaptic functions and signal processing
questions.modelAnswer:
Transmission of impulses
Convergence of impulse: Collection of Impulses — intensity of impulses (intensification)
Divergence of impulses: spreading of impulses
The site of action of drugs

questions.text: Compare between chemical synapse & electric synapse regarding Def. & Characteristics
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses use neurotransmitter release and receptor activation for unidirectional, slower, drug-sensitive transmission; electrical synapses use gap junctions for bidirectional, faster signaling with no drug sensitivity.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical vs electrical synapse characteristics
questions.modelAnswer:
Chemical synapse
Def. Occur by release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic terminal (terminal button) traverse the synaptic cleft & affect postsynaptic membrane
Characteristics: Less common, Unidirectional, Less fast, Drug sensitive, Excitatory or inhibitory
Electric synapse
Def. Occur by passage of ions & small molecules through gap junction between 2 adjacent cells
Characteristics: More common, Bidirectional, Faster, No drug sensitivity, Excitatory only

questions.text: Illustrate the mechanism of chemical neurotransmission in synapses
questions.explanation: Chemical neurotransmission involves calcium-dependent neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, ion channel modulation, postsynaptic potential changes, and subsequent neurotransmitter removal via reuptake, degradation, or diffusion.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanism of chemical synaptic transmission
questions.modelAnswer:
Release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic knob
NT crosses the cleft.
Combines with its specific receptor on postsynaptic membrane.
Changes the RMP of postsynaptic membrane by opening or closing channels.
Removal of NT.

questions.text: List the ways of removal of NT
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are removed from the synaptic cleft by presynaptic reuptake (active transport), enzymatic degradation at postsynaptic membrane, or passive diffusion away from the synapse.
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitter removal mechanisms
questions.modelAnswer:
Active Reuptake by the presynaptic membrane
Inactivation by enzyme on postsynaptic membrane.
Passive diffusion away.

questions.text:
Define:
Neurohormone
Neuromodulator
Neurotransmitter
questions.explanation: A neurotransmitter is rapidly inactivated and acts briefly between neurons; a neuromodulator acts more slowly and long-term to alter synaptic effectiveness; a neurohormone is released into blood to act at distant targets.
questions.keyConcept: Distinction between neurotransmitter, neuromodulator, and neurohormone
questions.modelAnswer:
Neurohormone: A chemical substance secreted by a neuron into blood
Neuromodulator: A slowly inactivated (long acting) chemical substance secreted
Neurotransmitter: A chemical substance secreted by neurons to stimulate or inhibit other neurons

questions.text: Mention the sites of release of Acetyl choline
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine is released at CNS synapses (cortex, thalamus), all neuromuscular junctions, all autonomic preganglionic terminals, all postganglionic parasympathetic terminals, and some sympathetic terminals (sweat glands, skeletal muscle vessels).
questions.keyConcept: Acetylcholine release sites in nervous system
questions.modelAnswer:
Brain (cortex, thalamus)
NM junction
All preganglionic neurons
All postganglionic parasympathetic neurons
Some postganglionic sympathetic as sweat glands and blood vessels of skeletal muscles.

questions.text: Mention effects of Norepinephrine
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is generally excitatory on alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction) and inhibitory on beta-2 receptors (bronchodilation, vasodilation), producing complex tissue-specific effects depending on receptor distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Norepinephrine receptor-specific effects
questions.modelAnswer: Stimulatory on α1 receptors Inhibitory on β2 receptors

questions.text: What is the effect of GABA?
questions.explanation: GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through GABA-A receptors to increase chloride ion influx, causing membrane hyperpolarization and neuronal inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: GABA inhibitory neurotransmission mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: Inhibitory, by increasing the influx of Cl- causing hyperpolarization

questions.text: Enumerate properties of receptors
questions.explanation: Receptors have specificity for particular stimuli, demonstrate adequate stimulus, exhibit variable sensitivity, show adaptation (phasic vs tonic), generate graded potentials, and have low threshold for activation.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor properties and adequate stimulus
questions.modelAnswer: Properties of receptors include: 1) Specificity (receptors are sensitive to a specific form of energy called the adequate stimulus). 2) Transduction (conversion of stimulus energy into generator/receptor potentials). 3) Adaptation (reduction in firing rate during constant stimulation, classified as rapidly or slowly adapting). 4) Threshold (minimum stimulus intensity needed to evoke a response). 5) Sensory coding (intensity, duration, localization, and modality are encoded by frequency, receptor type, and fiber projection).

questions.text: Illustrate mechanism of receptors adaptation
questions.explanation: Receptor adaptation involves sodium channel inactivation during sustained stimulation, reducing generator potential amplitude; rapidly adapting receptors have quickly inactivating channels while slowly adapting ones maintain depolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanism of receptor adaptation
questions.modelAnswer: Receptor adaptation occurs when a sustained stimulus produces a progressive decrease in generator potential amplitude despite constant stimulus intensity. Mechanisms include: 1) Inactivation or closure of ion channels responsible for the receptor potential. 2) Opening of potassium channels that hyperpolarize the receptor membrane. 3) Structural changes in the receptor capsule that reduce mechanical transduction (e.g., Pacinian corpuscle lamellae filter sustained pressure). 4) Inactivation of voltage-gated calcium channels at the sensory nerve terminal.

questions.text: Explain paradoxical cold sensation
questions.explanation: Paradoxical cold sensation occurs when skin temperature drops below 10C, activating cold receptors (normally activated at 10-40C) at the same time warm receptors are inhibited, creating the sensation of cold.
questions.keyConcept: Paradoxical cold sensation mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: Paradoxical cold sensation occurs when a warm stimulus applied to a cold spot (an area of skin rich in cold receptors) is perceived as cold. This happens because certain cold receptors can be stimulated not only by cold but also by very warm temperatures. The incorrect temperature perception arises from the specific pattern of nerve fiber activation rather than from true thermoreceptor specificity.

questions.text: Mention the mechanism of stimulation of pain receptors.
questions.explanation: Pain receptors (nociceptors) are stimulated by intense mechanical/thermal/chemical stimuli that cause tissue damage, releasing bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, and prostaglandins that sensitize and activate nociceptors.
questions.keyConcept: Nociceptor stimulation mechanisms
questions.modelAnswer: Pain receptors (nociceptors) are stimulated by: 1) Mechanical injury (deformation, pressure, stretching). 2) Thermal injury (extreme heat >45°C or extreme cold). 3) Chemical mediators released from damaged tissue (bradykinin, histamine, prostaglandins, substance P, hydrogen ions, potassium ions). 4) Ischemia leading to accumulation of acidic metabolites. Some nociceptors are polymodal and respond to multiple stimuli.

questions.text: Compare between nuclear bag fibers & nuclear chain fibers
questions.explanation: Nuclear bag fibers have central nuclei (multiple nuclei aggregated in fiber center), detect dynamic stretch, and innervated by large gamma motor neurons; nuclear chain fibers have elongated nuclei, detect static stretch, and innervated by smaller gamma neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Intrafusal fiber types and functions
questions.modelAnswer: Nuclear bag fibers are larger, have more nuclei clustered in an expanded central bag region, are more elastic, and respond primarily to dynamic stretch (rate of change in length). Nuclear chain fibers are smaller, have nuclei arranged in a linear chain, are less elastic, and respond mainly to static stretch (sustained length). Nuclear bag fibers signal muscle velocity, while nuclear chain fibers signal muscle position.

questions.text: What is coma?
questions.explanation: Coma is a state of unarousable unconsciousness where the person cannot be awakened by sensory stimuli, caused by bilateral cerebral hemisphere dysfunction or damage to ascending reticular activating system.
questions.keyConcept: Coma definition and causes
questions.modelAnswer: Unconsciousness from which the person cannot be aroused

questions.text: What is sleep?
questions.explanation: Sleep is a reversible physiological state of unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by sufficient stimulation, distinct from coma which is unarousable.
questions.keyConcept: Sleep definition and distinction from coma
questions.modelAnswer: Physiological and spontaneous unconsciousness from which a person can be aroused by stimuli

questions.text: What is the role of the piriform cortex in smell?
questions.explanation: The piriform cortex is the primary olfactory cortex responsible for perception and discrimination of odor quality, receiving direct input from the olfactory bulb via the lateral olfactory tract.
questions.keyConcept: Piriform cortex olfactory function

questions.text: What is the role of the enterorhinal cortex in smell?
questions.explanation: The enterorhinal cortex (area 28) is the major gateway for neocortical information to hippocampus, critical for forming and retrieving olfactory memories and spatial memory.
questions.keyConcept: Enterorhinal cortex memory function

questions.text: What is the role of normal limbic system in maternal & sexual behavior?
questions.explanation: Normal limbic system function is essential for maternal behavior (nurturing and bonding) and proper sexual behavior, with the medial preoptic area and limbic circuits coordinating these instinctual behaviors.
questions.keyConcept: Limbic system and reproductive behaviors

questions.text: What factors can modify sexual behavior?
questions.explanation: Sexual behavior is modified by multiple factors including prefrontal cortex (executive control), social/cultural influences, psychological state, hormones, and olfactory cues acting through the limbic system.
questions.keyConcept: Multifactorial control of sexual behavior

questions.text: Concerning synapses, which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are the most common type in the CNS and are susceptible to modulation by neurotransmitters, drugs, and toxins. Electrical synapses allow direct ionic coupling and are bidirectional.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical synapses are the predominant CNS synapse type and are targetable by drugs unlike electrical synapses.
options: Chemical synapses are not widely distributed in CNS.
Electric synapses are characterized by delayed transmission.
Electric synapse is a unidirectional synapse.
Chemical synapses are affected by many drugs and chemicals.

questions.text: Muscle tone is NOT reduced in the following condition:
questions.explanation: Parkinsonism is characterized by rigidity (lead-pipe or cogwheel), which represents increased muscle tone. UMNL lesions, cerebellar lesions, and tabes dorsalis all reduce muscle tone.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonism uniquely preserves or increases muscle tone, unlike other neurological conditions that cause hypotonia.

questions.text: The ankle jerk is exaggerated:
questions.explanation: In Parkinsonism, the ankle jerk is exaggerated due to increased muscle tone and rigidity affecting the stretch reflex arc. UMNL lesions, cerebellar lesions, and spinal transection initially cause hyporeflexia.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonism increases stretch reflex excitability, resulting in exaggerated tendon jerks despite normal peripheral nerve function.
options: Immediately after complete transection of spinal cord at mid-thoracic region.
On the right side after damage in the left internal capsule.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of the prefrontal association area?
questions.explanation: The prefrontal association area mediates working memory, decision-making, personality, and language (Broca's area handles speech production). Primary motor control resides in the primary motor cortex, not prefrontal area.
questions.keyConcept: The prefrontal cortex subserves executive functions and working memory, not direct motor execution.

questions.text: Contralateral representation of face and body is found in:
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory and motor cortices have contralateral representation (homunculus). The face representation is in the lateral hemisphere near the Sylvian fissure, while body representation is medial near the longitudinal fissure.
questions.keyConcept: Cortical representation is somatotopically organized with contralateral control for both motor and sensory functions.

questions.text: Postsynaptic inhibition in the CNS is primarily mediated by which neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on GABA-A receptors to cause chloride influx and hyperpolarization.
questions.keyConcept: GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, mediating most fast synaptic inhibition.

questions.text: Which statement best describes sensory adaptation?
questions.explanation: Sensory adaptation is the decrease in receptor response during sustained stimulation. Slowly adapting receptors maintain response to prolonged stimuli, while rapidly adapting receptors quickly cease firing.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory adaptation reflects receptor capability to maintain (slow) or reduce (rapid) firing during sustained stimuli.
options: Diminished sensation despite continuous application of the stimulus
Complete absence of sensation after brief stimulus
Activation of additional receptors over time
Conversion of one type of sensation into another

questions.text: Discrimination of stimulus intensity depends mainly on:
questions.explanation: Weber-Fechner law states that discrimination of stimulus intensity depends on the ratio of change to initial stimulus, not absolute difference. Just noticeable difference is proportional to the initial stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Intensity discrimination depends on proportional Weber fraction rather than absolute stimulus magnitude.

questions.text: Which explains areas with low two-point discrimination threshold?
questions.explanation: Areas with low two-point discrimination threshold (high resolution) like fingertips have higher cortical representation in the sensory homunculus. Smaller receptive fields and greater receptor density enable finer discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: Two-point discrimination inversely correlates with receptive field size and cortical magnification factor.
options: Less convergence of afferent nerve fibers
More convergence of afferent nerve fibers

questions.text: Which statement regarding sensory fiber conduction is correct?
questions.explanation: Sensory fiber conduction velocity correlates with fiber diameter: A-delta fibers (5-15 m/s) transmit fast pain; C fibers (0.5-2 m/s) transmit slow pain. Myelination increases conduction velocity.
questions.keyConcept: Conduction velocity in sensory fibers depends on diameter and myelination: A-delta > C fibers.
options: Crude touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Fine touch is carried on C fibers
Fine touch is carried on Aδ fibers
Vibration sense is carried on Aδ fibers
Nociceptive stimuli are carried on Aβ fibers

questions.text: Which type of pain is transmitted by Aδ nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers transmit fast, sharp, well-localized pain (first pain) via the neospinothalamic tract. C fibers transmit slow, dull, poorly localized pain (second pain) via the paleospinothalamic tract.
questions.keyConcept: A-delta fibers mediate fast, localized pain; C fibers mediate slow, diffuse pain.

questions.text: Sudden increase in skin temperature above 50 °C leads to:
questions.explanation: Heat above 50C stimulates thermal nociceptors (via TRPV1 channels) causing burning pain. Temperatures above 45C begin to activate pain receptors, with noxious heat stimulating C and A-delta fibers.
questions.keyConcept: TRPV1 receptors on nociceptors respond to temperatures above 43-45C, triggering burning pain sensation.
options: Transient impulses due to damage of cold receptors above 40 °C

questions.text: Which substance stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Bradykinin, substance P, histamine, prostaglandins, and serotonin are all algogenic substances that stimulate nociceptors and cause pain when released during tissue injury or inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Algogenic substances (bradykinin, prostaglandins, substance P) sensitize and activate nociceptors.

questions.text: Which nerve fibers transmit warm temperature sensation?
questions.explanation: Warm temperature sensation (30-45C) is transmitted by C fibers via the lateral spinothalamic tract to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamic nucleus, then to sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Warm receptors are C fiber thermoreceptors projecting via spinothalamic tract to VPL thalamus.

questions.text: Fast pain is characterized by which duration?
questions.explanation: Fast pain (A-delta fibers) has a brief duration (~0.1 seconds), occurring immediately after stimulus and enabling rapid localization of noxious stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain is brief (~0.1s) and well-localized due to A-delta fiber conduction.

questions.text: Which clinical sign is seen in chronic gastritis due to inflammation of the stomach wall?
questions.explanation: Chronic gastritis causing inflammation of the stomach body (where parietal cells are located) leads to loss of intrinsic factor and reduced acid production, resulting in pernicious anemia with neurological manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: Parietal cell destruction in body gastritis causes intrinsic factor deficiency and pernicious anemia.

questions.text: Acupuncture relieves pain mainly by:
questions.explanation: Acupuncture relieves pain primarily by stimulating A-beta fibers that activate descending inhibitory pathways from PAG to nucleus raphe magnus, releasing endogenous opioids.
questions.keyConcept: Acupuncture activates descending inhibitory pathways via A-beta fiber stimulation and endogenous opioid release.
options: Gate control theory and psychogenic excitation
Blockade of sodium channels in sensory nerves

questions.text: Deep pain is typically characterized by:
questions.explanation: Deep pain (visceral or deep somatic) is poorly localized, often aching or cramping, and may be referred to distant dermatomes. It is transmitted by C fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pain is dull, poorly localized, and may be referred due to convergence of deep and superficial afferents.
options: Rapidly conducted by Aδ fibers only

questions.text: Which is a cause of extracranial headache?
questions.explanation: Temporomandibular joint dysfunction is a cause of extracranial headache. Intracranial causes include meningitis, tumor, or vascular events.
questions.keyConcept: TMJ dysfunction and muscle tension are common extracranial headache causes originating from pericranial structures.

questions.text: The initial phase of a migraine attack is associated with which vascular event?
questions.explanation: The initial phase of migraine involves cortical spreading depression followed by vasoconstriction causing the aura. Later phases involve vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation.
questions.keyConcept: Migraine starts with cortical spreading depression and vasoconstriction (aura), followed by vasodilation causing headache.

questions.text: Stereognosis sensation is carried by which neural pathway?
questions.explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of form and texture) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway for fine touch and proprioception to reach the sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries stereognosis, fine touch, and proprioception for object recognition.

questions.text: Facilitation of stretch reflex is done by:
questions.explanation: Facilitation of stretch reflex is achieved by gamma motor neurons that contract intrafusal fibers, increasing spindle sensitivity and reflex excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons facilitate stretch reflex by contracting intrafusal fibers and enhancing spindle discharge.

questions.text: Oscillating, interrupted voluntary movements typically occur due to loss of which function?
questions.explanation: Loss of cerebellar function causes decomposition of movement and dysmetria. Oscillating interrupted movements (intention tremor) occur due to loss of coordination and timing.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesions cause intention tremor from loss of coordination and timing of voluntary movements.

questions.text: A patient presents with hypertonia, exaggerated reflexes, and signs of an UMN lesion. Which mechanism best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: An UMN lesion causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, and loss of superficial reflexes. The clasp-knife response is a characteristic feature.
questions.keyConcept: UMN syndrome includes spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, and loss of superficial reflexes with clasp-knife response.

questions.text: Which function is attributed to the pontine circuit in motor control?
questions.explanation: Pontine reticulospinal tracts facilitate extensor tone and antigravity muscles, important for posture and righting reflexes. They are part of the medial descending systems.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine reticulospinal tract facilitates extensor muscles for postural control and righting.
options: Storage of plan of skilled movement

questions.text: Which pattern of sensory loss is characteristic of peripheral neuritis?
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuritis causes stocking-glove sensory loss (distal symmetric loss) affecting all sensory modalities due to length-dependent axonal degeneration.
questions.keyConcept: Peripheral neuritis produces symmetric distal sensory loss in stocking-glove distribution from length-dependent neuropathy.

questions.text: In syringomyelia, sensory loss typically follows which pattern?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape' or 'jacket' distribution sensory loss due to the expansion of the syrinx affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia cord lesion pattern

questions.text: Which brain structure is typically damaged in left‑sided hemiballismus?
questions.explanation: Hemiballismus results from damage to the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, causing violent flinging movements of the opposite side of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Subthalamic nucleus lesions

questions.text: Glutamate is secreted by:
questions.explanation: Corticostriatal fibers (cortex to corpus striatum) use glutamate as their neurotransmitter, providing the major excitatory input to the striatum.
questions.keyConcept: Corticostriatal projection

questions.text:
The following sensation is not perceived by Somatosensory A 1:
A. Crude Touch.
B. Fast pain.
C. Vibration sense.
D. Proprioceptive sensation.
E. Stereognosis.
questions.explanation: Crude touch is transmitted by the anterior spinothalamic tract, not by somatosensory area 1 which processes fine/discriminative touch, vibration, proprioception, and stereognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 does not process crude touch (anterior spinothalamic does).

questions.text:
A high school student was trying to solve a math problem. Which of the following is the expected brain EEG waves in this case?
A. Alpha waves
B. Beta waves
C. Theta waves
D. Delta waves
E. Gamma waves
questions.explanation: Gamma waves (30-100 Hz) are associated with high-level cognitive processing and appear during complex problem-solving tasks requiring focused attention.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma waves: present during active problem-solving and cognitive tasks.

questions.text:
The memory of a sequence of events in which a person participated is called:
A. Semantic memory
B. Episodic
C. Implicit
D. Procedural
E. Conditional
questions.explanation: Episodic memory records personal experiences organized in time sequence (autobiographical memory), allowing recall of events in which one actively participated.
questions.keyConcept: Episodic memory: memory of personal events in sequence.

questions.text:
Semantic memory is characterized by which of the following?
A. It is the memory of personal events
B. A type of implicit memory
C. It is the memory of facts
D. It is non-declarative memory
E. It is a procedural memory
questions.explanation: Semantic memory is explicit/declarative memory for facts and knowledge about the world (general facts), distinct from episodic memory (personal events) and procedural memory (skills).
questions.keyConcept: Semantic memory: memory of facts (general knowledge).
options: It is the memory of personal events
It is the memory of facts

questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during the upstroke of the action potential. Na+ channels open rapidly causing an influx of Na+, creating the spike. K+ is responsible for repolarization during the downstroke.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium ion influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels is responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential.

questions.text: Discuss the physiological role of cortical motor function. The areas responsible for planning are premotor cortex (area 6) and supplemental motor area
questions.explanation: The cortical motor function involves multiple areas for movement planning and execution. Primary motor cortex (M1, area 4) is located in precentral gyrus and executes voluntary movements with contralateral representation (upside-down homunculus). Premotor cortex (area 6) plans movements based on sensory guidance and contains mirror neurons. Supplemental motor area (SMA, medial area 6) programs sequential movements and bilateral coordination. Key functions: 1) Planning voluntary movements; 2) Initiation of movement; 3) Coordination of bilateral movements; 4) Programming movement sequences; 5) Integration of sensory feedback for movement refinement. The premotor cortex receives visual and somatosensory information to guide movements externally, while SMA programs internally generated sequences.
questions.keyConcept: Motor planning involves premotor cortex (externally guided) and SMA (internally programmed sequences), executing via primary motor cortex.

questions.text: What is responsible for the conscious discrimination of odors?
questions.explanation: Conscious odor discrimination is mediated by the orbitofrontal and frontal neocortex, which receives processed olfactory information via thalamic relays, allowing identification and naming of odors.
questions.keyConcept: Neocortical olfactory discrimination
options: Lateral & VM hypothalamus, septum, Amygdala, thalamus & basal ganglia

questions.text: The supplementary motor area is primarily responsible for which function?
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) programs complex motor sequences and bimanual coordination, becoming active before voluntary movement initiation.
questions.keyConcept: SMA mediates motor sequence planning and bimanual coordination prior to primary motor cortex activation.
options: Control of complex movements of both hands

questions.text: Which structure is primarily responsible for the damping action that prevents tremors during voluntary movements?
questions.explanation: The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is responsible for the damping action that prevents overshoot and tremors during voluntary movements through its feedback loops.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar damping mechanism

questions.text:
The representational hemisphere is described by which one of the following?

questions.text: Compare the sensory manifestations of thalamic lesion with a lesion affecting the sensory cortex .Discuss thalamic syndrome.
questions.explanation: Thalamic syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) occurs with thalamic lesions affecting the VPL/VPM nuclei. Clinical features include: contralateral hemianaesthesia (loss of sensation), severe paroxysmal hemipain (thalamic pain), choreoathetosis, and transient hemiparesis. Unlike cortical lesions which preserve crude sensation but lose fine discrimination, thalamic lesions cause complete sensory loss including pain and temperature. The thalamus serves as the sensory relay station - it performs crude sensory processing and relays to cortex for fine discrimination. Cortical (SMI) lesions spare crude sensation but lose stereognosis, fine touch, and proprioceptive localization. Key difference: cortical lesions have 'loss of discriminatory sense only' while thalamic lesions have 'total sensory loss with thalamic pain'.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamic lesions cause total sensory loss with thalamic pain, while cortical lesions spare crude sensation but lose fine discrimination.

questions.text: Which sensory modality is primarily perceived at the level of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: Crude touch, pain, and temperature are primarily perceived at the thalamic level before cortical processing. Fine touch and proprioception require cortical (sensory cortex) discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamus serves as relay for crude sensory modalities; cortex refines discrimination for fine touch and proprioception.

questions.text: A cerebellar lesion is most likely associated with severe loss of equilibrium and drunken gait when the lesion involves:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the flocculonodular lobe causes severe equilibrium loss and drunken gait. Option D is correct. The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) receives vestibular input and controls balance. Lesions cause severe ataxia, especially of trunk and gait, with patients being unable to stand without support. The neocerebellum affects appendicular coordination, not truncal equilibrium primarily.
questions.keyConcept: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is essential for truncal stability and equilibrium.

questions.text: Regarding the cerebellum, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Cerebellum CAN initiate gross movements (Option B is INCORRECT). The cerebellum coordinates but does not initiate movements; the cerebrum initiates. Options A, C, D are true: cerebellum has reverberating circuits (via deep nuclei), prevents overshooting, and acts as a programmer for movements. The cerebellum fine-tunes motor commands but the cerebral cortex initiates voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum coordinates and refines motor commands but does not initiate voluntary movements.

questions.text: Patient with cerebellar lesion complains of the following except:

questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesions affect motor coordination (gait, speech, movement adjustment) but not autonomic functions.

questions.text: Which is NOT typically associated with a cerebellar lesion?

questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesions cause intention tremor, ataxia, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia; nystagmus is vestibular.

questions.explanation: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) is primarily concerned with equilibrium and balance, receiving input from the vestibular apparatus.

questions.text: Summarize functions of the semicircular canals, the utricle & the saccule?
questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus includes three semicircular canals (horizontal, superior, posterior) detecting angular acceleration/rotation, and two otolith organs (utricle and saccule) detecting linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity. Semicircular canals: each canal has an ampulla with crista containing hair cells. Endolymph movement during head rotation deflects the cupula, stimulating hair cells. The horizontal canal detects horizontal rotation; superior (anterior) canal detects rotation in the sagittal plane; posterior canal detects roll movements. Each canal works in push-pull pairs with the opposite canal. Utricle: detects horizontal linear acceleration (forward/backward movements) and head tilt in the lateral plane. Saccule: detects vertical linear acceleration (up/down movements) and head tilt in the sagittal plane. The vestibular nuclei integrate this information to maintain posture, balance, and coordinate eye movements (VOR).
questions.keyConcept: Semicircular canals detect angular acceleration; utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.

questions.text: Thiamine deficiency occurs most common with abuse of:
questions.explanation: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency most commonly occurs with chronic alcohol abuse. Alcoholics often have poor nutrition and impaired thiamine absorption/utilization. questions.text: Mention three different types of brain fuels
questions.explanation: The three main brain fuels are glucose, ketone bodies (β‑hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate), and lactate.
questions.keyConcept: The brain's primary energy sources are glucose, ketone bodies, and lactate, with glucose being the preferred fuel under normal conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: Three different types of brain fuels: (1) Glucose — the primary and preferred fuel for the brain under normal physiological conditions. It is metabolized via glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation to produce ATP. The brain consumes ~120 g of glucose per day (approximately 20% of body glucose utilization). Transport into the brain is via GLUT1 (endothelial cells) and GLUT3 (neurons). (2) Ketone bodies — β‑hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate become important brain fuels during prolonged fasting or carbohydrate restriction. They cross the BBB via monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1/2) and are metabolized in mitochondria via ketolysis. Can supply up to 60–70% of brain energy needs during starvation. (3) Lactate — increasingly recognized as an important brain fuel, particularly during exercise or ischemia. It is transported via MCTs and converted to pyruvate for oxidation. Lactate shuttling between astrocytes and neurons (astrocyte‑neuron lactate shuttle) is important for brain energy metabolism.

questions.text: Compare in three points between the metabolism in neurons and astrocytes.
questions.explanation: Neurons rely primarily on oxidative phosphorylation for energy, have fewer mitochondria and lower glycolytic enzyme expression, while astrocytes rely more on glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen (aerobic glycolysis).
questions.keyConcept: Neurons favor oxidative metabolism with numerous mitochondria; astrocytes preferentially use glycolysis even under aerobic conditions.
questions.modelAnswer: Three points comparing neuronal and astrocytic metabolism: (1) Glycolytic rate — astrocytes have a higher glycolytic rate than neurons (aerobic glycolysis), producing lactate even with adequate oxygen. Neurons have lower glycolytic enzyme expression (e.g., low PKM2) and depend more on glucose oxidation. This difference is linked to astrocytes' role in glycogen storage and the astrocyte‑neuron lactate shuttle. (2) Mitochondrial density and function — neurons have abundant mitochondria with high oxidative capacity suited to their high and constant ATP demand. Astrocytes have fewer mitochondria. Neurons are highly vulnerable to mitochondrial dysfunction (explaining selective neuronal loss in mitochondrial diseases). (3) Substrate preference — neurons preferentially oxidize glucose and lactate (not fatty acids) due to the blood‑brain barrier's limited fatty acid transport and neurons' limited β‑oxidation capacity. Astrocytes can metabolize a broader range of substrates including glycogen, glutamate (via glutamate dehydrogenase), and fatty acids.

questions.text: Why neurons make Slower glycolytic rate than astrocytes “Mention one cause”
questions.explanation: Neurons have a slower glycolytic rate than astrocytes primarily because they rely on oxidative phosphorylation for most of their ATP and express low levels of key glycolytic enzymes like pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2).
questions.keyConcept: Neurons have a slower glycolytic rate than astrocytes primarily due to their low expression of glycolytic enzymes and reliance on oxidative phosphorylation.
questions.modelAnswer: Cause of neurons' slower glycolytic rate compared to astrocytes: Neurons express low levels of the M2 isoform of pyruvate kinase (PKM2), which is the key rate‑limiting enzyme of glycolysis. PKM2 is replaced by the more active PKM1 in neurons (adult isoform), making glycolysis less active. Additionally, neurons have fewer glycolytic enzyme complexes and store less glycogen. Neurons are predominantly oxidative, with their glycolytic pathway serving mainly to support biosynthetic intermediates rather than ATP production. Astrocytes, in contrast, retain PKM2 and have robust aerobic glycolysis, converting glucose to lactate even under fully oxygenated conditions — a feature linked to their role in maintaining brain energy homeostasis and supporting neuronal function.

questions.text: Mention three examples of monoamines act as neurotransmitters.
questions.explanation: Dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and serotonin (5‑HT) are the three main monoamine neurotransmitters.
questions.keyConcept: The three monoamine neurotransmitters are dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin.
questions.modelAnswer: Three examples of monoamine neurotransmitters: (1) Dopamine — synthesized from tyrosine → L‑DOPA → dopamine by aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase (AADC). Acts on D1–D5 GPCRs. Functions: motor control (nigrostriatal pathway), reward (mesolimbic pathway), cognition (mesocortical pathway), prolactin inhibition (tuberoinfundibular pathway). Depleted in Parkinson's disease; excess in schizophrenia (positive symptoms). (2) Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) — synthesized from dopamine via dopamine β‑hydroxylase (requires vitamin C and copper). Acts on α1, α2, β1, β2 GPCRs. Functions: arousal, attention, stress response (locus coeruleus), blood pressure regulation. (3) Serotonin (5‑hydroxytryptamine, 5‑HT) — synthesized from tryptophan → 5‑hydroxytryptophan → 5‑HT by tryptophan hydroxylase (rate‑limiting) and AADC. Acts on 5‑HT1–5‑HT7 receptor families (GPCRs and ligand‑gated ion channels). Functions: mood regulation, sleep, appetite, pain modulation, thermoregulation. Implicated in depression (deficiency), anxiety, and migraine.

questions.text: Illustrate the rate limiting reaction of GABA synthesis and mention the name of vitamin needed in synthesis.
questions.explanation: GABA is synthesized from glutamate via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis rate is limited by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) which requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
questions.modelAnswer: Rate limiting reaction of GABA synthesis: Glutamate + H+ → GABA + CO2, catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), a pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)‑dependent enzyme. PLP is the active form of vitamin B6. GAD has two isoforms — GAD65 (pLPS‑dependent, localized to nerve terminals, responsible for rapid GABA production for neurotransmission) and GAD67 (constitutively active, involved in GABA synthesis for metabolic functions). The reaction requires glutamate as substrate (produced from glucose via astrocytic pyruvate carboxylation and neuronal transamination) and CO2 as product. Inhibitors of GAD (e.g., allylglycine) cause convulsions by blocking GABA synthesis.

questions.text: Illustrate the rate limiting reaction of catecholamine synthesis and mention its regulation.
questions.explanation: The rate‑limiting step of catecholamine synthesis is the conversion of tyrosine to L‑DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase, which is regulated by feedback inhibition, phosphorylation, and neural activity.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate‑limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, regulated by feedback inhibition and phosphorylation.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate limiting reaction of catecholamine synthesis: Tyrosine + O2 + NADPH → L‑DOPA + H2O, catalyzed by tyrosine hydroxylase (TH). Regulation: (1) Feedback inhibition — dopamine and norepinephrine inhibit TH activity at physiological concentrations. (2) Phosphorylation — TH is activated by phosphorylation at multiple serine residues via PKA, Ca2+/calmodulin‑dependent protein kinase (CaMKII), and MAP kinase pathways; phosphorylation decreases the enzyme's affinity for its tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cofactor and increases Vmax. (3) Long‑term regulation — nerve impulse activity increases TH gene expression via CREB phosphorylation. (4) BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) is an essential cofactor. Subsequent steps: L‑DOPA → dopamine (DOPA decarboxylase, requiring PLP/vitamin B6) → norepinephrine (dopamine β‑hydroxylase, requiring vitamin C and Cu2+) → epinephrine (phenylethanolamine N‑methyltransferase, requiring SAM).

questions.text: Mention the name of two enzymes used in catecholamine catabolism and mention the name of end product of epinephrine catabolism
questions.explanation: Catecholamine catabolism uses COMT and MAO; the end product of epinephrine catabolism is metanephrine and ultimately vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine catabolism involves MAO and COMT; epinephrine's end product is VMA (vanillylmandelic acid).
questions.modelAnswer: Two enzymes used in catecholamine catabolism: (1) Monoamine oxidase (MAO) — a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)‑containing enzyme located on the outer mitochondrial membrane. MAO‑A preferentially deaminates serotonin and norepinephrine; MAO‑B deaminates dopamine and phenylethylamine. Products: H2O2, NH3, and corresponding aldehydes (e.g., 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylacetaldehyde from dopamine). (2) Catechol‑O‑methyltransferase (COMT) — transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosylmethionine (SAM) to one of the phenolic hydroxyl groups of catecholamines, inactivating them. Products: e.g., normetanephrine from norepinephrine, metanephrine from epinephrine. End product of epinephrine catabolism: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) — formed from further metabolism of metanephrine via MAO and COMT; VMA is measured clinically as a urinary marker for pheochromocytoma.

questions.text: Give a short account on mechanism of action of α-methyl dopa.
questions.explanation: α‑Methyl dopa (methyldopa) is a centrally acting antihypertensive that is metabolized to α‑methyl norepinephrine, which acts as a false neurotransmitter at central α2‑adrenergic receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa acts as a false neurotransmitter at central α2‑receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow from the brainstem.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism of action of α‑methyl dopa: (1) α‑Methyl dopa enters the brain and is converted to α‑methyl norepinephrine (α‑MeNE) by dopamine β‑hydroxylase in the same pathway as endogenous norepinephrine synthesis. (2) α‑MeNE is a false neurotransmitter — it is stored in and released from synaptic vesicles instead of norepinephrine, but has lower potency at α‑adrenergic receptors. (3) In the brainstem (rostral ventrolateral medulla), α‑MeNE activates central presynaptic α2‑adrenergic autoreceptors more potently than norepinephrine, leading to profound reduction in sympathetic nervous system outflow. (4) Decreased sympathetic tone → reduced peripheral vascular resistance, heart rate, and blood pressure. (5) Also thought to reduce plasma renin activity and form false neurotransmitters peripherally. Note: Despite its central mechanism, it does not cross the BBB well, which limits its site of action to areas with an imperfect BBB.

questions.text: Name the tumor marker of pheochromocytoma.
questions.explanation: The tumor marker for pheochromocytoma is urinary or plasma metanephrines (and VMA).
questions.keyConcept: Pheochromocytoma is diagnosed biochemically by measuring urinary/ plasma free metanephrines and VMA.
questions.modelAnswer: Tumor marker of pheochromocytoma: The primary tumor markers are (1) Plasma free metanephrines (metanephrine and normetanephrine) — measured by liquid chromatography‑tandem mass spectrometry (LC‑MS/MS); most sensitive test. (2) 24‑hour urinary fractionated metanephrines — high sensitivity and specificity. (3) Urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) — less sensitive but specific. (4) Plasma chromogranin A — supportive marker. These markers reflect catecholamine metabolism by the tumor. Imaging (CT/MRI, I‑123 MIBG scan) follows biochemical confirmation for tumor localization.

questions.text: Name the tumor marker of carcinoid tumor “argintaffinoma”.
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors (argentaffinomas) produce serotonin; the tumor marker is urinary 5‑HIAA.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid tumor marker is urinary 5‑HIAA (5‑hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the serotonin metabolite.
questions.modelAnswer: Tumor marker of carcinoid tumor (argentaffinoma): Urinary 5‑hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5‑HIAA) — the primary biochemical marker. 5‑HIAA is the main metabolite of serotonin (5‑HT), which is synthesized and secreted by carcinoid tumors. Testing: 24‑hour urine collection for 5‑HIAA; dietary restrictions (avoid tryptophan‑rich foods: bananas, pineapples, walnuts) for 3 days before collection. Additional supportive markers: (1) Plasma chromogranin A — elevated in most neuroendocrine tumors including carcinoids; useful for monitoring disease progression. (2) Urinary serotonin — less specific. (3) Plasma serotonin — measured by platelet serotonin assay. Note: Some carcinoid tumors (foregut) may not produce 5‑HIAA as they lack the decarboxylase enzyme.

questions.text: Mention three causes of melatonin deficiency.
questions.explanation: Melatonin deficiency can result from aging, circadian rhythm disruption (shift work, jet lag), and insufficient light exposure during the day.
questions.keyConcept: Melatonin deficiency is caused by aging, circadian rhythm disorders, and insufficient exposure to natural daylight.
questions.modelAnswer: Three causes of melatonin deficiency: (1) Aging — melatonin secretion from the pineal gland declines significantly with age, with peak levels decreasing and circadian rhythm becoming less robust. Elderly individuals produce markedly lower melatonin, contributing to insomnia and circadian disturbances. (2) Circadian rhythm disorders — shift work, jet lag, irregular sleep schedules, and delayed sleep phase disorder disrupt the normal melatonin secretion pattern (which normally rises in darkness). Suppression or mistiming of melatonin release leads to deficiency during intended sleep periods. (3) Insufficient light exposure during the day and/or excessive light exposure at night — bright light (especially blue wavelength) in the evening suppresses melatonin secretion; inadequate bright light during daytime reduces the amplitude of the circadian rhythm, leading to suboptimal nighttime melatonin levels.

questions.text: Name the amino acids and coenzymes needed in serotonin synthesis
questions.explanation: Serotonin synthesis requires the amino acid tryptophan and the coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis requires tryptophan as the amino acid precursor and pyridoxal phosphate (PLP/vitamin B6) as the coenzyme.
questions.modelAnswer: Amino acid needed: L‑tryptophan (essential amino acid from dietary protein). Enzyme and coenzyme: Tryptophan hydroxylase (rate‑limiting enzyme, requiring tetrahydrobiopterin BH4 as cofactor) converts tryptophan → 5‑hydroxytryptophan (5‑HTP). Then aromatic L‑amino acid decarboxylase (AADC, requiring pyridoxal phosphate PLP as cofactor) converts 5‑HTP → serotonin (5‑hydroxytryptamine, 5‑HT). Note: PLP is the active form of vitamin B6. Dietary vitamin B6 deficiency reduces AADC activity, lowering serotonin synthesis.

questions.text: Name the amino acids, enzymes and coenzymes needed in Histamine synthesis
questions.explanation: Histamine synthesis requires the amino acid histidine and the enzyme histidine decarboxylase with pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine synthesis requires L‑histidine and histidine decarboxylase, which needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
questions.modelAnswer: Amino acid: L‑histidine. Enzyme: Histidine decarboxylase (HDC) — a PLP‑dependent enzyme that converts L‑histidine → histamine (by removing CO2). Coenzyme: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, active form of vitamin B6). Histidine decarboxylase is found in mast cells, basophils, enterochromaffin‑like cells, and neurons. Note: PLP is the cofactor for all amino acid decarboxylases including AADC (for dopamine, serotonin, and trace amines), DOPA decarboxylase, and histidine decarboxylase — explaining why vitamin B6 deficiency reduces synthesis of multiple neurotransmitters.

questions.text: Name the amino acids, enzymes and coenzymes needed in NO synthesis
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthesis requires the amino acid L‑arginine and the enzyme nitric oxide synthase (NOS) with NADPH, oxygen, and various cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: NO synthesis from L‑arginine requires nitric oxide synthase (NOS) and multiple cofactors including NADPH, FAD, FMN, tetrahydrobiopterin, and heme.
questions.modelAnswer: Amino acid: L‑arginine. Enzyme: Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) — three isoforms: eNOS (endothelial), nNOS (neuronal), and iNOS (inducible, activated by cytokines). Cofactors and co‑substrates: (1) NADPH — electron donor. (2) FAD and FMN — in the reductase domain of NOS. (3) Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) — required for coupling oxygen activation. (4) Heme — binds O2 in the oxygenase domain. (5) Calmodulin — required for eNOS and nNOS activity (iNOS is calcium‑independent). Reaction: L‑arginine + O2 + NADPH → L‑citrulline + NO + NADP+. Two-step mechanism: (1) N‑hydroxylation of guanidino nitrogen of arginine. (2) Oxidation to citrulline and NO.

questions.text: Mention two examples of purely ketogenic amino acids, and two examples of mixed.
questions.explanation: Purely ketogenic amino acids are leucine and lysine; mixed amino acids that are both ketogenic and glucogenic include isoleucine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, and tyrosine.
questions.keyConcept: Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic; isoleucine, tryptophan, phenylalanine, and tyrosine are mixed (ketogenic and glucogenic).
questions.modelAnswer: Purely ketogenic amino acids (yield only acetyl-CoA/ketone bodies, no glucose): (1) Leucine - degraded to acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA exclusively. (2) Lysine - degraded to acetoacetyl-CoA. Mixed amino acids (both ketogenic and glucogenic): (1) Isoleucine - yields both acetyl-CoA (ketogenic) and succinyl-CoA (glucogenic). (2) Tyrosine - yields fumarate (glucogenic) and acetoacetate (ketogenic). (3) Phenylalanine - yields fumarate (glucogenic) and acetoacetate (ketogenic). (4) Tryptophan - yields alanine (glucogenic) and acetyl-CoA/nicotinamide (ketogenic).

questions.text: Illustrate a biochemical reaction of transamination and mention the coenzyme needed.
questions.explanation: Transamination transfers an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid, catalyzed by aminotransferases with pyridoxal phosphate as cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Transamination is an amino group transfer reaction catalyzed by PLP-dependent aminotransferases.
questions.modelAnswer: Biochemical reaction of transamination: An amino acid (e.g., L-alanine) + an alpha-keto acid (e.g., alpha-ketoglutarate) <=> a new keto acid (e.g., pyruvate) + a new amino acid (L-glutamate). Catalyzed by aminotransferases with pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) as the essential coenzyme. PLP forms a Schiff base with the amino acid substrate, enabling reversible transfer of the amino group. Key aminotransferases: ALT (alanine aminotransferase) - alanine + alpha-ketoglutarate <=> pyruvate + glutamate (liver). AST (aspartate aminotransferase) - aspartate + alpha-ketoglutarate <=> oxaloacetate + glutamate (heart, liver, skeletal muscle). The nitrogen from transamination enters the glutamate pool for the urea cycle. Coenzyme: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, active form of vitamin B6).

questions.text: Illustrate a biochemical reaction of L- glutamate dehydrogenase and mention the coenzyme needed and regulation.
questions.explanation: L-glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia, using NAD+ or NADP+ and requiring ADP as activator and GTP as inhibitor.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate, regulated by GTP (inhibitor) and ADP (activator).
questions.modelAnswer: Biochemical reaction of L-glutamate dehydrogenase: L-glutamate + NAD(P)+ + H2O -> alpha-ketoglutarate + NAD(P)H + H+ + NH3. This is the major pathway for intracellular glutamate deamination and ammonia generation. Coenzyme: NAD+ or NADP+. Regulation: (1) GTP - allosteric inhibitor; energy-rich state suppresses ammonia production. (2) ADP - allosteric activator; energy-depleted state stimulates glutamate oxidation. (3) Leucine - allosteric activator. Significance: GDH is central to nitrogen metabolism - it channels nitrogen from amino acid catabolism into the urea cycle. The reaction is reversible, allowing glutamate synthesis from alpha-ketoglutarate during ammonia detoxification in astrocytes.

questions.text: Illustrate a biochemical reaction of non-oxidative deamination.
questions.explanation: Non-oxidative deamination of amino acids involves dehydration reactions (serine/threonine dehydratases) that remove nitrogen without redox change, using PLP as cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Non-oxidative deamination removes the amino group without oxidation via PLP-dependent dehydratases.
questions.modelAnswer: Biochemical reaction of non-oxidative deamination: Primarily seen with serine and cysteine. (1) Serine dehydratase (PLP-dependent): Serine -> pyruvate + NH3. The reaction involves dehydration followed by deamination, producing pyruvate and ammonia without requiring NAD+. (2) Cysteine desulfhydrase (PLP-dependent): Cysteine -> pyruvate + H2S + NH3. (3) Threonine dehydratase (PLP-dependent): Threonine -> alpha-ketobutyrate + NH3. Key features: (1) Does NOT use NAD+ or NADP+ (unlike oxidative deamination). (2) PLP is the coenzyme. (3) No redox change occurs - the amino group is removed without oxidation of the carbon skeleton. (4) The ammonia produced is channeled to glutamate dehydrogenase or glutamine synthetase for safe disposal.

questions.text: Illustrate two biochemical reactions that produce ammonia
questions.explanation: Two biochemical reactions producing ammonia are the oxidative deamination of glutamate by glutamate dehydrogenase and the deamination of AMP by AMP deaminase.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia is produced by glutamate dehydrogenase and AMP deaminase, among other reactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Two biochemical reactions that produce ammonia: (1) Oxidative deamination by L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH): L-glutamate + NAD(P)+ + H2O -> alpha-ketoglutarate + NAD(P)H + H+ + NH3. This is the primary source of ammonia in most tissues. GDH is allosterically regulated (activated by ADP, inhibited by GTP). (2) AMP deaminase (purine nucleotide cycle): AMP + H2O -> IMP + NH3. This reaction is important in skeletal muscle during intense exercise, contributing to ammonia production. The ammonia produced is converted to glutamine (by glutamine synthetase) or enters the urea cycle. Other ammonia sources: bacterial urease in the gut, and the intestinal mucosa via glutaminase activity.

questions.text: Mention three different sources of ammonia.
questions.explanation: Three sources of ammonia are: amino acid catabolism (transamination and oxidative deamination), purine nucleotide breakdown (AMP deamination), and gut bacterial metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia arises from amino acid catabolism, purine catabolism, and gut bacterial metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer: Three different sources of ammonia: (1) Amino acid catabolism (deamination) - the primary source. Oxidative deamination of glutamate by glutamate dehydrogenase. Aminotransferase reactions transfer amino groups to glutamate, which is then deaminated. Non-oxidative deamination of serine/threonine. Monoamine oxidase (MAO) deaminates biogenic amines (dopamine, serotonin) producing NH3. (2) Purine nucleotide catabolism - AMP deaminase converts AMP -> IMP + NH3 (important in skeletal muscle). Guanine deaminase converts guanine -> xanthine + NH3. (3) Gut bacterial metabolism - bacterial urease splits urea -> CO2 + 2 NH3. Also, bacterial deamination of unabsorbed amino acids. This accounts for 30-40% of daily urea turnover. The intestinal mucosa also contributes via glutaminase activity.

questions.text: Illustrate how ammonia is eliminated by the brain.
questions.explanation: The brain eliminates ammonia primarily by converting it to glutamine via glutamine synthetase in astrocytes, which is then transported to the liver and kidneys for disposal.
questions.keyConcept: The brain eliminates ammonia by converting it to glutamine in astrocytes, which is then exported for urea synthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: How ammonia is eliminated by the brain: The brain cannot perform the urea cycle (lacks all six urea cycle enzymes), so it converts ammonia to glutamine for safe transport. Process: (1) Glutamine synthetase (GS) - located in astrocytes, this enzyme catalyzes: Glutamate + NH3 + ATP -> glutamine + ADP + Pi + H2O. This is the primary ammonia detoxification pathway in the CNS. (2) Glutamine is released into the bloodstream and transported to the liver (via the portal circulation) and kidneys. (3) In the liver, glutamine is metabolized by glutaminase to regenerate glutamate and NH3, which enters the urea cycle for excretion. (4) In the kidneys, glutamine is deamidated to release NH3, which is excreted in urine as NH4+ (acid-base regulation). Clinical significance: Hyperammonemia (e.g., liver failure) causes brain edema because excess NH3 inhibits glutamine synthetase and glutamate transporters, leading to osmotic swelling of astrocytes.

questions.text: Illustrate the rate limiting step of urea cycle and its regulation.
questions.explanation: The rate-limiting step of the urea cycle is the synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate from NH3 and CO2 by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), which requires N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an obligatory activator.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, activated by N-acetylglutamate (NAG) derived from glutamate and acetyl-CoA.
questions.modelAnswer: Rate limiting step of the urea cycle: CPS I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) catalyzes: NH3 + CO2 + 2 ATP -> carbamoyl phosphate + 2 ADP + Pi. Location: Mitochondrial matrix. Regulation: N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is an obligatory positive allosteric activator of CPS I. NAG is synthesized from acetyl-CoA + glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS). NAG synthesis is stimulated when glutamate concentrations are high (e.g., after amino acid catabolism), ensuring the urea cycle is activated when nitrogen load increases. Inhibition: NAG deficiency (e.g., in NAGS deficiency) causes hyperammonemia. NAGS is activated by arginine - elevated when the urea cycle needs to be active. Upregulation: High protein diet, catabolic states increase NAG and CPS I activity.

questions.text: Mention two relationships between urea cycle and citric acid cycle.
questions.explanation: The urea and citric acid cycles are linked by fumarate (shared intermediate) and by the aspartate-argininosuccinate relationship.
questions.keyConcept: The urea and citric acid cycles are interconnected through fumarate and the aspartate-argininosuccinate relationship.
questions.modelAnswer: Two relationships between the urea cycle and citric acid cycle: (1) Fumarate as a shared intermediate - Argininosuccinate lyase in the urea cycle cleaves argininosuccinate to produce arginine and fumarate. Fumarate enters the citric acid cycle (via fumarase -> malate -> oxaloacetate), linking the two cycles directly. This is clinically relevant: in argininosuccinate lyase deficiency (ASAuria), fumarate accumulates, potentially affecting CAC function. (2) Aspartate-argininosuccinate relationship - In the urea cycle (mitochondrial): aspartate + citrulline -> argininosuccinate (catalyzed by argininosuccinate synthetase). Aspartate is an intermediate of the CAC (derived from oxaloacetate via transamination). Conversely, argininosuccinate lyase produces fumarate, linking to the CAC. The malate-aspartate shuttle also depends on CAC intermediates, supporting energy production while facilitating nitrogen disposal.

questions.text: Why increase ammonia is very toxic to brain “mention two causes”
questions.explanation: Elevated ammonia is neurotoxic because it depletes brain energy stores (inhibiting the CAC) and causes astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema via glutamine accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia neurotoxicity results from CAC inhibition and astrocyte swelling due to glutamine accumulation.
questions.modelAnswer: Two causes of ammonia neurotoxicity in the brain: (1) Inhibition of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle and depletion of energy stores - Ammonia directly inhibits key enzymes of the CAC, particularly alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (alpha-KGDH) and pyruvate dehydrogenase. Excess ammonia shifts glutamate toward glutamine formation, depleting alpha-ketoglutarate. The resulting energy failure impairs astrocyte function, neurotransmitter reuptake, and ion homeostasis. Additionally, ammonia stimulates glycolysis but impairs the use of pyruvate in the CAC, leading to ATP depletion. (2) Astrocyte swelling and cerebral edema - Ammonia causes osmotic swelling of astrocytes by: (a) Direct osmotic effect of glutamine accumulation (glutamine synthetase converts glutamate + NH3 -> glutamine, but glutamine accumulates in astrocytes and is osmotically active). (b) Glutamine-induced mitochondrial permeability transition, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). (c) Disruption of glutamate transporters (EAAT1/2), reducing glutamate reuptake and causing extracellular glutamate accumulation (excitotoxicity). Astrocyte swelling increases intracranial pressure, causing cerebral edema and hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.text: Name the defective enzyme in maple syrup disease.
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease is caused by a deficiency of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDH), which normally decarboxylates leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
questions.modelAnswer: Defective enzyme in maple syrup disease: Branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDH) - a multienzyme mitochondrial complex requiring thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, the active form of thiamine/B1) as a cofactor. This enzyme normally catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs): (1) Leucine -> acetoacetate. (2) Isoleucine -> acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. (3) Valine -> propionyl-CoA. In MSUD, BCKDH deficiency causes accumulation of BCAAs and their corresponding alpha-keto acids in blood, urine, and tissues. Clinical features: Characteristic maple syrup odor of urine, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, neurological deterioration, seizures, developmental delay, coma and death if untreated. Management: Dietary restriction of BCAAs, thiamine supplementation (if variant form), and liver transplantation in classic severe forms.

questions.text: Mention the name of three biochemical reactions need vitamin B1.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is required as thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) by three key biochemical reactions: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B1 (as TPP) is essential for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
questions.modelAnswer: Three biochemical reactions requiring vitamin B1 (as thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP): (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex - converts pyruvate -> acetyl-CoA (link reaction between glycolysis and the citric acid cycle). Requires TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, and FAD/NAD+. Deficiency blocks entry of pyruvate into the CAC, shunting pyruvate to lactate (lactic acidosis in B1 deficiency). (2) Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex - converts alpha-ketoglutarate -> succinyl-CoA in the CAC. Similar cofactor requirements to pyruvate dehydrogenase. Important for nitrogen metabolism via glutamate. (3) Transketolase - in the pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative phase). Catalyzes transfer of a 2-carbon unit between sugar phosphates. Transketolase activity in erythrocytes is used as a functional test for thiamine status (low activity indicates B1 deficiency).

questions.text: Mention two Biochemical tests of thiamine status
questions.explanation: Two biochemical tests for thiamine status are the erythrocyte transketolase activity assay and urinary thiamine excretion measurement.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine status is assessed by erythrocyte transketolase activity and urinary thiamine/TPP excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Two biochemical tests of thiamine status: (1) Erythrocyte transketolase activity (ETKA) - functional assay. Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway. In thiamine deficiency, erythrocyte transketolase activity is reduced. The test measures enzyme activity with and without added TPP in vitro. The TPP effect (percentage increase in activity when TPP is added) indicates the degree of deficiency: less than 15% = normal; 15-25% = marginal deficiency; greater than 25% = significant deficiency. This is the most sensitive functional test for B1 deficiency. (2) Urinary thiamine excretion - reflects recent dietary intake. Low urinary thiamine (less than 100 micrograms/24h) indicates deficiency. However, this reflects acute intake rather than tissue stores. Less reliable than transketolase assay because it fluctuates with recent dietary intake. Additional test: Blood thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) level via HPLC - direct but expensive.

questions.text: Illustrate the biochemical reaction of pyruvate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, requiring five cofactors: thiamine TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+.
questions.keyConcept: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is a multi-enzyme complex requiring TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+ to convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
questions.modelAnswer: Biochemical reaction of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH complex): Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA-SH + TPP + lipoic acid -> Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ + CO2. Location: Mitochondrial matrix. The PDH complex consists of three enzymatic components: (1) Pyruvate decarboxylase (E1) - requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP); decarboxylates pyruvate to hydroxyethyl-TPP. (2) Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2) - requires lipoic acid (covalently attached); transfers the acetyl group to CoA, generating acetyl-CoA and leaving reduced lipoic acid. (3) Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3) - requires FAD (from riboflavin) and NAD+ (from niacin); reoxidizes reduced lipoic acid back to its oxidized form, producing NADH. Regulation: Product inhibition by NADH and acetyl-CoA. Covalent regulation by PDH kinase (inhibits via phosphorylation) and PDH phosphatase (activates via dephosphorylation). Allosteric activation by pyruvate and ADP. Clinical significance: Thiamine deficiency (beriberi) causes accumulation of pyruvate and lactic acidosis due to impaired PDH function.

questions.text: Mention the name of two diseases from thiamine deficiency.
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (CNS) and wet beriberi (cardiovascular) as the two major disease manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (CNS) and wet beriberi (cardiovascular disease) primarily.
questions.modelAnswer: Two diseases from thiamine deficiency: (1) Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome - CNS manifestation of thiamine deficiency. Wernicke encephalopathy (acute): Classic triad - ophthalmoplegia (or nystagmus), ataxia, and confusion. Due to impaired glucose metabolism in brainstem and thalamic nuclei (mammillary bodies). Can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (chronic) - anterograde and retrograde amnesia, confabulation, personality changes. Most common in chronic alcoholics. (2) Wet beriberi - cardiovascular manifestation. High-output cardiac failure with peripheral vasodilation causing cardiomegaly, tachycardia, peripheral edema, and warm extremities. Due to impaired ATP production in cardiac muscle. Can rapidly progress to heart failure. (3) Dry beriberi - peripheral neuropathy with sensory and motor deficits (purely neurological, no cardiac involvement). All forms respond to thiamine replacement.

questions.text: Mention three causes and three symptoms of pellagra “niacin deficiency”
questions.explanation: Pellagra (niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency) results from dietary deficiency or conditions impairing tryptophan-to-niacin conversion; it presents with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
questions.keyConcept: Pellagra results from niacin deficiency and presents with the 3 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
questions.modelAnswer: Three causes of pellagra: (1) Dietary deficiency - inadequate intake of niacin and tryptophan. Common in populations relying heavily on corn (maize), as niacin in corn is bound and poorly bioavailable. (2) Malabsorption - conditions causing fat malabsorption reduce absorption of niacin and tryptophan. (3) Carcinoid syndrome - tumor diverts tryptophan away from niacin synthesis toward serotonin production, causing functional niacin deficiency. Hartnup disease is a genetic condition impairing tryptophan absorption. Other causes: chronic alcoholism, isoniazid therapy. Three symptoms: (1) Dermatitis - photosensitive dermatitis, particularly on sun-exposed areas (Casals necklace around the neck, or affecting hands and feet), with pigmented rash. (2) Diarrhea - inflammatory diarrhea due to mucosal atrophy. (3) Dementia - confusion, disorientation, and cognitive decline progressing to frank psychosis and death if untreated (the 4th D = death without treatment).

questions.text: Give a short account on two folate analogues “antagonists”.
questions.explanation: Two folate analogues are methotrexate and trimethoprim, which inhibit dihydrofolate reductase and thereby block purine and thymidylate synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Methotrexate and trimethoprim are folate antagonists inhibiting DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Two folate analogues (antagonists): (1) Methotrexate - a structural analogue of folic acid. It competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking conversion of dihydrofolate (DHF) to tetrahydrofolate (THF). This depletes all folate cofactors needed for: purine synthesis (via 10-formyl THF), thymidylate synthesis (via 5,10-methylene THF), and amino acid interconversions. Result: Impaired DNA and RNA synthesis, particularly affecting rapidly dividing cells. Used in: cancer chemotherapy (high dose), autoimmune diseases (low dose), ectopic pregnancy. Toxicity: myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity. Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescues from toxicity.
