(2) Trimethoprim - a folate antagonist that selectively inhibits bacterial DHFR (50,000x more potent against bacterial than human DHFR). Used in combination with sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) for UTI, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and other infections.

questions.text: Mention two different sources and two fates of methylene.
questions.explanation: Methylene (CH2) groups are derived from serine and glycine catabolism, and are consumed primarily in thymidylate synthesis and the methionine synthase reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Methylene (CH2) is derived from serine/glycine and is consumed primarily in dTMP synthesis and the folate cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Two different sources of methylene (CH2): (1) Serine - the primary source. Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) catalyzes: Serine + THF -> glycine + N5,N10-methylene THF. Serine provides the beta-carbon as the methylene group. This is the main source of one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis. (2) Glycine - also donates one-carbon units via its cleavage to CO2 + NH3 + N5,N10-methylene THF (by glycine cleavage enzyme system or SHMT in reverse). Two different fates of methylene: (1) Thymidylate synthesis - N5,N10-methylene THF donates both a methyl group and reducing power to convert dUMP -> dTMP (catalyzed by thymidylate synthase). This is the main fate of methylene THF and the basis of 5-fluorouracil chemotherapy. THF is oxidized to DHF in this reaction. (2) Methionine synthase reaction - methylene THF (as N5-methyl THF) donates its methyl group to homocysteine (via methionine synthase, requiring B12) to regenerate methionine. This is the only reaction that removes methylated THF from the folate pool.

questions.text: Mention two different sources of methenyl and formyl.
questions.explanation: Methenyl and formyl groups in one-carbon metabolism are derived from serine catabolism and from the catabolism of tryptophan and histidine.
questions.keyConcept: Methenyl and formyl groups derive from serine, tryptophan, and histidine catabolism, feeding into purine and formyl-Met-tRNA synthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Two different sources of methenyl: (1) Serine catabolism - N5,N10-methylene THF (from serine via SHMT) can be oxidized to N5,N10-methenyl THF by serine hydroxymethyltransferase in reverse or by methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase (MTHFD). Methenyl THF is an intermediate in the conversion of formyl groups to methylene groups and vice versa. (2) Tryptophan catabolism - the kynurenine pathway produces N-formylkynurenine, which generates one-carbon units at the formyl and methenyl oxidation levels. Two different sources of formyl: (1) Histidine catabolism - the catabolism of L-histidine produces N-formimino glutamate, which transfers a formyl group to THF (generating N10-formyl THF) via the formiminotransferase reaction. (2) Purine ring biosynthesis - N10-formyl THF provides two separate formyl groups for the synthesis of the purine ring (at positions C2 and C8 of the purine nucleus). These formyl groups are transferred by transformylases (GAR transformylase and AICAR transformylase) during de novo purine synthesis. Additionally, mitochondrial protein synthesis requires formyl-methionine (fMet) for the initiator tRNA.

questions.text: Which of the following may be measured in 24-hour urine to diagnose carcinoid syndrome (argentaffinoma, serotonin-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome (serotonin-secreting tumor) is diagnosed by measuring 5-Hydroxyindole-acetic acid (5-HIAA) in 24-hour urine - this is the main serotonin metabolite. 5-HIAA is elevated in carcinoid tumors. VMA is for pheochromocytoma. Phenylacetylglutamine is a phenylalanine metabolite.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid diagnosis: 24-hour urine 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite). VMA = catecholamine metabolite (pheochromocytoma).

questions.text: Which of the following may serve as a tumor marker?
questions.explanation: Both VMA (vanillylmandelic acid) and 5-HIAA can serve as tumor markers - VMA for neuroblastoma/pheochromocytoma, and 5-HIAA for carcinoid tumors. Phenylpyruvic acid is not a tumor marker.
questions.keyConcept: Tumor markers: VMA (neuroblastoma/pheochromocytoma), 5-HIAA (carcinoid). Both can be measured.

questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is Important for synthesis of both epinephrine and melatonin?
questions.explanation: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AAAD) converts 5-HTP to serotonin (for melatonin synthesis) and DOPA to dopamine (for epinephrine synthesis). This enzyme is required for both pathways, making it the shared enzyme.
questions.keyConcept: AAAD: converts 5-HTP→serotonin (→melatonin) and DOPA→dopamine (→norepinephrine→epinephrine).

questions.text: Catecholamines
questions.explanation: Catecholamines include dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. They function both as neurotransmitters (in the CNS and autonomic nervous system) and as hormones (epinephrine from adrenal medulla). Both statements (a) and (b) are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamines (dopamine, NE, E): both neurotransmitters and hormones. Synthesized from tyrosine.

questions.text: All of the following are ketogenic Amino acids except:
questions.explanation: Glycine is a glucogenic amino acid, not ketogenic. Leucine and isoleucine are purely ketogenic. Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic. Lysine is also purely ketogenic. Glycine is converted to serine (glucogenic) or to porphyrins.
questions.keyConcept: Purely ketogenic: leucine, lysine. Both glucogenic/ketogenic: isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan. Glucogenic: glycine, alanine, serine.

questions.text: The main sites for oxidative deamination are:
questions.explanation: Oxidative deamination (conversion of amino acids to keto acids with release of ammonia) occurs mainly in the LIVER and KIDNEY. These organs have the enzyme glutamate dehydrogenase. Other tissues lack significant oxidative deamination capacity.
questions.keyConcept: Oxidative deamination: liver and kidney (glutamate dehydrogenase). Produces ammonia for urea cycle.

questions.text: The urea cycle is active in cases of
questions.explanation: The urea cycle is active during protein intake (to excrete excess nitrogen) and during fasting (when protein breakdown increases to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis). Both conditions increase nitrogen waste that must be excreted as urea.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle: active during high protein intake and fasting (increased amino acid catabolism).

questions.text: The major end product of protein nitrogen metabolism in man is:
questions.explanation: Urea is the major end product of protein nitrogen metabolism in humans, produced exclusively in the liver via the urea cycle. It is excreted by the kidneys. Ammonia is toxic and must be converted to urea. Uric acid is from purine metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Major nitrogen waste product: urea (from hepatic urea cycle). Ammonia is converted to urea.

questions.text: If there were complete absence of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, what would be the source of urea in the blood?
questions.explanation: With CPS-I deficiency, urea cannot be synthesized via the cycle. However, some urea is produced by bacterial action on ammonia in the gut (bacterial urease). The liver's arginase cannot produce urea without upstream cycle intermediates.
questions.keyConcept: CPS-I deficiency: some urea from bacterial urease in intestine, not from hepatic urea cycle.

questions.text: N-acetyl glutamate is an essential allosteric activator of:
questions.explanation: N-acetyl glutamate (NAG) is an essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS-I), the first enzyme of the urea cycle in mitochondria. NAG is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase.
questions.keyConcept: N-acetylglutamate: allosteric activator of CPS-I (first urea cycle enzyme). Synthesized from acetyl-CoA + glutamate.

questions.text: Which of the following increases with deficiency of any enzyme of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: When any urea cycle enzyme is deficient, ammonia cannot be efficiently converted to urea. Glutamine synthesis (via glutamine synthetase) increases as an alternative ammonia detoxification pathway, so glutamine levels increase.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle deficiency: increased glutamine (alternative ammonia detoxification). Citrulline may decrease.

questions.text: Which of the following may be true about the glutamine synthetase reaction in the brain?
questions.explanation: Glutamine synthetase in astrocytes converts glutamate + ammonia → glutamine. This normally detoxifies ammonia. At high ammonia, glutamate gets depleted, reducing GABA synthesis (since GABA is made from glutamate), causing neurological symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glutamine synthetase: detoxifies ammonia; depletes glutamate → reduced GABA → neurological dysfunction.
options: At high ammonia concentration, it can deplete glutamate, with consequent decrease of GABA.

questions.text: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is normally used for synthesis of GLUTAMINE (via glutamine synthetase in astrocytes). The brain uses this pathway to detoxify ammonia. Alanine synthesis occurs in liver (not brain). Glutamate is made from alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia but requires different enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Normal ammonia disposal in brain: glutamine synthetase (astrocytes) converts glutamate + NH3 → glutamine.

questions.text: Ammonia toxicity to the brain is Probably through which of the Following mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Ammonia toxicity primarily inhibits the citric acid cycle (energy production) by depleting alpha-ketoglutarate and glutamate. It does NOT increase GABA (it decreases it). It causes alkalosis (not acidosis). Brain can still use amino acids.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibits TCA cycle (depletes alpha-ketoglutarate), depletes glutamate → decreased GABA → neurological symptoms.
options: Inhibition of energy production in brain Cells.
Production of increased amounts of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA.
Acidifying effect on the intra- and extracellular fluids.
Conversion to urea, increasing the Osmotic pressure.
Inability of the brain cells to utilize any of the amino acids.

questions.text: Hyperammonemia may be caused by
questions.explanation: Primary hyperammonemia results from genetic defects in any urea cycle enzyme. Secondary hyperammonemia results from liver failure (inability to convert ammonia to urea). Both causes lead to ammonia accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonemia: primary (urea cycle enzyme defect) or secondary (liver failure). Both cause ammonia accumulation.
options: genetic defect of any enzyme of urea cycle (primary hyperammonemia).

questions.text: The symptom of ammonia intoxication includes.
questions.explanation: Ammonia intoxication primarily affects the brain, causing mental confusion, asterixis (liver flap), and eventually coma. It does not typically cause visual blurring, constipation, or diarrhea as primary symptoms.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia intoxication: brain dysfunction → mental confusion, asterixis, coma. Does not cause GI symptoms primarily.

questions.text: Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia Levels are.
questions.explanation: Ammonia intoxication symptoms occur when brain ammonia levels are INCREASED (elevated). Normal brain ammonia is kept very low by glutamine synthesis and urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia intoxication: occurs when brain ammonia levels are elevated, disrupting glutamate/GABA metabolism.

questions.text: Primary hyperammonemia may be treated by
questions.explanation: Primary hyperammonemia (urea cycle defects) is treated with: low-protein diet (reduce nitrogen load), benzoic acid/phenylacetate (alternative nitrogen excretion as conjugated amino acids), and acidification of intestinal lumen (to trap ammonia as NH4+ for excretion).
questions.keyConcept: Primary hyperammonemia treatment: low protein, alternative nitrogen excretion (benzoic acid, phenylacetate), gut ammonia trapping.
options: agents that increase excretion of Conjugated amino acids, e.g., benzoic acid and phenylacetate.
acidification of the intestinal lumen to help get rid of ammonia as ammonium Ions.

questions.text: Maple syrup urine disease is an inborn error of metabolism of:
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease involves defective metabolism of BRANCHED CHAIN AMINO ACIDS (leucine, isoleucine, valine) due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Accumulated metabolites give urine a maple syrup odor.
questions.keyConcept: Maple syrup urine disease: branched-chain amino acid metabolism defect (BCKDH deficiency).

questions.text: Phenylketonuria is caused by deficiency of
questions.explanation: PKU results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This deficiency prevents the normal metabolism of phenylalanine, leading to accumulation and conversion to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate).
questions.keyConcept: PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → converted to phenylketones → intellectual disability if untreated.
options: Conversion of phenylalanine to  a phenylketoacid.
Production of phenylalanine from  a phenylketoacid.
Reaction of phenylalanine with an α-ketoacid.
Conversion of phenylalanine to another aminoacid.

questions.text: Conversion of Phenylalanine to tyrosine is catalyzed by phenylalanine hydroxylase which requires.
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, along with oxygen and NADPH. BH4 is also required for tyrosine hydroxylase (dopamine synthesis) and tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin synthesis).
questions.keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase: requires BH4, O2, NADPH. BH4 deficiency causes malignant PKU.

questions.text: The major contributor to the one-carbon pool?
questions.explanation: Serine is the major contributor to the one-carbon pool through its conversion to glycine, releasing a methylene group (-CH2-). The methyl group can be transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming N5,N10-methylene-THF.
questions.keyConcept: One-carbon pool: serine → glycine transfers CH2 to THF. Also from histidine, tryptophan, methionine.

questions.text: Methionine is synthesized in human body from:
questions.explanation: Methionine is synthesized from homocysteine and serine via methionine synthase (requires B12) and other enzymes. The pathway involves converting homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate.
questions.keyConcept: Methionine synthesis: homocysteine + serine → methionine (requires B12, folate). Cysteine is made from serine + homocysteine separately.

questions.text: Hyper-homocysteinemia may result from deficiency of
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of pyridoxine (B6, needed for transsulfuration to cysteine), cobalamin (B12, needed for remethylation to methionine), or folic acid (needed for the folate cycle that donates methyl groups).
questions.keyConcept: Hyperhomocysteinemia: B6, B12, or folate deficiency → elevated homocysteine → cardiovascular risk, neurological issues.

questions.text: What is the rate limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, converting tyrosine to DOPA; it requires tetrahydropteridine and iron as cofactors and is subject to end-product inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase rate-limiting step
questions.modelAnswer: Tyrosine hydroxylase (or tyrosine 3-monooxygenase) is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis. It converts tyrosine to L-DOPA, requiring tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor. This step is irreversible and tightly regulated by feedback inhibition.

questions.text: What is the fate of catecholamines?
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are cleared by active reuptake into presynaptic nerve terminals (uptake-1 mechanism) and enzymatic hydrolysis by enzymes like MAO and COMT, preventing prolonged receptor activation.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine termination mechanisms
questions.modelAnswer:
Active uptake by sympathetic nerve endings
Enzymatic hydrolysis

questions.text: What enzymes cause the oxidative deamination and inactivation of catecholamines?
questions.explanation: Monoamine oxidase (MAO), found in mitochondrial membranes of presynaptic terminals, causes oxidative deamination and inactivation of catecholamines, producing corresponding aldehydes.
questions.keyConcept: MAO catecholamine inactivation
questions.modelAnswer: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) is the primary enzyme catalyzing oxidative deamination of biogenic amines, including catecholamines and serotonin. It is located on the outer mitochondrial membrane and uses FAD as a cofactor. MAO inhibitors (MAOIs) are used as antidepressants.

questions.text: What is the primary end product of dopamine inactivation?
questions.explanation: Dopamine is primarily inactivated to homovanillic acid (HVA) via combined MAO and COMT activity; CSF HVA levels are used clinically to assess dopamine turnover.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine metabolic end product
questions.modelAnswer: Dopamine is primarily inactivated to homovanillic acid (HVA) via combined MAO and COMT activity; CSF HVA levels are used clinically to assess dopamine turnover.

questions.text: What is the primary end product of epinephrine and norepinephrine enzymatic inactivation?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are metabolized primarily to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) via combined MAO and COMT pathways; 24-hour urinary VMA is diagnostic for pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine urinary metabolite VMA
questions.modelAnswer: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are metabolized primarily to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) via combined MAO and COMT pathways; 24-hour urinary VMA is diagnostic for pheochromocytoma.

questions.text: What is the neurotransmitter produced in the CNS, gastrointestinal tract & platelets?
questions.explanation: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is synthesized in CNS neurons (raphe nuclei), enterochromaffin cells of GI tract, and platelets, where it acts as a neurotransmitter, hormone, and local signaling molecule.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis sites
questions.modelAnswer: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is synthesized in CNS neurons (raphe nuclei), enterochromaffin cells of GI tract, and platelets, where it acts as a neurotransmitter, hormone, and local signaling molecule.

questions.text: What is the end product of serotonin degradation?
questions.explanation: Serotonin is degraded to 5-hydroxyindolacetic acid (5-HIAA) via MAO; urinary 5-HIAA measurement is used to diagnose carcinoid tumors that overproduce serotonin.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA
questions.modelAnswer: 5-hydroxyindolacetic acid (5-HIAA)

questions.text: What tumor is characterized by increased production of serotonin and decreased production of nicotinic acid?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid tumors (argentaffinomas) produce excessive serotonin, causing flushing, diarrhea, and cardiac disease; they also decrease nicotinic acid (vitamin B3) synthesis because serotonin diverts tryptophan away from niacin production.
questions.keyConcept: Carcinoid tumor and niacin deficiency
questions.modelAnswer: Carcinoid tumor (Argentaffinoma)

questions.text: What happens in Vitamin B6 deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 (PLP) is the coenzyme for glutamate decarboxylase; deficiency reduces GABA synthesis, causing neuronal hyperexcitability, seizures, and hyperactivity.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B6 and GABA synthesis
questions.modelAnswer: Reduction in GABA levels with signs of hyperactivity and convulsions

questions.text: What factors can lead to melatonin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Melatonin deficiency can result from cigarettes (nicotine), caffeine, frequent stress, antidepressant drugs, and beta-blockers, all of which suppress pineal melatonin secretion.
questions.keyConcept: Melatonin deficiency factors
questions.modelAnswer:
Cigarettes
Caffeine
Frequent stress
Antidepressants
ß-blocker

questions.text: How is histamine formed?
questions.explanation: Histamine is formed by pyridoxal phosphate (B6)-dependent decarboxylation of histidine, catalyzed by histidine decarboxylase, producing histamine and CO2.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylase histamine synthesis
questions.modelAnswer: Histamine is formed by decarboxylation of histidine in a reaction requiring PLP

questions.text: What is the role of histamine?
questions.explanation: Histamine mediates allergic inflammation, stimulates gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors, acts as a CNS neurotransmitter modulating arousal, and causes vasodilation via H1 receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine diverse functions
questions.modelAnswer:
Histamine mediates a wide range of cellular responses, including allergic and inflammatory reactions, gastric acid secretion
Act as a Neurotransmitter in CNS
Powerful vasodilator

questions.text: What is the function of histamine in the brain?
questions.explanation: In the brain, histamine functions as a neurotransmitter in the tuberomammillary nucleus projections, promoting wakefulness and arousal through H1 receptor activation.
questions.keyConcept: Histaminergic arousal system
questions.modelAnswer: Histamine acts as a Neurotransmitter in parts of the brain by mediating arousal.

questions.text: What is the neurotransmitters that act as vasodilator?
questions.explanation: Histamine and nitric oxide are the primary neurotransmitter vasodilators; histamine acts via H1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle while NO acts directly on vascular smooth muscle to cause relaxation.
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitter vasodilators
questions.modelAnswer: Histamine and nitric oxide are the primary neurotransmitter vasodilators; histamine acts via H1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle while NO acts directly on vascular smooth muscle to cause relaxation.

questions.text: How is nitric oxide synthesized?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), producing L-citrulline and NO; this requires NADPH, oxygen, and tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: NO synthase reaction from arginine
questions.modelAnswer: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine in a reaction catalyzed by nitric oxide synthase enzyme

questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is derived from tyrosine?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine is the amino acid precursor for catecholamine neurotransmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine), which are synthesized via tyrosine hydroxylase, DOPA decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, and PNMT.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine-derived catecholamines
questions.modelAnswer: Catecholamines (Dopamine, Norepinephrine, Epinephrine)

questions.text: Where are dopamine and norepinephrine synthesized?
questions.explanation: Dopamine and norepinephrine are synthesized in the brain (as CNS neurotransmitters) and in adrenal medulla chromaffin cells (mainly norepinephrine which is then methylated to epinephrine).
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine and norepinephrine synthesis sites
questions.modelAnswer: In the brain and function as neurotransmitters

questions.text: Epinephrine is synthesized in_________ and the primary end product in the adrenal medulla of newborns is _________
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized in the adrenal medulla from norepinephrine via phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT); in newborns, the primary catecholamine end product is norepinephrine due to immature PNMT activity.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal medulla epinephrine synthesis pathway

questions.text: What happens to epinephrine with advancing age?
questions.explanation: With advancing age, epinephrine production dramatically increases, largely dependent upon cortisol levels since cortisol induces PNMT expression in the adrenal medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Age-related epinephrine changes
questions.modelAnswer: Dramatically raised, depending upon cortisol levels

questions.text: What is histamine synthesized from? And What is the enzyme required for histamine synthesis?
questions.explanation: Histamine is synthesized from histidine by histidine decarboxylase, a PLP-dependent enzyme, producing histamine and CO2; this reaction is irreversible.
questions.keyConcept: Histidine decarboxylase histamine synthesis
questions.modelAnswer:
Histidine
Histidine decarboxylase

questions.text: The coenzyme required for histamine synthesis is_________ and cells secrete it is_________
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, active form of B6) is the required coenzyme for histamine synthesis via histidine decarboxylase; histamine is secreted by mast cells, basophils, and enterochromaffin cells.
questions.keyConcept: PLP coenzyme and mast cell histamine

questions.text: What are the major functions of histamine? (Name two)
questions.explanation: Major histamine functions include mediating Type I hypersensitivity (allergic reactions), stimulating gastric acid secretion via H2 receptors, and acting as a CNS neurotransmitter promoting arousal.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine inflammatory and CNS roles
questions.modelAnswer:
Mediating allergic and inflammatory reactions.
gastric acid secretion.
as a neurotransmitter in parts of the brain.

questions.text: How is nitric oxide synthesized? And What enzyme catalyzes the synthesis of nitric oxide?
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide is synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS) enzyme, producing NO and L-citrulline in a five-electron oxidation reaction requiring multiple cofactors.
questions.keyConcept: NO synthase and L-arginine conversion
questions.modelAnswer:
From L-arginine
Nitric oxide synthase

questions.text: What is glycine synthesized from? And what is the enzyme catalyzes its formation?
questions.explanation: Glycine is synthesized from serine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT), which transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate, forming glycine and N5,N10-methylene THF.
questions.keyConcept: Serine to glycine conversion
questions.modelAnswer:
Serine
Serine hydroxy-methyltransferase

questions.text: How is glycine removed from the synapse?
questions.explanation: Glycine is removed from the synaptic cleft by high-affinity sodium-dependent transporters (GlyT1 and GlyT2), allowing rapid termination of inhibitory signaling and recycling for neurotransmitter reuse.
questions.keyConcept: Glycine synaptic reuptake
questions.modelAnswer: Reuptake through high-affinity transporter

questions.text: What are the biogenic amines neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Biogenic amine neurotransmitters include acetylcholine (not technically a biogenic amine but often grouped) and the monoamines: catecholamines (dopamine, NE, E), serotonin (5-HT), and histamine.
questions.keyConcept: Biogenic amine classification
questions.modelAnswer: Biogenic amine neurotransmitters include: (1) Catecholamines: dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and epinephrine (adrenaline); (2) Indolamine: serotonin (5-HT); (3) Imidazoleamine: histamine. They are synthesized from aromatic amino acids and act on G-protein coupled receptors.

questions.text: What is the primary end product of catecholamine synthesis in the adrenal medulla?
questions.explanation: In the adrenal medulla, norepinephrine is the primary catecholamine end product; most norepinephrine is subsequently methylated to epinephrine by PNMT, but norepinephrine remains a major secreted product.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenal catecholamine end products
questions.modelAnswer: The principal end product of catecholamine synthesis in the urine is vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), formed by the combined actions of MAO and COMT on epinephrine and norepinephrine metabolites.

questions.text: What is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through GABA-A (ionotropic, Cl- channel) and GABA-B (metabotropic, G-protein coupled) receptors.
questions.keyConcept: GABA as main inhibitory neurotransmitter
questions.modelAnswer: GABA (Gamma Aminobutyric Acid)

questions.text: What is GABA derived from?
questions.explanation: GABA is derived from glutamic acid (glutamate) via decarboxylation catalyzed by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), a PLP-dependent enzyme; this is an irreversible reaction.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis from glutamate
questions.modelAnswer: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is derived from glutamate (glutamic acid) via decarboxylation by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), requiring pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.

questions.text: What are the classification of neurotransmitters based on functions?
questions.explanation: Based on function, neurotransmitters are classified as excitatory (causing depolarization/action potentials), inhibitory (causing hyperpolarization), or modulatory (altering neuronal sensitivity without direct excitation/inhibition).
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitter functional classification
questions.modelAnswer: Based on function, neurotransmitters are classified as excitatory (causing depolarization/action potentials), inhibitory (causing hyperpolarization), or modulatory (altering neuronal sensitivity without direct excitation/inhibition).

questions.text: What are examples of excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: Excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters include glutamate (principal excitatory NT in CNS) and aspartate, both acting through ionotropic (NMDA, AMPA, kainate) and metabotropic receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS. It acts on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors, mediating fast synaptic transmission, plasticity, and excitotoxicity. It is cleared by astrocytic uptake and converted to glutamine.

questions.text: What is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting through NMDA, AMPA, kainate, and mGluR receptors; excessive activity causes excitotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate as principal excitatory neurotransmitter
questions.modelAnswer: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS. It acts on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors, mediating fast synaptic transmission, plasticity, and excitotoxicity. It is cleared by astrocytic uptake and converted to glutamine.

questions.text: Where are neurotransmitters stored?
questions.explanation: Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles (secretory vesicles) at presynaptic terminals, either small clear vesicles (acetylcholine, amino acids) or large dense-core vesicles (catecholamines, peptides).
questions.keyConcept: Neurotransmitter vesicle storage
questions.modelAnswer: In secretory vesicles (synaptic vesicles) before release into the synaptic cleft

questions.text: What are the substrates for glutamate transaminase?
questions.explanation: Glutamate transaminase (GOT/AST) uses alpha-ketoglutarate and L-aspartate as substrates to produce glutamate and oxaloacetate in a reversible PLP-dependent transamination reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate transaminase substrates
questions.modelAnswer: The substrates for glutamate transaminase (GOT / aspartate aminotransferase) are glutamate and oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate), yielding aspartate and glutamate as products. It requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor and plays a key role in transamination reactions.

questions.text: How is ammonia utilized in the conversion of glutamate to glutamine?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is incorporated into glutamate by glutamine synthetase to form glutamine, consuming ATP; this is the primary mechanism for removing ammonia in the brain and preventing neurotoxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine synthetase ammonia fixation
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonia is used by glutamine synthetase to convert glutamate to glutamine

questions.text: Which amino acids can produce both glucose and ketone bodies?
questions.explanation: Tyrosine, phenylalanine, tryptophan, threonine, and isoleucine are glucogenic-amino acids that can be converted to pyruvate or TCA intermediates (producing glucose via gluconeogenesis) and also generate ketone body precursors.
questions.keyConcept: Glucogenic and ketogenic amino acids
questions.modelAnswer:
Tyrosine
phenylalanine
tryptophan
threonine
isoleucine

questions.text: What is the main pathway of deamination for amino acids?
questions.explanation: Transamination (via aminotransferases using PLP) is the major pathway for amino acid deamination, transferring the amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate, which then undergoes oxidative deamination by GDH.
questions.keyConcept: Transamination as main deamination pathway
questions.modelAnswer: The main pathway of deamination for amino acids is oxidative deamination, catalyzed by L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH). GDH converts glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and NH3, using NAD+ or NADP+ as coenzymes. The released NH3 enters the urea cycle for excretion.

questions.text: What is the function of D-AA oxidase flavoprotein?
questions.explanation: D-AA oxidase flavoprotein converts D-amino acids to alpha-keto acids by removing the amino group, eliminating the asymmetry of the alpha-carbon atom and producing a racemic mixture with L-forms.
questions.keyConcept: D-AA oxidase racemization function
questions.modelAnswer: Conversion of D-amino acids to the α-keto acid will remove the asymmetry of the α-carbon atom.

questions.text: What is the product of the transdeamination of glutamine?
questions.explanation: Transdeamination of glutamine involves glutamine transaminase (producing glutamate and alpha-keto glutaramate) followed by omega-amidase, ultimately yielding alpha-ketoglutarate as the carbon skeleton product.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine transdeamination product
questions.modelAnswer: The product of transdeamination of glutamine is glutamate. Glutaminase deamidates glutamine to glutamate and NH3 in the mitochondria. Glutamate then undergoes oxidative deamination by GDH, completing transdeamination and releasing ammonia for the urea cycle.

questions.text: What is the role of glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing ammonia and NAD(P)H; this is the key reaction linking amino acid metabolism with TCA cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamate dehydrogenase oxidative deamination
questions.modelAnswer: Conversion of glutamate to α-ketoglutarate.

questions.text: What is the major pathway of oxidative deamination?
questions.explanation: L-glutamate dehydrogenase is the major pathway for oxidative deamination of amino acids in mammals, converting L-glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate with production of ammonia and NAD(P)H.
questions.keyConcept: L-GDH as main oxidative deamination enzyme
questions.modelAnswer: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) is the primary enzyme catalyzing oxidative deamination of biogenic amines, including catecholamines and serotonin. It is located on the outer mitochondrial membrane and uses FAD as a cofactor. MAO inhibitors (MAOIs) are used as antidepressants.

questions.text: Which organs mainly carry out oxidative deamination?
questions.explanation: Liver and kidney are the primary organs for oxidative deamination, but heart, brain, and skeletal muscle also carry out this reaction, contributing to amino acid nitrogen disposal.
questions.keyConcept: Organ sites of oxidative deamination
questions.modelAnswer:
Liver, kidney
heart, brain, and muscle

questions.text: What coenzyme is required for L-glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: L-glutamate dehydrogenase requires NAD+ (for oxidative deamination) or NADP+ (for reductive amination) as coenzymes, reflecting its reversible nature in nitrogen metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: L-GDH NAD/NADP coenzyme requirement
questions.modelAnswer: NAD+ (or NADP+) is the coenzyme required for L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH). GDH catalyzes the oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and NH3, using NAD+ as cofactor. This reaction is reversible and occurs in the mitochondria.

questions.text: NAD+ is used in oxidative deamination and NADP+ in reductive amination.
questions.explanation: True: NAD+ is the coenzyme for oxidative deamination ( glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate), while NADP+ is used in reductive amination (alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate), maintaining redox balance.
questions.keyConcept: NAD+ vs NADP+ in deamination

questions.text: What stimulates L-glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: ADP and GDP (guanosine diphosphate) allosterically stimulate L-glutamate dehydrogenase, increasing ammonia production during energy deficit states when more amino acids need to be catabolized.
questions.keyConcept: L-GDH allosteric activators
questions.modelAnswer: L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is stimulated by GDP, ADP, and other purine nucleotides (positive allosteric effect), which increase its affinity for glutamate. These activators promote oxidative deamination, particularly during fasting when ammonia disposal is needed.

questions.text: What inhibits L-glutamate dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: ATP, GTP, and NADH allosterically inhibit L-glutamate dehydrogenase, preventing excessive ammonia production when energy status is adequate and reducing glutamate catabolism.
questions.keyConcept: L-GDH allosteric inhibitors
questions.modelAnswer: L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is inhibited by GTP, ATP, and high concentrations of glucocorticoids. These negative allosteric regulators suppress GDH activity to conserve glutamate for other metabolic processes and prevent excessive ammonia production.

questions.text: What is the coenzyme of the enzyme D-AA oxidase?
questions.explanation: D-amino acid oxidase is a flavoprotein requiring FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) as its prosthetic group, which accepts electrons during the oxidative deamination reaction.
questions.keyConcept: D-AA oxidase FAD coenzyme
questions.modelAnswer: FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide). D-amino acid oxidase is a flavoprotein that uses FAD as its prosthetic group to accept electrons during the oxidative deamination of D-amino acids.

questions.text: In which organs is D-AA oxidase found?
questions.explanation: D-amino acid oxidase is found primarily in liver and kidney peroxisomes, where it metabolizes D-amino acids from dietary sources and bacterial cell walls.
questions.keyConcept: D-AA oxidase organ distribution
questions.modelAnswer: D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO) is found in the liver, kidneys, and brain (cerebellum). It catalyzes the oxidative deamination of D-amino acids to their corresponding keto acids, producing H2O2 and NH3. Deficiency is linked to schizophrenia.

questions.text: What substrates does Ketoglutarate-D-AA oxidase flavoprotein act on?
questions.explanation: Ketoglutarate-D-AA oxidase flavoprotein acts on D-amino acids and glycine as substrates, performing transdeamination reactions that link amino acid metabolism to TCA cycle intermediates.
questions.keyConcept: Ketoglutarate-D-AA oxidase substrates
questions.modelAnswer: Ketoglutarate-D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO) flavoprotein acts on neutral D-amino acids such as D-serine, D-alanine, and D-proline. It uses FAD as a prosthetic group and produces alpha-keto acids, H2O2, and NH3.

questions.text: What happens to glutamine in the liver?
questions.explanation: In the liver, glutamine is cleaved by glutaminase to produce glutamate and ammonia; the ammonia enters the urea cycle while glutamate enters energy metabolism or gluconeogenesis.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic glutaminase reaction
questions.modelAnswer: Cleaved by glutaminase enzyme to produce ammonia

questions.text: What amino acids can’t go through transamination?
questions.explanation: Lysine, threonine, proline, and hydroxyproline cannot undergo transamination because they lack an alpha-amino group or have secondary amino groups that are not recognized by aminotransferases.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acids excluded from transamination
questions.modelAnswer:
Lysine
Threonine
Proline
Hydroxyproline

questions.text: What enzyme converts pyruvate to alanine in muscles?
questions.explanation: Alanine transaminase (ALT) catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to alanine in muscles, using glutamate as the amino donor; this is part of the glucose-alanine cycle transporting nitrogen to liver.
questions.keyConcept: ALT pyruvate to alanine conversion
questions.modelAnswer: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT / alanine transaminase) converts pyruvate to alanine in muscles. This reaction transfers the amino group from glutamate to pyruvate, forming alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate. Alanine is then transported to the liver for gluconeogenesis.

questions.text: What is the function of L-AA oxidase?
questions.explanation: L-amino acid oxidase catalyzes the oxidative deamination of L-amino acids to corresponding alpha-keto acids, producing hydrogen peroxide and ammonia; FMN is its required cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: L-AA oxidase oxidative deamination
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidative deamination of L-amino acids.

questions.text: What is the process of non-oxidative deamination for glutamine and asparagine?
questions.explanation: Non-oxidative deamination of glutamine and asparagine is catalyzed by specific deamidases (glutaminase, asparaginase), releasing NH3 which enters the urea cycle in liver or is excreted in urine by kidneys.
questions.keyConcept: Glutamine and asparagine deamination fate
questions.modelAnswer: Deamidases release NH3 which enters urea cycle in the liver, or passes in urine in the kidney.

questions.text: Where does NH3 released by deamidases in the liver go?
questions.explanation: NH3 released by hepatic deamidases enters the urea cycle in hepatocytes, where it is combined with CO2 and ammonia from other sources to form urea for renal excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic ammonia to urea cycle
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonia (NH3) released by deamidases in the liver enters the urea cycle. It is first converted to carbamoyl phosphate by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) in the mitochondria, then combines with ornithine to form citrulline, ultimately leading to urea synthesis for excretion.

questions.text: Where does NH3 released by deamidases in the kidney go?
questions.explanation: NH3 released by renal deamidases is not converted to urea but diffuses into the tubular lumen and is excreted directly in urine as ammonium ion.
questions.keyConcept: Renal ammonia excretion in urine
questions.modelAnswer: NH3 released by deamidases in the kidney is excreted in urine as NH4+ (ammonium ion). Renal ammoniagenesis involves deamination of glutamine by glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase, producing NH3 which diffuses into the tubular lumen and binds H+ to form NH4+ for excretion.

questions.text: What are the sources of ammonia NH3?
questions.explanation: Sources of ammonia include amino acid catabolism (transamination, oxidative deamination), purine/pyrimidine catabolism, glutaminase action, amine oxidation, and intestinal bacterial metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia metabolic sources
questions.modelAnswer:
Catabolism of amino acids
catabolism of purine and pyrimidine
glutaminase enzyme
Catabolism of amines
intestinal bacteria

questions.text: What is the synthetic fates of ammonia?
questions.explanation: Synthetic fates of ammonia include incorporation into non-essential amino acids via reductive amination (glutamate from alpha-ketoglutarate) and glutamine synthesis via glutamine synthetase.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia biosynthetic utilization
questions.modelAnswer:
Synthesis of non essential amino acids
Synthesis of glutamine

questions.text: What is the major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver?
questions.explanation: The major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver is urea synthesis via the urea cycle, which converts two molecules of ammonia (one free, one from aspartate) into one urea molecule.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic urea synthesis ammonia disposal
questions.modelAnswer: The major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver is urea synthesis via the urea cycle, which converts two molecules of ammonia (one free, one from aspartate) into one urea molecule.

questions.text: How is hepatic encephalopathy diagnosed?
questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy is diagnosed by excluding other causes of altered mental status, identifying precipitating factors (infection, bleeding, electrolytes), and observing rapid improvement with ammonia-lowering treatment.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic encephalopathy diagnosis
questions.modelAnswer:
Exclusion of other causes of encephalopathy
identification of the precipitating cause
rapid response to empiric treatment

questions.text: How does lactulose help in the reduction of ammonia production?
questions.explanation: Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying colonic contents (conversion to lactic/acetic acid), reducing ammonia absorption, and decreasing ammonia-producing bacteria through osmotic catharsis.
questions.keyConcept: Lactulose mechanism in HE
questions.modelAnswer: Inhibits intestinal ammonia production by reducing colonic bacterial load and acidifying the gut lumen

questions.text: Name three substances used to increase ammonia clearance.
questions.explanation: Sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, and sodium phenylacetate are ammonia scavengers used to increase nitrogen excretion in urea cycle disorders and hepatic encephalopathy.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia scavenger drugs
questions.modelAnswer:
Sodium benzoate
sodium phenylbutyrate
sodium phenylacetate

questions.text: How does sodium benzoate contribute to ammonia clearance?
questions.explanation: Sodium benzoate conjugates with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is rapidly excreted in urine, effectively removing one nitrogen atom from the body per molecule of benzoate.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium benzoate hippurate conjugation
questions.modelAnswer: Interacts with glycine to form Hippurate, which is then excreted in the urine

questions.text: What is the role of L-ornithine-L-aspartate in hepatic encephalopathy treatment?
questions.explanation: L-ornithine-L-aspartate (LOLA) stimulates the urea cycle by providing substrates (ornithine and aspartate) for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, enhancing ammonia fixation and disposal.
questions.keyConcept: LOLA urea cycle stimulation
questions.modelAnswer: Stimulates the urea cycle, leading to the loss of ammonia

questions.text: What is the effect of hyperammonia on brain function?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonia decreases Krebs cycle activity and ATP production, reduces GABA synthesis (causing hyperexcitability), disrupts cerebral electrical activity, causes cerebral edema, and increases serotonin production.
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonia brain toxicity mechanisms
questions.modelAnswer:
Decrease in Krebs’ cycle and ATP production
decrease in GABA (neurotransmitter)
interference with electric activity in the brain
cerebral edema, and increased serotonin production

questions.text: What are the causes of hyperammonemia?
questions.explanation: Hyperammonemia causes include acquired forms (liver cirrhosis, hepatitis, portosystemic shunts) and congenital forms (urea cycle enzyme deficiencies, ornithine transporter defects, N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency).
questions.keyConcept: Hyperammonemia etiology
questions.modelAnswer:
Acquired hyperammonemia due to liver diseases
congenital hyperammonemia due to deficiencies in urea cycle enzymes, membrane-associated ornithine transporter, or N-acetyl glutamate synthase

questions.text: What is the first step of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The first step of the urea cycle is carbamoyl phosphate synthesis from ammonia and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondrial matrix, consuming 2 ATP.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle initiation step
questions.modelAnswer: The first step of the urea cycle is the formation of carbamoyl phosphate from NH3 and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) in the mitochondrial matrix. This step consumes 2 molecules of ATP and requires N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an obligatory activator.

questions.text: What is the enzyme catalyzing the second step of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the second step of the urea cycle, transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, forming citrulline.
questions.keyConcept: Ornithine transcarbamoylase step
questions.modelAnswer: Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the second step of the urea cycle, transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, forming citrulline.

questions.text: What is the second step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The second step of the urea cycle is citrulline synthesis, catalyzed by ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC), occurring in the mitochondrial matrix.
questions.keyConcept: Citrulline synthesis step
questions.modelAnswer: The second step of the urea cycle is the synthesis of citrulline from carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine, catalyzed by ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC). Citrulline is then transported to the cytosol for the remaining steps.

questions.text: What is the third step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The third step of the urea cycle is argininosuccinate synthesis, catalyzed by argininosuccinate synthetase, where citrulline combines with aspartate in the cytosol.
questions.keyConcept: Argininosuccinate synthesis step
questions.modelAnswer:
Argininosuccinate synthesis
Argininosuccinate synthetase

questions.text: What is the fourth step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The fourth step of the urea cycle is cleavage of argininosuccinate by argininosuccinate lyase to form arginine and fumarate in the cytosol.
questions.keyConcept: Argininosuccinate cleavage step
questions.modelAnswer:
Cleavage of argininosuccinate
Argininosuccinate lyase

questions.text: What is the final step of the urea cycle? And it’s enzyme?
questions.explanation: The final step of the urea cycle is cleavage of arginine by arginase to form urea and ornithine, with ornithine being transported back to mitochondria to repeat the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Arginase final step
questions.modelAnswer: The final step of the urea cycle is the hydrolysis of argininosuccinate to form arginine and fumarate, catalyzed by argininosuccinate lyase. Arginine is then cleaved by arginase to produce urea and ornithine, completing the cycle.

questions.text: What is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate and subject to substrate availability control.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I rate-limiting enzyme
questions.modelAnswer: Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I)

questions.text: Synthesis of urea occurs in the liver and excretion by the kidney
questions.explanation: Urea synthesis occurs exclusively in the liver mitochondria and cytosol, while excretion is performed by the kidneys; the liver synthesizes urea from ammonia and the kidneys filter and excrete it in urine.
questions.keyConcept: Urea synthesis and excretion分工
questions.modelAnswer: Urea is synthesized in the hepatocytes of the liver via the urea cycle, which converts toxic ammonia (from amino acid deamination) into urea. The urea cycle consumes ammonia, bicarbonate, and aspartate to produce urea, fumarate, and water. The synthesized urea is then transported via the bloodstream to the kidneys, where it is filtered by the glomeruli and excreted in urine, representing the primary route for nitrogen disposal from protein metabolism.

questions.text: Which enzyme is present in the cytosol and used in pyrimidine synthesis? And what is its other mitochondrial enzyme used in urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrial enzyme used in pyrimidine synthesis is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II), distinct from the cytosolic enzyme; the question may refer to amidophosphoribosyltransferase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
questions.keyConcept: Cytosolic vs mitochondrial pyrimidine enzymes
questions.modelAnswer: The mitochondrial enzyme used in pyrimidine synthesis is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II), distinct from the cytosolic enzyme; the question may refer to amidophosphoribosyltransferase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.

questions.text: How many ATP molecules and high energy bonds are utilized in the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle consumes 3 ATP molecules (equivalent to 4 high-energy phosphate bonds): 2 ATP for CPS I reaction and 1 ATP for argininosuccinate synthetase (AMP + PPi effectively = 2 ATP).
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle ATP requirement
questions.modelAnswer: The urea cycle consumes 3 ATP molecules (equivalent to 4 high-energy phosphate bonds): 2 ATP for CPS I reaction and 1 ATP for argininosuccinate synthetase (AMP + PPi effectively = 2 ATP).

questions.text: What is the main fate of urea?
questions.explanation: The main fate of urea is renal excretion in urine; approximately 20-25g of urea is filtered and excreted daily in adults, with small amounts lost in sweat.
questions.keyConcept: Urea urinary excretion
questions.modelAnswer: The main fate of urea is excretion in urine. Urea is filtered by the glomerulus and partially reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. About 60-70% of filtered urea is excreted daily, with plasma concentration maintained at 2.5-7.5 mmol/L.

questions.text: What activates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I)?
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (NAG), synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase, is the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.
questions.keyConcept: NAG as CPS I activator
questions.modelAnswer: N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is the obligatory activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). NAG is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS), and its synthesis is stimulated by arginine, the product of the urea cycle.

questions.text: What is the relationship between the urea cycle and the citric acid cycle?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle and citric acid cycle are linked through fumarate (from argininosuccinate cleavage) which enters the TCA cycle, and aspartate (from TCA cycle transamination) which provides nitrogen for urea synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Urea and TCA cycle connection
questions.modelAnswer: The urea cycle and citric acid cycle are metabolically linked through aspartate and fumarate. The urea cycle consumes aspartate (donating its amino group to form argininosuccinate). Fumarate, a byproduct of argininosuccinate cleavage, enters the citric acid cycle and can be converted to malate and then oxaloacetate. Oxaloacetate can be transaminated back to aspartate, completing the cycle. Additionally, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I uses bicarbonate derived from TCA cycle intermediates.

questions.text: What is phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin), preventing conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine.
questions.keyConcept: PKU phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency
options: A condition caused by a deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin reductase
A condition caused by a deficiency of dihydrobiopterin biosynthesis
A condition caused by a deficiency of homocystinuria

questions.text: What are the clinical pictures of phenylketonuria?
questions.explanation: PKU clinical features include intellectual disability (if untreated), hypopigmentation (decreased tyrosine reduces melanin), and characteristic mousy/musty odor from phenylacetate accumulation in urine and sweat.
questions.keyConcept: PKU clinical manifestations
options: Urine with a bad mousy odor

questions.text: How is phenylketonuria treated?
questions.explanation: PKU treatment involves lifelong dietary phenylalanine restriction with tyrosine supplementation (since tyrosine becomes essential); with defective BH4 metabolism, DOPA and 5-HTP supplementation is also required.
questions.keyConcept: PKU dietary and pharmacological treatment
options: A diet low in phenylalanine, supplementation of tyrosine
Giving DOPA and serotonin if there is dihydrobiopterin deficiency

questions.text: What is maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) results from deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine and their ketoacids.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD branched-chain dehydrogenase deficiency
options: A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in branched-chain amino acid catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in phenylalanine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tyrosine catabolism
A condition resulting from a deficiency of the dehydrogenase complex involved in tryptophan catabolism

questions.text: What are the effects of maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: MSUD manifests as mental retardation, developmental delay, feeding difficulties, and characteristic sweet maple syrup/burnt sugar odor of urine from accumulating branched-chain ketoacids; untreated cases often fatal in infancy.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD clinical presentation
options: Mental retardation and may lead to early death
The urine has a sweet smell-like maple syrup or burned sugar

questions.text: What is the treatment for maple syrup urine disease?
questions.explanation: MSUD treatment requires lifelong restriction of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) in diet, with careful monitoring of amino acid levels to prevent neurological damage.
questions.keyConcept: MSUD branched-chain amino acid restriction
options: A diet low in branched-chain amino acids

questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute requirement for the brain at all times?
questions.explanation: The brain absolutely requires glucose and oxygen at all times; it cannot use fatty acids as an energy source and depends almost exclusively on glucose oxidation for ATP production.
questions.keyConcept: Brain absolute glucose requirement

questions.text: In fasting conditions, glucose is provided for the brain by
questions.explanation: In fasting, brain glucose comes from hepatic glycogenolysis (immediately) and gluconeogenesis from lactate, amino acids, and glycerol (sustained); intestine is not a source during fasting.
questions.keyConcept: Fasting brain glucose sources

questions.text: Brain cells oxidize glucose to
questions.explanation: Brain cells completely oxidize glucose to CO2 and H2O via aerobic metabolism in mitochondria, producing 30-32 ATP per glucose molecule.
questions.keyConcept: Brain glucose complete oxidation

questions.text: In brain cells, glucose is phosphorylated by
questions.explanation: Brain uses hexokinase (not glucokinase) to phosphorylate glucose, giving it high affinity for glucose and allowing uptake even at low blood glucose concentrations.
questions.keyConcept: Brain hexokinase glucose phosphorylation

questions.text: Glucose 6-phosphate is utilized in which pathway in brain cells?
questions.explanation: Glucose 6-phosphate in brain cells enters glycolysis; the pentose phosphate pathway also operates for nucleotide synthesis, but glycolysis is the main utilization pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Brain G6P glycolysis pathway

questions.text: What is the importance of HMP pathway in the brain cells?
questions.explanation: HMP pathway's main importance in brain is generating NADPH for antioxidant defense (via glutathione reductase) and nucleotide synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: HMP pathway brain antioxidant role

questions.text: Hormones and neurotransmitters
questions.explanation: Hormones and neurotransmitters are signal molecules for cell-cell communication, derived from amino acids (nitrogenous) but also include non-nitrogenous compounds like steroid hormones.
questions.keyConcept: Signal molecules characteristics
options: are signal molecules used for cell-cell communication.
are mostly polypeptides or nitrogenous compounds, both derived from amino-acids.

questions.text: Which of the following aminoacids may act as a neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glycine, glutamic acid (glutamate), and GABA are all amino acid neurotransmitters; glycine and GABA are inhibitory, glutamate is excitatory.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acid neurotransmitters

questions.text: Gamma-amino-butyric acid (GABA) is produced by
questions.explanation: GABA is produced by decarboxylation of glutamic acid via glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), requiring PLP (vitamin B6) as cofactor; both a and c are correct.
questions.keyConcept: GABA synthesis glutamate decarboxylase
options: a reaction that requires vitamin B6 derived cofactor.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about the aminoacid neurotransmitters?
questions.explanation: All statements about amino acid neurotransmitters are true: glutamate is excitatory, glycine/GABA are inhibitory; glycine is in collagen; glutamate produces MSG; all above is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Amino acid NT properties
options: Glutamic acid is an excitatory, while glycine and GABA are inhibitory neurotransmitters.
Glycine constitutes one third of the collagen aminoacids, and glutamic acid is largely produced from other aminoacids.
Monosodium glutamate is a widely used food additive.

questions.text: L-Dopa (Dihydroxyphenylalanine) is
questions.explanation: L-DOPA is produced from tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase (not from dopamine); dopamine is synthesized from L-DOPA by DOPA decarboxylase. Option D (neither) is correct.
questions.keyConcept: L-DOPA synthesis pathway
options: converted to tyrosine by a hydroxylase enzyme.

questions.text: The rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis is
questions.explanation: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step by hydroxylating tyrosine to form DOPA; both formation of DOPA and hydroxylation of tyrosine describe the same step.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine hydroxylase rate limiting

questions.text: Norepinephrine is produced by
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is synthesized from dopamine via hydroxylation by dopamine beta-hydroxylase, which requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and copper as a cofactor. This is the primary pathway for norepinephrine production in the adrenal medulla and CNS neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Catecholamine synthesis pathway and dopamine beta-hydroxylase reaction

questions.text: Production of norepinephrine from dopamine requires
questions.explanation: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase catalyzes the hydroxylation of dopamine to norepinephrine. This enzyme is a copper-containing monooxygenase that requires vitamin C as an electron donor and tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor. Both cofactors are essential for activity, hence answer D.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase cofactors: copper, vitamin C, and tetrahydrobiopterin

questions.text: Production of epinephrine from nor-epinephrine requires
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is synthesized from norepinephrine by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which uses S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. PNMT is expressed primarily in the adrenal medulla. The combination of PNMT enzyme and SAM availability makes both factors necessary.
questions.keyConcept: PNMT methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine using SAM as methyl donor

questions.text: Catecholamines are catabolized by
questions.explanation: Catecholamines are catabolized by both MAO (monoamine oxidase) and COMT (catechol O-methyltransferase), acting sequentially or independently. MAO acts first in mitochondria, followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase; COMT O-methylates catecholamines directly. Both pathways contribute to VMA production.
questions.keyConcept: Dual catabolism of catecholamines by MAO and COMT pathways
options: monoamine oxidase (MAO), followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase.

questions.text: The end product of adrenaline and noradrenaline catabolism is
questions.explanation: Vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) is the primary urinary metabolite of both epinephrine and norepinephrine. It is formed through combined MAO and COMT action on catecholamines, then further metabolism to VMA. Elevated VMA is a key diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: VMA as the end product of catecholamine catabolism and tumor marker

questions.text: Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan results in formation of
questions.explanation: 5-hydroxytryptophan is decarboxylated by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (ALAD) to form serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine).
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin synthesis from 5-hydroxytryptophan via decarboxylation

questions.text: Serotonin is
questions.explanation: Serotonin is chemically 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), synthesized from tryptophan. It is not a tyrosine derivative (that would be catecholamines); rather, it is an indoleamine derived from tryptophan. Melatonin is formed from serotonin by N-acetylation and O-methylation, not the reverse.
questions.keyConcept: Serotonin (5-HT) as an indoleamine, not a catecholamine
options: produced by N-acetylation and O-methylation of melatonin.

questions.text: Serotonin is catabolized by
questions.explanation: Serotonin is catabolized primarily by monoamine oxidase (MAO), which oxidatively deaminates it to 5-hydroxyindoleacetaldehyde, further converted to 5-HIAA. COMT does not significantly metabolize serotonin since it is not a catecholamine.
questions.keyConcept: MAO as the primary catabolic enzyme for serotonin

questions.text: Which of the following increases in 24-hour urine with pheochromocytoma (adrenaline-secreting tumor)?
questions.explanation: In pheochromocytoma, excess catecholamines are secreted and metabolized, producing elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). VMA is the end product of both epinephrine and norepinephrine catabolism and is routinely measured as a diagnostic marker for this tumor.
questions.keyConcept: VMA elevation in urine as diagnostic marker for pheochromocytoma

questions.text: Histamine is formed from histidine by
questions.explanation: Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine, and this enzyme requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase also participates in histamine metabolism in some contexts, requiring the same cofactor.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine synthesis from histidine requiring PLP cofactor
options: a reaction that requires pyridoxal phosphate.

questions.text: Tyramine
questions.explanation: Tyramine is formed by bacterial decarboxylation of tyrosine in aged foods (cheese, wine). It displaces catecholamines from synaptic vesicles, and in patients on MAO inhibitors, this can cause massive catecholamine release leading to hypertensive crisis (the 'cheese effect').
questions.keyConcept: Tyramine in aged foods and cheese effect with MAO inhibitors
options: is the decarboxylation product of tyrosine, which is present in aged food.
can displace catecholamines from their stores.
may precipitate a hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAO inhibitors as anti-depressant.

questions.text: Nitric oxide is a hormone and a neurotransmitter produced
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized from arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS), which requires oxygen and NADPH. Glycine is not a precursor for NO; it is involved in purine metabolism and as a neurotransmitter. The NOS reaction also produces citrulline.
questions.keyConcept: NO synthesis from arginine by NOS requiring O2 and NADPH
options: by the action of nitric oxide synthase.

questions.text: Nitric oxide synthase
questions.explanation: Nitric oxide synthase exists as three isozymes: neuronal (nNOS), endothelial (eNOS), and phagocytic/inducible (iNOS). All isoforms convert arginine to citrulline and NO using NADPH and oxygen. The reaction produces both citrulline and nitric oxide as products.
questions.keyConcept: Three NOS isoforms: neuronal, endothelial, and phagocytic
options: acts on arginine and needs Oxygen and NADPH.
has three isozymes: neuronal, endothelial and phagocytic.

questions.text: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is
questions.explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages.
questions.keyConcept: iNOS as calcium-independent NOS isozyme in phagocytes

questions.text: Urea cycle is a pathway that
questions.explanation: The urea cycle occurs exclusively in the liver (hepatocytes) and is the body's mechanism for converting toxic ammonia (NH3) into urea for excretion. It does not produce ammonia from urea; that would be the reverse reaction which does not occur physiologically.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle location in liver and its role in ammonia detoxification
options: takes place mainly in the liver cells.

questions.text: In the urea cycle, urea is produced from
questions.explanation: Arginine is cleaved by arginase to produce urea and ornithine in the final step of the urea cycle. Fumarate is produced earlier from argininosuccinate. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase initiates the cycle by fixing ammonia and CO2.
questions.keyConcept: Arginase cleavage of arginine to produce urea and ornithine
options: carbon dioxide and ammonium ions by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase.

questions.text: Although arginine is formed in the urea cycle, it is considered an essential amino-acid. Why?
questions.explanation: Although the urea cycle synthesizes arginine, the rate of endogenous synthesis is insufficient for the demands of rapid growth in infants and children, making it a conditionally essential amino acid during development. Adults normally synthesize adequate arginine.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine as conditionally essential amino acid in children
options: It must be broken down by arginase enzyme.
Its rate of synthesis is not enough for growing children.
It is formed in the cytosol, therefore it cannot be used.
It is formed in the D-configuration.

questions.text: Two reactions of the urea cycle take place in the mitochondria. These are
questions.explanation: The first two reactions of the urea cycle occur in mitochondria: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate, and ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine. The remaining reactions occur in the cytosol.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondrial steps of urea cycle: CPS I and OTC
options: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamoylase.

questions.text: Which of the following is a high energy compound formed in the urea cycle?
questions.explanation: Carbamoyl phosphate is a high-energy compound formed in the first step of the urea cycle, consuming 2 ATP equivalents. It donates its energy to drive the subsequent reaction. Ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not high-energy compounds.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamoyl phosphate as the high-energy intermediate of urea cycle

questions.text: Which of the following aminoacids is formed in the urea cycle and used in protein synthesis?
questions.explanation: Arginine is the only urea cycle intermediate that is incorporated into proteins; ornithine, citrulline, and argininosuccinate are not standard proteinogenic amino acids.
questions.keyConcept: Arginine as the only proteinogenic amino acid in urea cycle

questions.text: Ornithine is an aminoacid formed from
questions.explanation: Ornithine is produced from arginine by arginase and can be transaminated to glutamate via ornithine aminotransferase. Conversely, glutamate can be converted to ornithine through acetylation (N-acetylglutamate) and subsequent reactions in the urea cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Ornithine-glutamate interconversion in nitrogen metabolism
options: arginine and can be transformed to glutamate in two steps.
glutamate and can be transformed to arginine in the urea cycle.
arginine and transformed to aceto-acetate on fasting.

questions.text: N-acetyl-glutamate
questions.explanation: N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase. NAG is an obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I), and its concentration increases after protein-rich meals when glutamate is abundant.
questions.keyConcept: NAG as allosteric activator of CPS I, increasing postprandially
options: is an allosteric activator of ornithine transcarbamoylase.

questions.text: In the urea cycle, which aminoacids should be transported between the mitochondria and the cytosol in either direction?
questions.explanation: Ornithine must be transported from mitochondria to cytosol (where it combines with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline), and citrulline must travel back to mitochondria for the next step. This mitochondrial-cytosolic transport is essential for urea cycle function.
questions.keyConcept: Mitochondrial-cytosolic transport of ornithine and citrulline

questions.text: Which of the following is produced by the urea cycle with the production of urea?
questions.explanation: The urea cycle produces fumarate when argininosuccinate is cleaved by argininosuccinase. Fumarate can enter the TCA cycle.
questions.keyConcept: Fumarate production from argininosuccinate in urea cycle

questions.text: How many carbon and nitrogen atoms are there in a urea molecule?
questions.explanation: Urea has the formula (NH2)2C=O, containing ONE carbon atom and TWO nitrogen atoms.
questions.keyConcept: Ammonia toxicity: inhibition of TCA cycle enzymes and glutamate accumulation

questions.text: Which of the following is the source of urea carbon?
questions.explanation: The carbon of urea comes from CO2 (as bicarbonate) via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondria.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I as rate-limiting enzyme requiring NAG for activation

questions.text: Which of the following gives one nitrogen atom of the urea molecule?
questions.explanation: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (Citrullinemia type I) leads to citrulline accumulation. The diagnosis is confirmed by elevated citrulline in plasma and urine. This is the third enzyme of the urea cycle, encoding the ASS1 gene.
questions.keyConcept: Citrullinemia type I from ASS deficiency with citrulline elevation

questions.text: Which of the following is a source of urea nitrogen?
questions.explanation: X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency is the most common urea cycle disorder. Males are more severely affected; female carriers may be asymptomatic or have mild symptoms. Plasma glutamine rises compensatorily when urea cycle is blocked.
questions.keyConcept: OTC deficiency as most common X-linked urea cycle disorder

questions.text: Glutamate can be the source of both nitrogen atoms of urea through which reactions?
questions.explanation: Glutamate provides nitrogen via both glutamate dehydrogenase (oxidative deamination) and glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase (transamination).
questions.keyConcept: Glycine cleavage system in mitochondria for glycine catabolism

questions.text: Ammonia is introduced in the urea cycle by
questions.explanation: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) catalyzes the reversible interconversion of serine and glycine in the cytosol and mitochondria. This reaction transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate, forming 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate, essential for nucleotide synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Serine-glycine interconversion via SHMT generating one-carbon units
options: reacting as ammonium ion with carbon dioxide and ATP.
making a part of N-acetyl glutamate.

questions.text: How is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I different from carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II?
questions.explanation: CPS I is mitochondrial and participates in the urea cycle (using ammonia and CO2), while CPS II is cytosolic and involved in pyrimidine synthesis (using glutamine). CPS I requires N-acetylglutamate as an allosteric activator; CPS II does not.
questions.keyConcept: CPS I (mitochondrial, urea cycle) vs CPS II (cytosolic, pyrimidine synthesis)
options: I is mitochondrial while II is cytosolic.
I is used for pyrimidine synthesis but II is for urea synthesis.
I does not need N-acetyl glutamate as allosteric activator, unlike II.
I uses glutamine not ammonia as a nitrogen donor.

questions.text: Which of the following is an energy-producing pathway?
questions.explanation: The citrate (Krebs) cycle produces energy by oxidizing acetyl-CoA, generating NADH, FADH2, and GTP. The urea cycle consumes energy (4 ATP equivalents) and does not produce ATP; its purpose is ammonia detoxification.
questions.keyConcept: Citric acid cycle as energy-producing pathway, urea cycle as energy-consuming

questions.text: How many ATP (energy currency) are used in one turn of urea cycle?
questions.explanation: One turn of the urea cycle consumes 4 high-energy phosphate bonds: 2 ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, 1 ATP to form argininosuccinate (AMP + PPi, counting as 2), with fumarate oxidation linking to the TCA cycle to recover some energy.
questions.keyConcept: Urea cycle energy cost: 4 ATP equivalents per turn

questions.text: Which of the following reactions linked to urea cycle may help covering its energy cost?
questions.explanation: The fumarate produced in the urea cycle enters the TCA cycle where malate dehydrogenase regenerates oxaloacetate, which is transaminated back to aspartate (used in argininosuccinate synthesis). Glutamate dehydrogenase and glutaminase provide ammonia for the cycle.
questions.keyConcept: TCA cycle link to urea cycle via fumarate and aspartate regeneration
options: Malate dehydrogenase involved in aspartate regeneration from fumarate.
Glutamate dehydrogenase involved in provision of ammonia.
Glutaminase involved in provision of ammonia.

questions.text: ATP is consumed in which of the following reactions?
questions.explanation: ATP is consumed in the CPS I reaction (2 ATP to 1 ADP) and the argininosuccinate synthetase reaction (ATP to AMP + PPi, effectively 2 ATP). Ornithine transcarbamylase does not require ATP; it transfers the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine.
questions.keyConcept: ATP consumption at CPS I and ASS steps of urea cycle

questions.text: What is the use of glutamate for the urea cycle?
